This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of this premise through a new estimate that demonstrates the ground state's smoothness in the specified function space, achieved through a proof utilizing a representation of the eigenvalues of a specific Jacobian matrix and associated Perron-Frobenius theory. As a direct application, we derive an upper bound for the smoothness of the ground state within a specific space for quadratic family functions on a $d$-dimensional cube. Investigating orbital resonances enables the restriction of planetary properties in compact systems. The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five proposed to be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, necessitates the analysis of its planets' potential resonant behavior. By using existing parameters in N-body simulations, our analysis confirms that nearly all simulations (99.2%) produce a chain of 3:2 resonances; however, fewer (11%) demonstrate a five-planet resonance chain. We successfully employ resonances to confine the orbital periods and masses of the planets. We examine the likelihood of this system forming in situ and through disk migration, as well as explore the potential planetary compositions using a computational planet structure model. Our results also propose observable signs, like brightness variations and gravitational redshift, that could be detected in the system due to tidal interactions. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers studied the molecular structure of water in hexagonal ice (Ih) and low-density amorphous ice (LDA) at low temperatures under high pressure conditions. When subjected to this pressure, both types of ice transform into a high-density amorphous ice (HDA) in a sudden, drastic phase transition. An innovative measure, based on the structural analysis of ice clusters, allows the researchers to detect the presence of Ih domains within the LDA structure. Interestingly, the appearance of Ih domains is linked to a specific temperature below which LDA and HDA exhibit equivalent structural characteristics. Below this temperature, known as the crossover temperature (Tc), the LDA and HDA structures undergo a drastic transformation. An analysis of the thermal evolution of the LDA structure, using high-pressure conditions, reveals that the LDA and HDA states coexist with Ih domains at all temperatures but become stable only when Tc is exceeded. When subjected to pressure and temperature conditions imitating Mars' polar climates (about 140 K), the LDA contains Ih domains. Thus, the researchers propose that the sudden transformation from LDA to HDA, under high-pressure conditions in Martian climates, results from the stabilization of large Ih domains within LDA. This finding has significant implications for investigating planetary ices, particularly in Martian climates, involving sudden, drastic transformations at low temperatures. In an effort to address these issues, the researchers carry out additional simulations. An initial simulation, replicating ice in Martian polar climates and then slowly warming it over 100 days, eventually transforms LDA into HDA. However, the HDA formation in this simulation is slowed by the presence of small Ih domains. An additional simulation, using high-density amorphous ice as a starting point, yields contrasting results. An extremely short time frame of just 2 days is required for the transformation of HDA into LDA with small Ih domains. Notably, the size of Ih domains correlates with the cooling rate during HDA formation in LDA and, conversely, the size of HDA domains during the transformation of HDA into LDA. These findings provide a basis for the sudden, drastic transformations at low temperatures in ice and its relevance in Martian polar climates. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, for instance: examining the patterns of contribution among authors to understand how to enhance collaboration and visibility within the community; investigating how to streamline learning Isabelle with the aim of increasing participation rates; analyzing the structure of Isabelle documents to identify methods for clarifying and simplifying their complexity; and evaluating and refining existing strategies for tagging and annotating Isabelle code to facilitate browsing and search. Ultimately, my research goals are centered on identifying effective methods to prioritize content, refine search results, and propagate usage metadata, as well as exploring their applications in other areas of formal verification. Moreover, I aim to demonstrate the practical value of these concepts by implementing and evaluating them in the context of Isabelle, for example, tagging and producing usage data for Isabelle documents, incorporating the tool's source code into the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, and enabling more effective browsing and search experiences. Although my primary focus is the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, I also consider other areas of controlled theorem collections, such as Coq's Galileo and Lean's Lean Collection, with the goal of identifying commonalities that could lead to the development of standardized best practices. Ultimately, the ultimate goal of this research is to develop a comprehensive understanding of effective content prioritization and management methods, as well as to encourage the development and maintenance of reusable, accessible, and searchable formal verification content. This research proposal outlines my planned exploration into these concepts, with the ultimate goal of contributing to the creation of a cohesive ecosystem that facilitates the discovery and reuse of a diverse array of formal verification content. Audification is a straightforward way to turn oscillatory data into audio, retaining all the original information but potentially making magnetospheric wave observations go by too fast to fully grasp. Consequently, audio scaling techniques used in music have been adapted and tested for ULF wave data, with a discussion on the most suitable techniques that balance speed and detail, and a summary of the existing research in this area. Additionally, two methods of extracting magnetospheric wave periods from time-series data are presented, aimed at enhancing audio representations for enhanced understanding. Specifically, one approach involves identifying individual wave events through their polarity reversal in high-resolution data, and then using a Fourier-based method for confirming the results. These techniques have been applied to multiple case studies from various locations in the outer heliosphere, including planetary magnetospheres, the outer heliosphere, and Jupiter's magnetotail. These observations have implications on understanding large-scale magnetospheric oscillations, and discuss how certain patterns may be linked to the occurrence of substorms and pulsar radio emissions, as well as the structure of the outer heliosphere and Jupiter's magnetotail. Ultimately, audio representations of magnetospheric waves offer a valuable insight into understanding solar and magnetic activity. A small-step operational semantics in a programming language breaks down computations into discrete, indivisible steps, directly reflecting how the language is implemented.  A previous semantics for GP 2 is incomplete because its loop and branching commands utilize big-step operations.  This paper presents an accurate small-step operational semantics for GP 2, effectively capturing the nature of divergent computations. This semantics provides a clear understanding of the nature of divergent computations in GP 2 and serves as a foundation for various GP 2 program analyses. A moving dielectric medium can alter the path of light traveling through it, a phenomenon termed the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect. The induced deviation in the path is directly proportional to the velocity of the medium. Our investigation documents a previously unreported instance of the optical drag effect where the path deviation remains proportional to the medium's velocity but is oriented in a direction counter to the medium's motion. To observe this anomalous effect, we conducted an optical drag experiment under the conditions of electromagnetic transparency and monitored the angle between polarization axes under a magnetic field strong enough to induce a parallel change in the medium's properties. Upon application of the magnetic field, the path deviation exhibited a dramatic shift, transitioning from a typical, velocity-dependent effect to the anomalous, opposite-in-direction effect at specific magnetic field intensities corresponding to the medium's electromagnetic transparency thresholds. A theoretical model and calculation based on Berestetskii, Litovskii, and Sudov electromagnetic hydrodynamics support our findings. Our study opens the possibility of a new optical drag effect observation, prompting a description of this effect as an optical drag effect opposite-in-direction-under-strong-magnetic-field conditions. Additionally, we propose a set of comprehensive conditions for electromagnetic hydrodynamics vacuum-like properties and, as an aside, prove the existence of a hermitian-matrix representation for a dielectric medium's tensor that depends on the medium's velocity, a fact not widely recognized in the literature. Our optical drag effect research, being a dielectric-medium-based investigation, is distinct from research involving antiparticles, such as Z-bosons, in a different context. A future investigation of this effect using spin polarized electrons could lead to a groundbreaking discovery, but our study primarily opens the door to a cutting-edge experimental inquiry into novel optical drag effects. Moreover, our study is a pioneering exploration into the fundamental principles governing optical drag effects, a topic still shrouded in mystery. By leveraging electromagnetic hydrodynamics vacuum-like properties as a guiding principle, we propose a set of general conditions for a novel optical drag effect, thereby bringing order to this effect and its various manifestations. Building on Sodemann and Fu's theory of the nonlinear Hall effect established in 2015, 
a semiclassical framework where it arises from Bloch electrons' anomalous velocity as a geometric property,
a broader theory is presented, encompassing correlated and disordered systems. Within this theory, a generally applicable nonlinear Response function is defined, encompassing both linear and nonlinear Hall effects, from which a nonlinear Hall conductivity is derived. It is demonstrated that interaction and disorder share a symmetric effect, both altering the nonlinear Hall effect in proportion to a given parameter. Additionally, through a disorder-driven transition, a transition is observed where a liquid with quasiparticles gives way to a topologically insulating state, with the nonlinear Hall effect serving as a hallmark for this transition. Furthermore, at the critical interaction required for this transition, a scaling phenomenon is observed in the nonlinear Hall effect, where it remains proportional to the critical parameter. Lastly, under complete interaction, a scaling phenomenon is observed in the nonlinear Hall effect in the correlated system, with it being proportional to the square of the critical parameter. It is hoped that this investigation may lead to the observation of this nonlinear Hall effect in experiments and provide insights into the nonlinear response of systems under varying influences of disorder and interactions. It is also anticipated that this investigation may provide significant breakthroughs in the understanding of quantum Hall effect in systems with interactions as well as systems with Fermi liquids. It is also anticipated that this investigation may provide significant insights into the non-Abelian geometry of quasiparticles that may arise in quantum mechanics. A crucial challenge in the study of rarefied gas dynamics lies in determining the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation efficiently. The conventional iteration method often achieves rapid convergence for highly rarefied systems but is severely hampered by prolonged and error-prone computations when applied to near-continuum flow regimes. Building on gas kinetic models, certain schemes like UGKS and its variants have notably improved efficiency, yet their iterations remain significantly higher than those in the highly rarefied domain. This paper introduces a comprehensive iterative approach, integrating elements from the spectral decomposition of the collision operator and efficient iterative solutions to the macro-model, with the intent of minimizing the number of iterations needed to obtain the steady-state solution in near-continuum regimes. A number of theoretical justifications and experimental studies demonstrate that this approach can achieve a substantial reduction in the number of iterations needed, ultimately proving to be a valuable tool in rarefied gas dynamics. Furthermore, through experimental analysis, it is shown that this method may be applied effectively to a broad range of Knudsen numbers spanning from extremely rarefied to near-continuum regimes. The results suggest that this iterative approach can serve as a valuable benchmark for evaluating the efficiency of various iterative methods for near-continuum flow regimes. Lastly, the paper concludes by considering the underlying mechanics of the proposed iterative method and exploring potential avenues for further optimization of iterative solutions in near-continuum regimes. Moreover, to improve the efficiency of iterative methods, a preconditioning technique for non-linear iterations is first implemented in rarefied gas dynamics, followed by suggestions for integrating mesoscopic approaches to achieve higher speeds while preserving accuracy. A final suggestion is provided for the development of iterative methods that combine elements from the spectral decomposition of the collision operator and macro-models to optimize computational performance. The main body of this work has been completed prior to 2021, with the final sections offering additional insights up to 2023. As such, the ideas presented not only reflect my research interests but also my gradual growth in understanding iterative methods over the years. The study ultimately concludes with a variety of potential future directions for efficient iterative methods in rarefied gas dynamics. Its completion marks a natural conclusion to my research in this area. The ZNN method is derived from the concept of an ordinary differential equation (ODE), translated into a corresponding algebraic form for discrete application, often relying on a matrix exponential function. Consequently, an alternative formulation of the ZNN model has been explored to provide a novel computational method that can be applied to a broad range of dynamic matrix problems. The new formulation is grounded in the theory of the predictive computing framework for multistep predictive problems. By assuming the presence of 4 focusing mirrors with a Wolter I geometry, we've identified the potential for significant gains in efficiency by simulating the overlapping fields of view of the various Astonish concept iterations. By optimizing certain design parameters in an ordered sequence, we've successfully reduced the number of required Monte Carlo simulations from thousands to just two. Through these simulations, we've gathered essential metrics such as effective area, angular resolution at specific energies, and wide-field angular resolution at 1 keV, 3 keV, and an intermediate value. Additionally, we've developed an open-source repository to facilitate the reproduction of our results, which we plan to expand to accommodate a broader range of telescope designs, including those with multiple Wolter I and II parameters, as well as a combination of both (e.g., Wolter I:1 and Wolter II:1). Furthermore, we've devised a strategy for identifying and prioritizing the most promising design prescriptions within a given area of investigation. Specifically, we've suggested the use of a systematic approach to explore designs with increasingly large off-axis angles and a step-size of 10 degrees, allowing us to identify optimal results within this search space. However, our method does not provide the best results for area-based investigations, which may result in a lack of understanding of the optimal designs for applications requiring both wide-field and field-of-view sensitivity, a crucial consideration for future X-ray wide-field mission proposals, which we'll address in the future. Researchers frequently apply synthetic control techniques to determine the effect of treatment on a single treated entity within data sets that span multiple years or decades. The goal of synthetic control is to create a weighted average of units without treatment that mimics the treated entity's pre-intervention outcome trajectory. Initially, the weights used in synthetic control calculations are derived by correlating pre-intervention outcomes of the treated entity with those of units without treatment. It has been discovered, however, that traditional estimation techniques can be inconsistent. To resolve this challenge, this paper introduces a novel analytical framework, which formalizes the process of determining and making inferences regarding treatment effects using synthetic controls. The new framework enhances the estimation technique's consistency across various outcome types and can also be applied to differential intervention problems, including instances where interventions occur in multiple treated entities. Additionally, the proposed framework facilitates model-free inferences about treatment effects that do not rely on outcome space assumptions or causal order constraints. Using data on Venezuelan migrants, this paper demonstrates that synthetic control weight estimates can be inconsistent when applied to post-intervention outcomes, even when assuming linear or generalized linear models. In contrast, the proposed framework yields consistent estimates and reliable model-based inferences, which are robust to non-linear interventions. The empirical findings suggest that synthetic control weight estimates should not be used directly for evaluating post-intervention treatment effects and that correct inferences require careful model specification, including the correct inclusion of time effects as standalone variables. The proposed framework also yields reliable Bayesian inferences, which do not rely on outcome space assumptions or the correct specification of a causal model. Ultimately, the practical application of synthetic control weights should be confined to pre-intervention years and unit-level data. The proposed framework is compatible with novel synthetic control weight estimation techniques or modifications that involve temporal covariates, including lags of treated entity outcomes or difference equations. By using a state-of-the-art particle code and a novel technique to simulate extremely high-intensity laser beams, we discovered a unique electron pattern forming in a high-intensity laser-matter interaction experiment. This distinct electron configuration creates a well-defined plasma bubble, setting the stage for a nanometer-scale plasma accelerator. This research has also generated new insights into plasma bubble formation and electron dynamics, allowing for a new way to tailor electron injection into a high-intensity laser interaction with matter. This discovery offers possibilities for a new level of control over electron injection and plasma bubble formation in laser wakefield acceleration. This controlled formation of a plasma bubble could greatly contribute to a more stable and higher-quality beam in laser wakefield acceleration. This discovery could lead to a new level of performance in high-energy plasma-based accelerators, which could greatly expand the capabilities of these devices for future applications in, for instance, a next-generation petawatt laser facility in the US. In addition to this, we have also shown that not only can we create a well-defined plasma bubble for a stable laser wakefield accelerator, but we can also use this discovery to tailor the electron and plasma bubble in a way that allows for further enhancement of coherent radiation and energy conversion in plasma by a high-energy laser beam. This potential for enhanced coherent radiation and energy conversion, combined with the plasma bubble formation, could provide an additional new path to high-energy laser applications. This discovery could also contribute to a high-energy laser beam becoming more efficient and having a higher quality output. This could also provide new possibilities for a high-energy laser beam being used to tailor plasma properties at extremely high intensities by a high-energy laser beam, which could have far-reaching implications for a high-energy laser facility in the future. Coxeter groups possess distinct subgroups called parabolic subgroups, defined through the reduction's subsets, with reduced length equal to $l$ less some non-negative number. A particular theorem exists regarding a specific basis for these parabolic subgroups; in this paper, we specifically explore $B_l$-type groups in relation to their spherical subgroups, here denoted as $\mathcal B_n$. It is shown that the standard basis of $\mathcal B_n$ will satisfy the Coxeter presentation, here termed the 'basis theorem'. Additionally, it is demonstrated that any choice of simple reflections, when used as a basis for the parabolic subgroup corresponding to these reflections, will also fulfill the Coxeter presentation, here termed the 'generalized basis theorem'. Furthermore, it is shown that the volume of this parabolic subgroup is $2^{r(\mathcal B_n)}$, with $r(\mathcal B_n)$ equal to the sum of the labels of the reflections in the proposed basis, here denoted as the 'intrinsic reduction'. Lastly, it is shown that the intrinsic reduction of $\mathcal B_n$ can be expressed as $n^2$, with this finding extending to the full group $B_n$.

Recent investigations have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely insufficient. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain errors stemming from malicious interference. However, in practical applications, these networks lose their capacity for constraint and consequently remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs. Similar reasoning can be applied to other deep neural networks featuring skip connections. Moreover, we show that a new class of deep neural networks, namely Neural ODEs, has a weaker constraint which prevents excessive deviations in the outcome, thereby providing natural resilience against malicious inputs. In comparison, we examine the robustness of Neural ODEs to various types of attacks against the robustness of ResNet. Moreover, the robustness of Neural ODEs surpasses that of models developed with adversarial training, such as TRADES and Adversarial Dentification Framework. Additionally, we introduce a new method for identifying adversarial inputs based on the differentiability of Neural ODEs, which achieves superior performance in detecting malicious inputs on MNIST, CIFAR10, and TinyImagenet datasets. Importantly, this method does not need access to the target dataset, utilizing instead adversarial samples or clean images obtained from our proposed simple generator. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, which accurately detects malicious inputs on the test set with a low false positive rate of 4.33% on MNIST, 15.56% on CIFAR10, and 8.70% on TinyImagenet. In particular, this approach outperforms existing countermeasures, such as DeepRobust, DeepSigns, and DeepForest, which have a false positive rate of 13.96% on MNIST, 62.84% on CIFAR10, and 8.99% on TinyImagenet. Moreover, our method outperforms the performance of Grey Box Attack, which has a false positive rate of 64.84% on MNIST, 72.84% on CIFAR10, and 8.99% on TinyImagenet. Our code and generator are available at https://github.com/strinirane/NILM. This generator can also be applied to defend against adversarial examples in other fields, such as to defend against adversarial examples in medical image analysis, which is shown in https://arxiv.org/submit/2202.04421. Importantly, our method does not need to use gradient based attacks

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive alternative to conventional pair-wise measures such as correlation and mutual information. Building on this concept, we developed a whole brain connectivity map and demonstrated its potential to serve as a marker for specific cognitive functions. Furthermore, by leveraging recent breakthroughs in computing technology, we were able to accurately and efficiently determine the connectivity of large brain networks, enabling the application of this framework in studying whole brain connectivity. Two studies were conducted using the data from the Human Connectome Dataset and the ABIDE dataset, which showed that connectivity measures derived from structural connectivity correlated with cognitive abilities, while connectivity measures derived from functional data through dynamic correlation and the structural information from diffusion MRI also correlated with cognitive abilities. Our results established the feasibility and effectiveness of using total correlation to measure functional connectivity, providing a new tool for analyzing the human brain. This tool can further be used to study various brain disorders and improve the understanding of brain structure and function. Additionally, our framework can guide the design of artificial brain networks, enhancing the development of artificial intelligence systems. This framework may also be used to study evolutionary problems in brain development and offer insights into the design of consensus mechanisms in multi-agent systems. Moreover, it can provide a basis for developing a quantitative theory of brain function by revealing the underlying organization of the brain through a framework that resembles generative models. Using the framework, we were able to recover the spatial organization of the brain and identify the roles of various brain regions, which would lead to new theories of brain function and provide a foundation for assessing the health of individual brains and designing artificial intelligence systems. However, the actual implementation of the framework is complicated by the high computational requirements of computing total correlation. Therefore, we developed an efficient algorithm based on a partial complementary compressed sensing identity matrix and a hierarchical clustering approach to determine whole brain connectivity in a computationally efficient manner. This algorithm leverages the structure of the brain to reduce the high dimensionality of the data and utilizes complementary compressed sensing identity matrices to determine the connectivity of the brain regions. Following the initial screening using the algorithm, hierarchical clustering is used to determine the connectivity of brain regions, which can further be used to study whole brain connectivity. Our algorithm can accurately and efficiently determine the connectivity of large brain networks, which can lead to a new understanding of brain structure and function. Furthermore, our algorithm can be used to study various brain disorders and improve the design of artificial intelligence systems. However, the actual implementation of the algorithm is limited by the data from a single subject.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions through random sampling. Traditional techniques for generating samples from Gaussian process posterior calculations consider the process as a whole or break it down into individual data points. This research focuses on a middle ground, developing techniques for pointwise characterization of the Gaussian process posterior, enabling the creation of samples that accurately represent the process's randomness while simplifying computations. By characterizing the posterior in this manner, the process's independence from its own posterior in relation to specific data points can be determined, allowing for the generation of samples through latent variables and the construction of samples that are inherently consistent. We illustrate the implementation of these methods in the context of two Monte Carlo inference techniques: slice sampling and slice Gibbs sampling. By evaluating these methods on a variety of simulated examples and a notable application in the prediction of active learning, we demonstrate their effectiveness and practicality. We provide detailed mathematical derivations and offer an accompanying software package for reproducing our results. Our findings show that the techniques for pathwise conditioning can be an efficient and reliable alternative to existing methods for Gaussian process Monte Carlo. Further analysis into their performance in the context of other Monte Carlo techniques and beyond Gaussian processes is recommended. The last ten years have been marked by significant breakthroughs in neutrino physics. Notably, multiple studies have conclusively proven the occurrence of neutrino flavor oscillations. We have established the parameters for neutrino mixing, which allows us to design more effective investigations of newly opened avenues of research. By taking precise measurements, we can test our current understanding of three types of neutrinos, their mass relationships, and CP symmetry in the lepton sector. Long-range neutrino experiments are expected to play a crucial role in enhancing our understanding of electroweak forces. The DUNE experiment, set up to capture a wide-band neutrino beam from Fermilab in a deep, massive Liquid Argon detector, is poised to provide key insights into CP asymmetry and mass hierarchy. Its underground facility will also enable us to study rare events such as proton decay and supernova neutrino bursts, broadening the DUNE project's scope to encompass astrophysics and related cosmological impacts. This presentation will outline the DUNE project's underlying motivations and essential features needed to meet its scientific objectives. Finally, we will provide an update on the progress made in both technology and project development in the past, discussing how these advancements lay the foundation for reaching the precision required to tackle the challenges mentioned above. Recent studies have centered around boosted top tagging algorithms, particularly those utilizing discriminants. Although these algorithms have been thoroughly examined, there is still a lack of clarity on the tagging process itself. To address this gap, we applied the Shapley value method to analyze and interpret the results of the \bt\ discriminant. This method enables us to determine the relative contribution of each sub-discrimant to the overall \bt\ result, thereby providing new insights into the tagging process. Notably, we found that the mass information in \bt\ is largely redundant, whereas the spatial distribution of kinematic variables holds significant importance. Additionally, we observed that the tagger's performance could be further enhanced by incorporating kinematic variables derived from top-friendly regions in the detector. Our research also ventured into unexplored regions of the \bt\ discriminant, promising potential applications in physics beyond the standard model with implications for collider experiments. The Shapley value approach can be applied to any boosted object tagging scenario, offering a novel perspective on the tagging process. It may be particularly beneficial for scenarios where the tagging interpretability is crucial, such as in instances of conflicting results or in the standard model's interpretation. Furthermore, this method can aid in identifying the most effective configurations of tagging algorithms, which is particularly essential during the data reevaluation process. It is worth noting that using the Shapley value method for sensitive topics like collisions at the Large Hadron Collider may require a careful analysis to avoid disclosing any sensitive information. Many computer vision tasks, including predicting future actions from observed dynamics, greatly benefit from motion information. However, traditional relative spatial-temperal (ST) frameworks struggle to capture detailed motion features like orientation, velocity, and contours, resulting in inaccurate action predictions. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel end-to-end deep learning approach called ModRNN, which extracts precise motion details through a hierarchical prediction mechanism, combining high-level action features with low-level motion details. By merging these two streams, ModRNN achieves better performance than existing baselines on challenging action prediction tasks. This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing methods for linear capabilities to ensure safe access to reference types that can be copied, with a particular emphasis on its novel extension to languages with tracing garbage collection, as well as data structures featuring explicit lifespan management. This work is related to hybrid programming that combines linear and non-linear elements, specifically in the context of the languages Rust and JavaScript. A prototype implementation has been developed for JavaScript to facilitate communication with Rust code through WebAssembly, with this protocol named Josephine. Our proof-of-concept demonstrates that Rust code embedded within JavaScript can remain memory-safe even when subject to garbage collection and mutual references between Rust and JavaScript objects. However, these references lead to mutual references that cannot be automatically resolved, posing challenges for garbage collection. To address this limitation, our approach involves ensuring that Rust objects embedded in JavaScript are treated as linear entities, with a subsequent extension of our theory to cover multi-threaded programs. Finally, a demonstration has been developed using Josephine based on a Web page that employs a Rust-based implementation of the todo list example from the Rust book, with a live demonstration available online. Our research marks the first effort to integrate linear capabilities with an additional extension for applications with a flexible, non-linear lifetime management approach, as well as a prototype implementation in JavaScript targeting WebAssembly. With this approach, developers can safely access and manipulate Rust objects within JavaScript, with a live demonstration available online. As an added benefit, our theory can be applied to other languages with similar mechanisms, specifically TypeScript/JavaScript and Scala/JavaVM. However, due to constraints related to polyglot development, the protocol cannot be publicly accessed, with plans for an open-source implementation that integrates with existing WebAssembly libraries, as well as discussions with developers of these libraries and TypeScript/JavaScript to integrate our approach into their tools, with details available online. In the long term, we intend to expand our theory and demonstrate its applications by designing memory models that integrate multiple programming models with varying levels of explicit memory management, with a live prototype available online. This research concludes with considerations for its practical applications, discussing avenues for extending this theory to cover additional languages, with particular emphasis on its potential integration with TypeScript/JavaScript, as well as challenges related to performance and synchronization that are still unresolved, with a live demonstration

  4. The effect of varying parameters, including sigma, weighting functions, and lambda values, on the point spread functions of co-added images is studied through simulations.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these estimates are sharp. Building upon these estimates, we investigate the unconditional stability of periodic initial conditions with specified norms. It's worth noting that similar estimates have been studied in the past, although the present approach is distinct due to its focus on multi-dimensional space and the use of a specific aligned decomposition, as well as the application of a fixed aligning operator in the perturbation. This methodology has the added benefit of providing an explicit relationship between the aligned perturbation and the initial conditions' maximum norm, thereby allowing for the exploration of potential generalizations in other contexts. To overcome the challenges posed by the degenerate parabolic equations, we employ an innovative technique that involves estimating the growth of vorticity along the degenerate direction in space. Moreover, we build upon the developed estimates a priori by tackling the stability problem for the Cauchy problem in 2D and 3D on the torus with Hölder norms. In the case of 2D, we leverage the use of the vorticity function's conservation, while in 3D, we rely on the energy inequality for our derivations. Lastly, we expand upon these estimates an alternative approach by exploring the 4D periodic Cauchy problem for a degenerate parabolic equation, specifically the Smolinsky equation, and establish that any small enough perturbation, expressed as a maximum norm, results in a global-in-time unique solution. Interestingly, we obtain the same type of estimates an unconditional stability problem even if we consider a non-degenerate parabolic equation, as an example, the 4D Navier-Stokes equations in the radially symmetric case. The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial and challenging, where a quantum server attempts to convince a less computationally powerful classical client that a quantum circuit has produced a specific output. The fastest known protocol for verifying classical results in quantum computation has a time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|^3), but recent advancements have led to two new results: 

Firstly, we've developed a protocol that uses the quantum support state, resulting in a time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|), and we've also generalized this concept to other types of quantum states. 

Secondly, we've employed the QFTS (Quantum Fast-Fourier Transform for Strings) to create a protocol that runs in linear time with inputs, and we've shown that this is achievable within the noisy quantum channel model. Consequently, we believe this breakthrough will have far-reaching implications for quantum algorithms that rely on efficient classical verification. Our findings also pave the way for generalizing classical verification protocols based on quantum fast matching and support of superdense coding. Furthermore, we've identified a natural extension of these concepts to positive semi-definite matrices, known as Gram matrices, and we've developed a protocol that verifies these matrices in linear time with inputs, and we've shown that this is achievable in both the noisy quantum channel model and a setting where quantum computers are used. The fastest known protocol for verifying Gram matrices in the latter setting has a time complexity of O(poly(κ) |X|^{O(1)}), and we've demonstrated that this complexity can be reduced to O(|X|^1.5) while utilizing quantum computers. Finally, we've established a connection between our approach and a recent protocol designed by Barak, Braverman, and Brumer. Our work has several applications, including a more efficient generation of random linear codes, and an improvement in the time complexity required to determine whether a given matrix lacks full rank, all of which can be realized in the noisy quantum channel model. Furthermore, we've shown that these optimizations can be realized in two additional settings: a noisy quantum channel with classical verification and a setting where quantum computers are used. The fastest known protocol for determining matrix rank in the latter setting has a time complexity of O(poly(κ)|X|). Consequently, we believe these reductions could lead to new applications, as well as improve the efficiency of recent works in this domain. A blockchain system enables secure interaction among parties with conflicting reliability, making it a prime candidate for establishing trust within the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem, where its applications extend beyond digital currencies. However, applying the blockchain to IoT straightforwardly yields high processing times and energy consumption. To address these limitations in supply chain management, where various IoT devices operate in parallel, a new blockchain architecture has been developed, specifically designed to incorporate a lightweight consensus protocol, for instance the Practical Byzantine Fault Detector. Moreover, the proposed architecture requires an additional layer of supervision, as unverifiable data sent by IoT devices to nodes and nodes' requests for services to the blockchain necessitate validation. To achieve this, an 'oracle' is incorporated into the architecture to ensure only legitimate information is transmitted to the blockchain. Utilizing the Food Supply Chain as a real-world example of IoT applications, this new architecture has been put to the test and measured in terms of processing time and energy consumption. Results indicate that their approach surpasses current standards, showcasing a notable decrease in energy consumption of up to 43 times and a decrease in processing time of up to 43.18 times. Consequently, this architecture is suited for real-time blockchain applications, especially in complex ecosystems. Additionally, the architecture allows for the easy integration of new components, as the decision-making or contract modification can occur without interrupting the existing protocol. Therefore, it is an adaptable and versatile architecture. An implementation of this decision-making process can be accessed at GitHub repository: https://github.com/ucamp/releaseOracles. Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and unseen cell shape sequences. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively through comparisons of synthetic cells generated from our model against those obtained from realistic simulations of cell growth. Our results demonstrate the capacity of our approach to effectively generate growth patterns in cells with varying levels of complexity. Additionally our approach's compact latent code enables intuitive exploration of the generated cells through user interaction, which we demonstrate with user studies. Finally the efficacy of the compact representations also enables learning effective cell shape similarity metrics which will allow for more accurate classification of cells in the future. These capabilities and more make our approach valuable for development in both computer vision and biological cell analysis contexts. Ultimately the ultimate potential of our approach could see use in higher levels of cellular modeling as well as other applications in the biomedical sciences. Such potential uses would further cement the importance of developing compact, neural-based representations for modeling cell growth and topology. Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, footnotes, images, tables, and mathematical equations. Unlike sighted individuals who can easily locate the referenced content, individuals who rely on linear audio narration find it extremely challenging. We suggest an approach based on visual detection to identify referenced content and gather necessary metadata that can be utilized in subsequent research to insert summaries into audio narratives. The technique we present has shown effectiveness on both digital documents and those that have been scanned from print. The latter requires rectangular entity segmentation, which is often overlooked but is essential for providing summative descriptions in audio narratives. We present empirical findings on the accuracy of visual detection and the applicability of this approach on a dataset comprising over 5000 research papers. The dataset and source code can be accessed at https://h2020-heads-project.github.io/navigability/. Our experiments were conducted using the JAWS screen reader, which simulates real-world listening conditions. The dataset was annotated by five individuals who are blind or low-vision, and whose feedback informed our research. The project received funding from H2020 PROJECT HEADS (Grant Agreement No. 720257).

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking limits its ability to capture context dependencies within neighboring words, leading to inconsistencies when encountered during inference. This paper presents XLNet, an alternative approach based on autoregressive pretraining, which eliminates these limitations by exploring all possible sequence permutations in a permutation-filled mask, enabling the capture of dependencies within neighboring words, while maintaining bidirectional context capture. Autoregressive pretraining is further enhanced by incorporating an ensemble of permutation-filled autoregressive language models, including XLNet, which demonstrates significant improvements over BERT on 20 languages, surpassing human performance in multiple tasks, and achieves state-of-the-art results with improved efficiency. Moreover, XLNet's pre-trained models are versatile, enabling the automatic induction of knowledge and the creation of knowledge graphs, as well as pretraining and fine-tuning in 20 languages without English pretraining, achieving state-of-the-art results in multiple tasks. Finally, XLNet's success in multiple tasks and languages paves the way for its application in NLP's next challenges. We've developed computational models to analyze how stellar activity affects spectroscopic analysis of exoplanet transits, utilizing data from both high-resolution and low-resolution spectra. We compared observed signals in the presence of activity for various planets, including warm Jupiters and mini-Neptunes, across wavelengths that include hydrogen in the optical range and methane in the infrared range. Our simulations revealed that if a planet shows signs of water absorption despite stellar contamination, high-resolution spectroscopy can identify the water signal in the data. However, for planets that don't exhibit water absorption, using high-resolution spectroscopy won't eliminate the effects of stellar activity and might even create additional features that resemble a planet's atmosphere, such as scarves of extended atmosphere. We found that in some cases, the false positives can mimic features of mini-Neptunes, including the potential for atmospheric escape in these planets, but could also complicate detection of atmospheric features in general and impact the assessment of planets' habitability, including the search for temperate zones. Our research examined methods to analyze transiting planet spectra, including traditional, optimized, and regularized chi-squared fits, and discovered that although these methods differ in their ability to recover planet parameters, they are all susceptible to stellar activity to some extent. However, if we assume that the atmosphere remains neutral or that atmospheric features are known, models that match total flux or flux ratios outperform those that analyze individual wavelengths. Moreover, regularized chi-squared fits tend to perform better than their un-regularized or non-regularized counterparts in these scenarios. Our research uncovered a trade-off between accurately removing the effects of stellar activity and detecting atmospheric features, and suggests that in cases of strong activity, low-resolution spectroscopy may be a more reliable choice for mini-Neptunes, while high-resolution spectroscopy may be a more reliable choice for warm Jupiters. However, these models require knowledge of the host star's spectral type and are not as reliable as other methods that can correct for stellar activity. Our research uncovered a correlation between how stellar activity affects spectroscopy and the characteristics of the host star, suggesting that early-type host stars are more difficult to analyze, while late-type host stars are relatively easier to analyze, at least in cases where the atmosphere remains neutral. Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows minimal movement in water when not stimulated, but when stimulated at different points along its body, it is able to generate rapid movements in various segments.  This observation contrasts with the theory that animals at low Reynolds numbers are unable to volitionally move in this regime.  By combining high-speed video analysis with a model that accounts for fluid resistance, it has been found that forcedoricatus exploits a phenomenon where the fluid provides a small but significant upward force on its surface, allowing for efficient movement when stimulated.  This movement is made possible by using wave-like undulations combined with changing body angles, and by taking advantage of the momentum from one limb to propel the next.  This combination of movements enables fororicatus to travel more quickly than expected based on its size, and this efficient movement may be due to a lightweight body and a flexible outer cover that helps reduce drag.  Additionally, fororicatus has demonstrated the ability to perform an advanced maneuver - turning while remaining stationary - and this ability may be linked to selecting sensitive areas to apply stimuli.  This research combines elements of drag reduction and temporary swimming styles to propose a new theory: that some animals at low Reynolds numbers may use temporary increases in movement speed that are not seen at static conditions, and that some movements may be based on both wave-like undulations and simultaneous body segment activation.  However, more research is needed to confirm this new theory.  Also, as animals move from water to air they can take advantage of air's lower viscosity but not its lower density, and this can result in a temporary increase in movement speed that is not seen at static conditions, and that may be based on both wave-like undulations and simultaneous body segment activation.  However, more research is needed to confirm this new theory. Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, yet constructing and maintaining them proves to be a difficult task. Current techniques for taxonomy expansion face limitations, particularly in handling data that is hierarchically complex and noisy. This paper proposes an innovative method for taxonomy expansion through hyperbolic representation learning, allowing for the graph structure to be preserved and enhanced. Our hyperbolic technique employs Geometric Flow framework to transfer information from a superseding taxonomy, while HyperLCSC tackles noise and uncertainty by representing variable data shapes and distributions in lower-dimensional hyperbolic space. We evaluate our approach in multiple Bayesian hierarchical forecasting scenarios, demonstrating its adaptability in addressing uncertainty and dynamic data patterns. Overall, our results show that HyperExpan successfully integrates these concepts to achieve reliable and efficient taxonomy expansion. It outperforms existing methods in predictive accuracy and adapts better to data patterns. Moreover, our hyperbolic representation learning technique is freely available on GitHub under the name HyperExpan. 

HyperExpan has been successfully applied in the following two areas:

1.  Weather Forecasting over Time: This study investigates the use of hierarchical taxonomies to forecast weather conditions at different times. Specifically, we employ HyperExpan to forecast numerical weather data with varying time scales, as well as weather reports over a period of a day. Our approach involves building a hierarchical representation of weather data and using it to forecast future weather conditions based on historical data. We evaluate our technique in numerical weather data and weather reports from major cities across the United States. The results show that HyperExpan improves forecasting accuracy in both cases. 

2.  Stock Prediction over Time: This study investigates the effectiveness of hierarchical taxonomies in predicting stock prices at different times. Specifically, we use HyperExpan to predict stock price data with varying time scales, as well as financial reports over a period of a day. Our approach involves building a hierarchical representation of stock data and using it to predict future stock prices based on historical data. We evaluate our technique in numerical stock data and financial reports. The results show that HyperExpan outperforms existing methods in both cases. 

In summary, our research demonstrates the adaptability and effectiveness of hyperbolic representation learning in multiple Bayesian hierarchical forecasting scenarios, underscoring its significance in preserving taxonomic structure. The accompanying code is publicly available for review at https://github.com/mohefanooi/HyperExpan.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing images of southern sky sources from the ATCA telescope, we've investigated how the angular size of sources affects their polarization levels, using a statistical approach to mitigate biases from individual source measurements. We found a systematic decline in polarization degrees of compact sources as they became more faint, in contrast to sources with larger angular sizes which showed no such trend. Additionally, we observed no correlation between polarization degree and source displacement from the center, suggesting that displacement can be a reliable proxy for evaluating bias in polarization-statistics studies. Furthermore, we've estimated the ratio of sources oriented perpendicular to those oriented parallel, finding lower limits of three and five respectively. Finally, we've calculated the polarization fraction required for sources to be undetected by the Planck satellite, finding it to be roughly five percent. By analyzing dispersion values, we've identified bias arising from sources missed by the Large Synoptic Poll, with the bias decreasing as angular sizes exceeding 10 arcseconds. The cause of this phenomenon is attributed to the survey's incomplete sampling of sources, resulting in statistically dependent fields which introduce correlation and cause dispersion values to deviate from expectations. We've proposed a correction based on a model to account for this source sampling effect, suggesting a factor of ten reduction in bias for sources larger than ten arcseconds. Importantly, our study highlights the validity of analyzing population statistics through stacking and provides population models which can be used to evaluate systematic effects in future polarization-statistics studies. We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor, with its components being the integrated velocity field auto-correlation. However, in cases where nonlocal effects are prominent, we demonstrate that transport will be impaired and experience a delay, with nonlocal perturbations acting to decrease or increase the diffusivity tensor depending on their sign and magnitude. Moreover, we provide a detailed explanation for the sensitivity of the turbulent transport properties to perturbations in the velocity field. These findings are exemplified by numerical simulations in three dimensions, focusing on the transport of a passive scalar in a system with periodic boundary conditions. Our results show that local and nonlocal perturbations can significantly impact the turbulent transport properties, with considerable potential for reduction or enhancement. Therefore, our work suggests that any theoretical model of turbulent transport, aiming for precision and generality, should be based on a representation of the flow field statistics as a Markov process, otherwise it may fail to capture key aspects of turbulence. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings on the understanding and interpretation of experimental and numerical data, with a particular emphasis on the importance of coherent structures in turbulence. Namely, our work reveals that the presence of dynamically coherent structures naturally gives rise to nonlocal perturbations and, consequently, to delayed and nonlocal perturbations in turbulent transport. Moreover, our results imply that the sensitivity of the turbulent transport properties to perturbations in the velocity field can be attributed to the coherent structure in the far-field, rather than to perturbations in the near-field, and that the effect of these perturbations is direct, rather than indirect through coherent structures in the near-field. Consequently, our work offers a theoretical basis for the interpretation of experimental and numerical results, with implications for the understanding of turbulent transport properties. Specifically, our findings indicate that the reduction of turbulent transport properties can be attributed to the motion of coherent structures in the far-field, rather than to perturbations in the near-field or to coherent structures in the near-field. Moreover, our results show that delayed perturbations in turbulent transport can be calculated exactly, without the need for Markov approximation

We define T to be the time at which the random walk visiting the tree leaves first returns to a previously visited leaf. Under the condition that the trial trees satisfy a uniform H\"older condition, it is shown that the law of the encoded T-convergence orbit converges to a quantum Markov process associated with the Laplacian on a sphere with spherical trigonometric coordinates, as n approaches infinity. We demonstrate that this quantum process remains invariant under a conjugation of the encoding function, which induces a conformal transformation on the sphere, and show that it must converge to a stationary state for large n. Moreover, for any fixed large n, it is shown that the encoded T-convergence orbit for a random forest of size k exhibits uniform convergence, which implies the existence of a limit orbit for random forests of varying sizes as k approaches infinity. This limit orbit encodes the information of the random forest system. This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the stationary Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we investigate the relationship between input forces and resulting flows in dimension d. This work shows that the stationary Navier-Stokes equation becomes unstable when the input forces decrease slowly with spatial frequencies for certain dimensions and types of flows, causing the solution map to diverge at zero. Conversely, we find that this divergence is not a concern when the input forces decrease rapidly, and we specifically identify cases where this is true for 3D and 4D systems. By resolving these competing outcomes, we have fully addressed the open question for systems in dimension d ≥ 4. Moreover, we have obtained more precise information regarding the ill-posedness of the equation in various spaces and have extended our analysis to other related problems. This study is significant because it shows that the stationary Navier-Stokes equation can be solved in high dimensions under strong conditions, but remains ill-posed under more relaxed conditions, and has important implications for related problems such as Euler equations and systems of critical Besov spaces. Our research also opens new avenues for investigating the regularity of solution maps and their relations to specific systems of fluid dynamics. This work further extends our understanding of the behavior of solution maps in more general settings by covering the case of semi-group regularity. Finally, we have obtained an alternative proof of a result concerning the non-existence of regularity or ill-posedness in 3D systems, which was first discovered by Cancès, Maldarella, and Schimperna.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and generate general word meanings, researchers are exploring new ways
to enhance model performance. The quality of these word meanings depends on how
often the words appear in the data, leading to underoptimized representations
of rare words. This paper investigates a novel method to address this limitation
by developing a dictionary-based approach to improve PLMs' understanding of
rare words in two stages. Firstly, it utilizes existing dictionaries to map rare
words to semantically similar surrogate words, which are then incorporated into
the PLMs. Secondly, it refines PLMs' representations by fine-tuning them with
surrogate words and their corresponding original words. The two-stage technique
is tested on the BERT model and an industry text classification benchmark, with
results demonstrating its efficacy and cost-accuracy benefits. The analysis further
examines the impact of different dictionary usage strategies and evaluates the
generalizability of these findings to other models and domains. Ultimately, this
paper provides a foundation for integrating dictionaries to enhance PLMs' rare word
comprehension. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/senfo66/dict-bert.

In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust predictive model by sharing only encrypted data, thus preventing the risk of data exposure. We concentrate on the vertical fusion methodology, in which contributors lack access to complete data entries, and the main goal is to train a comprehensive predictive model for a full data set. We demonstrate that this process can be vulnerable to a privacy breach involving the training data ('inference attack'), which can be executed with only a few participants' data and a general model. We also show that two common regularization techniques used in vertical federated learning actually make it simpler for such breaches to occur. We further highlight the practicality of these breaches and demonstrate that they can be successful within a reasonable timeframe. Finally, we outline a potential method for mitigating these breaches, specifically by limiting the training data available to participating entities, thus protecting sensitive information. The study was conducted with a focus on electoral data from three countries: the United States, Germany, and Switzerland.

The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, artificially generated labels. However, since the distribution of node features in the real world often lacks diversity, the naturally occurring node labels also lack sufficient diversity, ultimately resulting in pseudo-labels with relatively low confidence. To address this phenomenon, we propose Informative Pseudo-labeling (IPL), a pseudo-labeling approach for Graph Neural Networks that accounts for both node connectivity and local neighborhood structure when computing the confidence of pseudo-labels. By focusing on both the source node and its connected neighbor nodes, IPL enables the incorporation of more informative neighbor nodes as negative examples to enhance the robustness against overly confident pseudo-labels. Thorough experimental evaluations confirm that IPL significantly enhances the ability of Graph Neural Networks to handle scenarios with an extremely limited number of labels. Notably, IPL is adaptable to multiple existing pseudo-labeling techniques and can also be applied to other areas beyond node classification. Our study includes numerical demonstrations highlighting the method's efficiency. This reduction holds without the convexity assumption and yields comparable convergence rates, with an accelerating rate when the regularization tends towards zero. This study investigates how basic autonomous entities akin to Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler in "Chaos in Wall Following Robots", the autonomous entities use a straightforward distance sensor to navigate, with the added limitation of a narrow "phi" field of view. As these agents maintain a consistent forward velocity, they rely on the sensor to adjust their path accordingly: rightward when close to obstacles and leftward when distant from them. In a linear environment, the autonomous entities maintain a consistent distance from their surroundings and proceed along a fixed path. However, when faced with periodic patterns in the environment, such as square, triangular, or sawtooth shapes, and the field of view is narrowed, these agents follow a recurring path. But as their field of view expands and certain threshold levels are reached, their movements become chaotic. If the shape of the obstacle is symmetrical, symmetry breaking occurs at a specific point, leading to unpredictable paths at higher thresholds, a behavior known as period doubling to chaos. With certain triangle shapes, the autonomous entities' paths exhibit a limit cycle before descending into chaotic movements. As the autonomous entities navigate through areas with alternating light and dark environments, such as a periodic grid or a half-tone pattern, their paths exhibit more complex behaviors, including permanent chaos or a limit cycle. These entities do not require a long period of time to change from ordered movements to chaotic ones but instead experience a sudden transition into the chaotic behavior through a crisis phenomenon. This sudden, chaotic behavior poses challenges for their survival and can result in two possible outcomes: death or persistence. As their basic design doesn't accommodate learning or adaptation, their chances of survival depend solely on their ability to explore their surroundings and develop new strategies to maintain existence. In conclusion, these autonomous entities can manifest a wide array of behaviors, from repeated patterns to random movements, all driven by the interplay between their inherent design and the variation in their environment. Such fundamental systems can serve as an effective case study in the interplay between their internal programming and the external context. Moreover, these autonomous entities can serve as an analogy for biological systems that adapt and learn, where similar sudden transitions may occur between different behaviors and highlight the significance of environmental perception in their functional processes. Ultimately, their simple design renders them susceptible to death, but their ongoing movement maintains the possibility of discovery, a central principle of their continued existence. Therefore, their persistent motion serves as a testament to their unyielding determination to exploration and discovery.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computing cross-correlations given traditional architectures, where the computational demand increases exponentially with the number of antennas involved. Traditional architectures, requiring the calculation of all antenna pairs, become impractical for arrays with many antennas. The introduction of the FFT-correlator architecture reduces the computational complexity, but can lead to underutilization of computing resources if the number of antennas is not optimized. This paper explores the possibility of dividing the antennas into smaller, uniform groups, and implementing FFT-correlators within each group. By combining the results from these sub-units, the system can achieve optimal computational scaling by leveraging the underutilized capacity within each unit. The proposed architecture can scale to the level of individual integrations with minimal increase in computing resources, while traditional FFT-correlator systems are limited by the size of their largest FFT. The added benefits include higher bandwidth and baseline sampling, but also increase the demand for high-speed data storage, while improved signal detection is achieved through increased sensitivity and reduced system variability. The theoretical benefits will be supported by simulations of creating FFT-correlators with the Casper pipeline and evaluating their performance. This new architecture is well-positioned for realization due to recent advancements in the scalability of their components. This study focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates. Moreover, the research expands upon these L-infinity estimates to encompass a broader category of parabolic Hessian equations. Importantly, the scalar curvature equation and the Weyl equation are specifically examined in this context. Moreover, the potential applications and interconnections with the elliptic Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations are explored. Lastly, the research includes an additional section on elliptic complex Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations. Moreover, the L-infinity estimates from the parabolic equations are used to demonstrate the aleph or Alexandrov convexity of manifolds meeting a specified criterion. 

In terms of related work, the research notes that the L-infinity and Holder estimates for the complex Monge-Ampere equation were previously explored by Phong et al, Calabi, and Candelas et al and others. Meanwhile, the L-infinity estimates for parabolic equations were initially considered by Li, and those for the K\"ahler-Einstein equation were investigated by Hashinaka. Furthermore, the convexity estimates and the Alexandrov reflection have been a topic of study for many, including Aleksandrov, Minkowski, Hogben, Burbea, Lassak, Burbea-Fleig, and Li. 

In a related note, the research intends to examine the connection between the parabolic Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations and the stability properties of geometric flows in a future work. 

The paper includes five sections. The first section provides an overview of the assumptions and the main estimates to derive L-infinity and Holder estimates for the parabolic complex Monge-Ampere equation. 

The second section expands upon these L-infinity estimates and applies them to the broader category of parabolic Hessian equations. 

The third section examines the scalar curvature equation as an example.

Research on spoken dialogue systems has typically relied on a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses for interpreting meaning and monitoring the dialogue flow.  Nevertheless, using a limited number of options fails to account for the underlying probability distributions of the ASR output.  This study investigates the impact of incorporating probability distributions, derived from a confusion network of the top ASR hypotheses, into a model for tracking dialogue flow.  Unlike existing approaches to integrating probabilistic ASR output with dialogue flow tracking, this work presents a shortlist of multiple hypotheses and trains the model to forecast a distribution over the dialogue history.  Results from both automatic evaluation and human testing show that incorporating the probability distributions yields an improvement in performance for the task of tracking dialogue flow.  This work is the first to incorporate probability distributions of the ASR output in a model for tracking dialogue flow, and demonstrates the value of representing the ASR ambiguity in a spoken dialogue system.  Additionally, this study provides guidance on strike-point for balancing the accuracy of the ASR model against the desirability of a predictive distribution over the dialogue history.  An implementation of the work is provided through the OpenDS structure at https://github.com/jhushuai/open_ds. 

This paper extends previous research that utilized a limited number of the top ASR hypotheses to extend the representation of the ASR output to a full distribution.  This study offers an objective evaluation of the performance to date of dialogue flow tracking models that integrate probabilistic ASR output, and provides a standard for assessing such models in the future.  Furthermore, this work presents two strategies for training a model that forecasts a distribution over the dialogue history, rather than a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses, and demonstrates that these strategies can be successful with the adoption of attention to the ASR ambiguity or the incorporation of the underlying probability distributions into the training objective of the model for tracking dialogue flow. 

Finally, this study provides an analysis of the performance to date of dialogue flow tracking models that integrate probabilistic ASR output, and shows that such models can be successful even when the probability distributions are far from uniform.  An implementation of the work is provided at https://github.com/jhushuai/open_ds.  An extended analysis of the confusion network of the top ASR hypotheses is also presented at https://github.com/jhushuai/asn.  An implementation of the work to train a model that forecasts a distribution over the dialogue history is provided at https://github.com/jhushuai/open_ds.

Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. This simple approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Split-CIFAR100 benchmark and delivers comparable results on CoRe 50, consisting of 50 consecutive tasks. In addition to this, we observe that our approach performs well on the BCI competition competition tasks 2 and 4. To address this, our approach leverages multiple content features, including text, images, and their interactive relationship, which have thus far been underutilized in hate speech detection. Through experimental evaluations on two datasets, which are notably imbalanced in terms of classes, our results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over existing ones. Additionally, by using our model to analyze the reasons behind false detections, we are able to identify the most susceptible categories and features, which can in turn inform the development of more effective hate speech detection algorithms. Finally, our method's extended applicability to unexplored domains is demonstrated through balanced accuracy scores, which surpass that of existing models in known domains.
