A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate on non-Euclidean data, making it suitable for processing graph-structured data across various fields. Recently, research into GNN has been rapidly accelerating as more effective methods for training have been developed, particularly in contexts involving decentralized data, lacking a centralized server. This article focuses on the application of GNN in wireless communication systems. Initially, we provide an in-depth examination of GNN models, review their practical applications in wireless communication systems, and explore both centralized and decentralized estimation techniques from a theoretical perspective. Furthermore, we analyze the practical challenges associated with implementing GNN in wireless communication systems, discussing for instance, how device mobility can cause digitial channel fluctuations. This motivates the proposal of a novel GNN design with built-in sparsity, incorporating state division, filtering, and regularization schemes to trade-off sparsity, depth, and generalized performance. An empirical study is then conducted using wireless communication channel measurement data to verify the efficacy of this approach. Lastly, we explore the future research opportunities arising from the integration of GNN in wireless communication systems. This research offers insights into potental extensions to various other domains where graph data is involved, aiding the formulation of decentralized estimation challenges and guiding future research into GNN applications. variance $\sigma^2$ in stochastic gradients and (ii) problem-dependent parameters.
When optimizing smooth, strongly-convex functions with condition number $\kappa$, we 
prove that $T$ iterations of SGD with step sizes that decrease exponentially and 
know the value of $\sigma^2$ yield an $\tilde{O}(\kappa \sqrt{\log(T)} / M T)$ 
regret after $T$ iterations. We also show that SGD with statically chosen step sizes is 
only able to reach $\tilde{O}(\sigma \sqrt{T} / M)$. We then derive accelerated, adaptive 
SGD, proving it yields $\tilde{O}(\log(T) \log(1 / \delta) (\kappa \sqrt{\log(T)} / M) +
(\sigma^2 / (M \T^2 \kappa^2 \theta^2 + \kappa \log(1 / \delta) / M))$ regret, which greatly 
surpasses acceleration when optimizing with known variance and statically chosen step 
sizes. We further provide a sample-based acceleration technique, which can be applied 
independently, and which we prove recovers these results exactly under the specified 
conditions, thereby providing a foundation for truly adaptive, accelerated SGD in 
practice. We then test these methods in four functions: the hyperbolic tangent, the 
and the $\ell_1$-norm. We also test them on a real, distributed, training job in 
tensorflow train (https://github.com/google-research/tensorflow-training-workbench), 
specifically, on 32 GPUs, a function that is nonconvex and has very large gradient 
noise. We test several varieties of adaptive, accelerated SGD, some of which are known, 
theoretical, and some that are simple, practical. Ultimately, we can reduce training time 
exactly in line with theory when the variance is known precisely. When the variance is 
only estimated, we can actually lower training time below what theory predicts, up to

Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object-grasping fields, dexterous grasping has been understudied, mainly due to a shortage of extensive datasets. To address this issue, our study introduces DexGraspNet - a large-scale simulated dataset - designed specifically for robotic dexterous grasping, paired with an efficient synthesis method for diverse dexterous grasps. By employing a highly accelerated force closure estimator, we have successfully generated millions of stable and diverse grasps for multiple robotic applications. Utilizing the ShadowHand gripper, our dataset includes over 1.3 million grasps for over 5,300 objects from 133+ categories, all validated through physics simulations. In comparison to a previous dataset based on object features, our proposed dataset exhibits a significant increase in diversity and quality, demonstrated by successful experiments in both force closure and dexterous grasping tasks. Furthermore, cross-domain evaluation shows that our dataset leads to state-of-the-art performance in dexterous grasping, outperforming prior approaches by a large margin. Our research dataset and finding are available at: https://dx.grasp.ml/2022/09/24/dex-grasp-net.html. Additionally, our code for the synthesis pipeline is openly sourced at: https://dx.grasp.ml/2022/09/24/dex-grasp-net-code.html. In terms of future contributions, our study paves the way for efficient dexterous grasping in contact-rich environments, specifically in the domain of cooking. Moreover, our study highlights various strategies to expand existing grasping datasets, enhancing their quality and diversity. In terms of potential societal impacts, our study may lead to advancements in collaborative robots cooking meals safely and efficiently. In summary, our study makes available the considerable DexGraspNet dataset, along with multiple other datasets, their underlying synthesis protocols, and our dexterous grasp synthesis code, which are now open to the public. This dataset has the potential to fuel advancements in robotic research, whereas our dexterous grasp synthesis code can be applied to various other challenging object-manipulation tasks. Ultimately, our study advocates for the expansion of existing datasets to enlarge their capabilities and facilitates seamless transfer of these advancements to other related fields. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of ascending and descending data points (AP) to minimize effects from respiratory motion. Compensating for motion in-plane shifts data to the center of k-space during each phase, while an adapted reconstruction technique utilizing central k-space data achieves high resolution without diminishing contrast. Evaluations through phantom tests and human studies have confirmed high quality images with resolution of 256x256 pixels and frame rates of up to 10 per second. Additionally, our method has demonstrated comparable image contrast to conventional breath-held sequences and superior image contrast to free-breathing sequences. Therefore, it offers an excellent alternative for situations involving breathing constraints. Image data is now available online through the MRIQual database (https://mriqual.institute-of-physics.sk). Our source code for the motion-compensated sequence is available at https://github.com/IMECHE-EPFL/AP_MC. Our method has the potential to replace standard sequences in clinical practice with the goal of creating a new standard. An accompanying video showcasing human study results is available at https://youtu.be/1RZrZK9Oo4k. Further research aims to reduce sequence parameters, such as decreasing the acquisition window from 4 seconds to shorter periods and shortening sequence duration, which would ultimately lead to the development of a new standard four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence for routine applications in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. An associated patent has been submitted. A thorough safety assessment has been performed and a related clinical study is currently being conducted in humans. Large, complex models like those for image recognition and speech synthesis require significant computational resources and cannot be directly compressed due to the way modern neural models are constructed. However, these models can be simplified through knowledge distillation, transferring knowledge from a larger, trained model to a smaller, less computationally intensive one. Currently, knowledge distillation involves adjusting model parameters to match the performance of a pre-trained larger model, which does not ensure the transfer of complex, high-level information. Following this, the adjustments made to the model are often optimized, which may improve the model's ability to accurately replicate its larger counterpart, but may also eliminate important details. Our proposed method, InDistill, preserves key information flows within the model by incorporating them into the adjustment process and learning procedure, thereby ensuring that the model replicates not only its larger counterpart's outputs, but also the complex patterns and relationships within those outputs. InDistill significantly outperforms current top-distillation methods by an average of 4.4% for model compression of various tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness for compressing complex models and improving model efficiency without decreasing its accuracy. Our research showcases the methods' applications in compressing the CNNS, which powers the successful ImageNet classification model, resulting in a model that achieves comparable performance with only 79% of the original model's parameters. Additionally, the InDistill methods' applications in compressing the Transformer, which powers the recent SynLG speech synthesis system, resulting in a model that achieves comparable performance with only 4% of the original model's parameters. As the interest in accelerating neural models continues to grow, our research advances model compression, enabling the creation of more accurate and efficient models through synthesis systems. Our research and development is based on the SynLG dataset, which is now available at https://github.com/ResearchSystems/SynLG. Our research code and model configurations for model compression are available at https://github.com/ResearchSystems/InDistill. The study of mathematical models for the development of plant populations highlights the impact of environmental variations, interaction distances, and water availability. The inherent complexity of these systems can be simplified by using spatially-based stochastic models. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on adaptive information from previous input vectors. Under such conditions, the classic sketch can fail to identify the top elements, even up to a constant factor. Interestingly, the CountSketch sketch remains robust when considering non-adaptive inputs, retaining a constant factor approximation for vectors up to a low dimension relative to m, where m is the number of measurements. This study aims to investigate sketches that provide robust analysis for a variety of input types, including adaptive and nearly adaptive inputs. A new family of sketches is introduced, leveraging pairwise linear measurements to reduce dimensionality. The analysis showcases the capability of these sketches to maintain a constant factor approximation for a significantly broader class of input vectors, including adaptive ones, while retaining approximation to top elements with essentially the same number of measurements as before. The analysis also addresses a long-standing question regarding the feasibility of achieving this level of robustness. The primary results mentioned above hold true for a broader class of dimensionality reduction tasks involving approximate matrix multiplications. The study provides a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving this level of robustness, in addition to proposing new algorithms that offer a constant factor reduction in dimensionality, while maintaining nearly constant number of measurements. These sketches not only provide a robust solution to low-dimensional approximation problems but also contribute to a well-known open problem in approximation algorithms, namely finding a feasible factor of density d and edge expansion edge expansion ε for any given graph; this question has remained unsolved for nearly two decades. The study reveals that achieving this level of robustness is feasible using sketches, while maintaining a level of density d' and edge expansion ε' where d'< d and ε'< ε. The proposed method demonstrates the feasibility of sketch-based solutions to problems that have been analyzed from an algorithmic perspective. The study compares the performance of sketches on various types of input vectors, including non-adaptive and adaptive ones, and highlights the need for a more precise input classification scheme that captures both known and unknown relationships between input vectors, which the authors believe presents an interesting research direction. The program's functionality is substantiated through calculations of electron-transport properties in systems with step-like density-invariant functions and transport-mediated phase transitions in a minimal model of $d$-wave superconductivity on the honeycomb lattice. These examples demonstrate ipie's potential in investigating diverse quantum many-body systems and their associated properties. The program's source code, documentation, and executable installer are accessible at https://ipiepy.github.io/. We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the mechanism or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust mechanisms capable of handling intermediaries that offer the highest bid to multiple agents, regardless of their private valuation profiles. To tackle this issue, we introduce the concept of "revenue maximization" defined as the maximum expected revenue generated by a mechanism when faced with intermediaries making fixed-bid pricing offers. We outline the conditions necessary for a mechanism to maintain a revenue maximization ratio of $\frac{1}{e}-\epsilon$ for any $\epsilon>0$. We investigate mechanisms capable of handling intermediate classes and present examples of mechanisms that come close to achieving a robust revenue ratio of $\frac{1}{e}$ but fall short of it by any arbitrarily small $\epsilon$ amount. Furthermore, we show that a mechanism designed by Ausubel is not robust in the presence of certain intermediate classes, while outlining an intermediate-class specific mechanism capable of $\Omega(\sqrt{m})$ times better revenue compared to the posted price mechanism, for $m$ denoting the number of agents. We investigate mechanisms capable of handling the widest range of intermediaries and present a simple mechanism: Second Price Plus Bid that attains a $\frac{1}{e}-\Omega(\frac{\log k}{k})$ fraction of the optimal revenue not accounting for intermediaries. To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity chains, and training transformer models to predict these chains, and subsequently generate summaries conditioned on them. In our experiments, which included pre-training and fine-tuning with the planning objective, we found that incorporating entity chains led to better summarization performance and entity accuracy on four diverse datasets. Notably, this method outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of Rouge metrics for the XSum and SAMSum datasets. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating entity chains allows for more effective hallucination control, and we were able to improve faithfulness of generated summaries by prompting the model to omit irrelevant information. Finally, our results demonstrate the applicability of this method to other generation tasks, such as abstractive text generation. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/tony313/Planning-with-LEAP. Through thorough analysis, our work highlights key planning and grounding choices that can aid future research in these areas. A preliminary version of our paper was presented at the Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL 2021). Our accompanying video can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KpF9QOo6R9g.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of quasiparticle excitation energies per particle in three theoretical models of the fractional quantum Hall effect: Laughlin, Correlator, and Jain. The goal of these analyses is to determine the phase boundary between the particle and hole phases within these theories. The phase diagrams obtained from the exact energy per particle calculations are compared with the phase diagrams based on the entanglement entropy. The exact energy per particle in the Correlator theory exhibits two distinct minima that shift towards lower filling fractions as the number of particles increases. The exact energy per particle also displays minima in the Jain theory, however, they do not lie below the energy per particle of the ground state. Both theories predict that the particle and hole phases do not coexist. The phase diagrams obtained from the exact energy per particle as well as entanglement entropy are identical, suggesting the phase diagrams based on entanglement entropy are reliable. The exact energy per particle in the Correlator model can be interpreted as a Hall conductivity, indicating that even in the case when the energy per particle does not demonstrate minima, the relationship between the exact energy per particle and its second derivative bears resemblance to the conductivity. In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact-related issues in marine ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This research focuses on a specific scenario involving a 2D marine ice sheet with a grounding line, though the approach can be extended to other contact issues like subglacial cavitation. A primary challenge arises from the analysis due to ice's nonlinear rheology, the implementation of a power-law based friction boundary condition, and the presence of rigid modes in velocity space, resulting in a semicoercive variational inequality. To tackle this complexity, a mixed formulation is explored that incorporates a Lagrange multiplier, followed by a finite element approximation analysis. This research derives error estimates by employing a specially constructed projection operator to account for the rigid modes, leveraging a Korn-type inequality, under the condition that rigid modes do not contribute to error, with results analogous to those obtained in recent polynomial approximation analyses. To confirm these findings, stable, quasi-Complementary Gradient schemes are demonstrated with both Bubnov-Galerkin and Petrov-Galerkin approaches. Furthermore, a comprehensive numerical study illustrates the effectiveness of these methods. This research's conclusions have potential implications for other contact-related issues in glaciology and could potentially be extended to other fields. A comprehensive code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/quasarml/quasarml.github.io. A visualisation of the numerical results is also available at https://quasarml.github.io/quasar-ml-website/fem-stokes-variational-inequality.html. A related movie is available at https://youtu.be/4n0v0B4HgG8. Furthermore, a note on non-conformal methods is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10351. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using artificial datasets and a real-world example involving diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal images. This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination via template fitting techniques. Our findings, expressed as percentage errors, demonstrate that radiative corrections to the top quark's partial width are minimal, beneath the 1% threshold, but have a more substantial effect on the fractional decay width of top quarks, impacting certain differential distributions by up to 10% and often more. Additionally, we discover that non-resonant contributions can significantly alter results, amounting to 20-30% changes in specific distributions, especially for events with leading b-quarks. We have also evaluated the impact on a set of differential distributions that are traditionally used for template fitting, revealing that corrections to these observables are generally small, but that they can be quite diverse, with some cases exhibiting variations of over 10% in specific template constructions. Our analysis indicates that these orders-of-magnitude estimates hold true for various final states other than those involving dileptonic decays of top quarks. Ultimately, these findings will allow researchers to assess whether the comprehensive, off-shell computation is truly necessary for top quark mass extraction or if the narrower approximation can suffice. Our analysis also includes a comparison with a computation that is currently available but based on the leading order piece-by-piece method, which shows significant differences with observable-dependent magnitudes of variation of over 30% in some cases. This comparison not only sheds light on the level of errors introduced by this approximation but also provides valuable insights into the piece-by-piece method's strengths and weaknesses, and how it could be modified into a more efficient approach, particularly by including a leading-order piece-by-piece description of the ttj process. This modification would likely yield results that closely mirror the comprehensive, off-shell computation, thus representing an important improvement. Moreover, our analysis of the extraction of the top quark's pole mass, which is crucial in many theoretical interpretations of LHC data, has also been left for future investigation. Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes lacking instruction due to the synchronization bottleneck. A notable issue in APEAs occurs when parent selection is based on fitness values. The chosen parents often tend to have similar fitness levels, leading to an uneven distribution in workload, thereby exacerbating evaluation time bias. This results in underutilization of computing resources and prolonged convergence. To address this, we present an alternative parent selection approach based on frequency, aimed at decreasing the impact of evaluation time bias and enhancing diversity, thereby accelerating convergence and achieving better results. Our proposed method is evaluated using six test functions in comparison to the standard fitness-based approach. The results indicate that the new selection method leads to a notable improvement in computational efficiency, specifically providing a factor of 2 to 5 times faster convergence rate despite slight increases in computation time. Moreover, we also found that when combined with a novel local search operator inspired by the nature of extinction, the proposed selection method results in superior output quality compared to existing local search approaches. Finally, the proposed parent selection is integrated into a novel online parallel coevolutionary algorithm and compared against established baselines, resulting in significant quality improvements with a notable increase in computation time proportion of 6.08. The source code for the presented approach is available for public use at https://github.com/hust-hilma/frequency-parent-selection. The experimental results can be found at https://github.com:hust-hilma/frequency-parent-selection/results. The investigation into evaluation time bias is documented at https://github.com/hust-hilma/evaluation-time-bias-in-asynchronous-peas. Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate an image's sharp version and the point spread function used to blur it, without any prior knowledge. This difficult problem has been partially overcome by assuming that the image belongs to a specific category, such as natural scenery or text. However, even with this limitation, there remains an uncertainty about which category the image belongs to. To tackle this issue, we present a novel model called the Kernel Mixture (KM) model that allows for various images to be blended in a single blurred image. This model represents the blurred image as a combination of clear images and the PSF that relates to their categories. To solve this complex problem, we develop an algorithm that starts with an initial estimation of image categories, followed by refining the estimates of images and the PSF based on these initial assumptions. By repeating this process, we achieve a stable final estimate of the images, the PSF, and the weights representing the image categories. This proposed method performs well on a range of official datasets as demonstrated by our experiments. Moreover, we introduce several datasets comprising blended images and show that our proposed method excel on these additional datasets. The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle. An accompanying plot displays the locations 
where these energetic particles entered Earth's atmosphere, leaving their data unanalyzed. 
Additionally, analyses of 27 events above 150 EeV investigate possible connections 
to the cosmic microwave background's radiation patterns, temperature, and density 
along the particles' paths. However, no strong evidence is found to support an 
explanation for the phenomenon. Furthermore, studies on particle intensities 
throughout the southern hemisphere also reveal possible fluctuations in the data. 
Finally, combining Auger and other high-energy particle data from both hemispheres 
reveals a slight excess in the east-central region of the southern hemisphere, 
particularly around 110 degrees longitdudinal position, although no clear source 
has been identified. These findings await further verification by data from other 
observatories.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The current approach relies on predicting link-level traffic conditions.
However, this method is inefficient due to the excessive data required for a small benefit.
Alternatively, a novel method called Traffic4CastTCN incorporates a traffic feature representation scheme called TrafficSnippets.
This innovative approach forecasts local traffic changes at intersection levels, reducing redundancy.
The TrafficSnippets scheme utilizes a self-contained video clip representing traffic evolution and is trained alongside an end-to-end recurrent neural network model.
The incorporation of TrafficSnippets enhances forecasting performance and efficiency.
Experimental results demonstrate that Traffic4CastTCN exhibits a notable improvement in NMAE accuracy of 15% when using TrafficSnippets over a baseline method.
Additionally, TrafficSnippets enables a substantial reduction in required data, requiring only 50% of traffic videos to maintain comparable performance. 
Such capabilities make Traffic4CastTCN an attractive option for city-scale deployments. 
The proposed framework showcases through experiments that Traffic4CastTCN outperforms existing approaches across various evaluation metrics and cities due to its adaptability and versatility. 
A notable adaptation is presented, utilizing TrafficSnippets and EyeOfTTCN that achieves state-of-the-art performance across three cities while requiring only 10MB of storage per intersection. 
Such a lightweight model has the potential to be adopted as an edge computing application in the future. 
Moreover, extending Traffic4CastTCN leads to advancements in other relevant applications like urban planning and urban design.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method that uses an extended 2D multi-orientation approach with automatic pre-processing and orientation alignment. We compared this method with other recent deep learning techniques in two datasets: the public HarP dataset and an in-house epilepsy dataset, HCUnicamp. Despite surpassing other methods in terms of Dice score, our approach as well as other compared methods failed to completely avoid false positives in resection regions when applied to epilepsy patients, indicating room for further improvement. While our method outperformed other deep learning hippocampus segmentation methods in terms of reliability and applicability to various domains, it still presented some limitations in specific cases, particularly for epilepsy patients where other methods and hippocampus segmentations often fail. Nevertheless, our results show that automatic hippocampus segmentations in epilepsy patients can be as accurate as those in other populations. This study also highlights that a thorough evaluation of any new hippocampus segmentation method is essential to ensure its reliability and applicability to various domains and clinical scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/icml2021/HCUnicamp.

Finally, we frame the problem of two pairs of particles meeting their destinations within $V_{2}$ time as a quantum $k$-intersection game, and we offer some quantitative estimates for the duration $V_{2}$ based on the player's skills. Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to calculate proton radiation at low Earth orbit by simulating the interaction between cosmic ray particles and the Earth's atmosphere, followed by transportation in the magnetosphere. This model accurately predicts the proton radiation characteristics at low Earth orbit by accounting for variations in energy, atmospheric depth, and trapped proton populations. Analysis of data from the STPSAT-1 spacecraft reveals agreement between our model and observations, confirming its effectiveness. This model can be applied for predicting proton radiation in the inner belt and near Earth's atmosphere due to variations in cosmic ray flux and atmospheric conditions. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the potential implications of changes in global atmospheric nuclear resonance absorption on proton radiation. The model also provides insights into the potential of using neutron detectors on spacecraft near the Earth to monitor variations in cosmic ray intensity. A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, consisting of global model reduction, weight refinement, and weight 
redistribution among links. By applying a dynamic shrinking strategy to model 
structure, we can streamline graph models efficiently. Subsequently, we use 
gradient-based methods to refine model weights, then reassign links dynamically 
to optimize the model topology. Experiments using ResNet-50, GoogLeNet, and 
graph classification with the NELL dataset verify the effectiveness of our new 
training strategy, yielding improved outcomes and faster training times with 
less model weight. Notably, our method achieves comparable results with state-of-the-
art performance on image classification using limited models, outperforms prior 
link reassignment techniques, and accelerates training by approximately 2-3 times. 
Moreover, our approach surpasses existing models with more robust node 
distinguishability in graph classification tasks. Our code is publicly available on 
GitHub.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The evidence suggests that a uniform grain composition is most consistent with the observed patterns of infrared polarization, and the established ratio between optical and infrared polarization. A detailed analysis reveals that a combination of astrodust and PAHs accurately replicates the properties of galactic extinction and emission from interstellar dust while adhering to existing constraints on dust abundance. The associated data and software have been made publicly accessible for further research. Additionally, we explore potential implications of our model in the context of the UV-to-mid-IR spectral energy distribution of the Milky Way, particularly the Lupin and Fainberg templates. The model presents an opportunity for the development of a comprehensive, referential model of interstellar dust, and has significant implications for the study of dust in other galaxies, and for the interpretation of data from various space observatories. The model also offers new possibilities for the use of interstellar dust as a tool in the investigation of PAHs' molecular structures. Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which involves changing all lights off in a specific arrangement. Inspired by the original Lights Out game from Tiger Electronics, we're investigating an extension known as the Most Clicks Problem, which revolves around determining the most clicks required to solve a given instance, regardless of the solution path or order of clicks. Unlike the original problem with a known NP-completeness status, this variant has an unknown complexity and presents a new research area with ongoing research focusing on solving instances with specific light configurations, such as full or half-lit states, as well as exploring general and practical algorithms for solving generic instances. Furthermore, we're examining the problem in specific contexts, such as grid-based graphs, where we're making theoretical assessments and providing example-based analyses. In addition, we're investigating the problem within specific subgraphs, such as cycles and the complete graph, while also delving into variations of the problem in directed graphs known as the Strong Lights Out Problem. A practical implication of our research is that we're improving the efficiency of a specific rehabilitation toy, which our experiments with real users have demonstrated to be more effective and intuitive than the original version. Additionally, we're analyzing the computational complexity of the problem across different graph types and designing efficient algorithms with proven bounds that demonstrate the problem's distinct characteristics, such as its non-data-retrievable and coNP-completeness, as well as the hardness of approximating it within a certain ratio. Lastly, we're investigating the parameterized complexity of the problem across different graph types and designing algorithms with various targets in mind, such as the problem with a focus on the number of colors involved and the problem with a focus on the distance between lights in a specific graph. Analyzing these problems, we're investigating the problem's complexity with respect to different parameters, which could potentially be useful in developing more efficient algorithms in related contexts, such as a generalization of the problem known as k-Color Lights Out. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can handle these distorted images by modeling the image data as a combination of smooth regions and clear boundaries within images. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach produces highly accurate segmentations and effectively restores high-quality image data, particularly in images with varying color schemes. Our model also enjoys convexity and optimal partial recovery guarantees, ensuring robust results. This paper showcases the capabilities of this approach through successful segmentations of diverse images, including brain tumors, statistical shape models, and colored images of coral skeletons and sharks. Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, before applying approximations again and then interpolating. The proposed approach is based on the identification of domains where these transitions wouldn't result in losses, though a thorough exploration of all such domains is generally infeasible. A specific framework was developed for sparse sets, allowing for its practical application in common contexts like reachability analysis. The application of this approach to other domains is also discussed, as well as its potential for improving analysis precision and reducing computational requirements. Experimental results demonstrating a 30 times speedup and a 100 times higher precision were also obtained on a benchmark suite of cryptographic systems. The implementation of the proposed approach is available as an additional layer on top of existing AI tools, making it compatible with existing AI-based analysis and verification approaches. Moreover, the underlying theory provides opportunities to integrate other precision increasing techniques in similar ways, thereby enhancing the range of available Abstract Interpretation techniques. Finally, a complementary decoupling approach that takes a different direction than sparse sets is also presented and shown to provide additional ways to improve analysis precision and speed. The suggested decoupling approach can be combined with the one proposed in this paper to further enhance the performance and precision of Abstract Interpretation based analysis and verification tools. Moreover, through the underlying general underlying theory, other decoupling techniques can be identified and added, thereby opening the door to a larger set of possible improvements. The suggested decoupling and decoupling-based layers can be used independently or together with existing layers, thereby allowing existing analysis and verification tools to be upgraded with these new precision increasing modules. Moreover, when used within the analysis and verification process these layers can be used for free. The suggested decoupling and decoupling layers can be used within existing contexts, as well as new contexts, to improve the performance and precision of analysis and verification tools, thereby opening the door to a new generation of more accurate and faster analysis and verification tools. The suggested layer can be used to improve the performance and precision of context-free analysis, by temporarily switching to a more precise representation of the semantic domain, before applying other layers that introduce new approximations, or other context-dependent analysis layers. Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Large-scale data processing in these fields requires more efficient outlier detection algorithms that can handle standard databases optimized for transitive closure, allowing for distance calculations to be joined with data processing pipelines to determine the prevalence of objects and identify outliers. To achieve this, we propose the OUTL-Outlier Detection System, leveraging proximity graphs to extract proximity information from database queries and improve the overall performance of outlier detection. A thorough experimental evaluation showcases the effectiveness and efficiency of OUTL in comparison to current approaches. Furthermore, we have made OUTL publicly available to the research community. The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror. An attempt to apply a scalar model to the Rindler horizon in a cosmological context reveals inconsistencies in derived probabilities that conflict with established principles, particularly detailed balance. A related analysis involving a two-level atom exposes difficulties in obtaining consistent results depending on whether the atom is at rest with a moving mirror or the mirror is at rest with a moving atom. These challenges stem from the fact that momentum transfer affects the electromagnetic field and atomic states differently in these scenarios. However, an approach involving a systematic expansion in powers of the coupling constant may circumvent such difficulties. Furthermore, an evaluation of radiation spectra resulting from the acceleration of an two-level atom demonstrates that, aside from the principal peaks, the spectrum exhibits empty bands due to the restriction of allowed dipole transitions by the mirror, with bands opening up as the atom approaches resonant frequencies corresponding to transitions within the atom. These findings suggest that in any coherent or non-convex model where momentum transfer affects the electromagnetic field and atomic states dissimilarly, they must be treated independently, with such momentum transfer related to the Poynting vector. However, in the context of an atom near a Rindler horizon, even a consistent coherent model yields an unphysical outcome since this regime lacks a well-defined Poynting vector. Specifically, for an atom at rest with a moving mirror (the Rindler horizon), the probability to jump up from the ground state to an excited state is not the mirror's reverse counterpart when the mirror moves with an acceleration twice that of the atom. However, in the latter scenario, the spectral intensity reduces to a well-known quantity from the radiation emitted by an atom in a laboratory setting. As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures node-level fairness by incorporating the effects of distant nodes and incorporates neighborhood sensitivity into various GNN architectures. Through fair graph representation learning, our approach yields more transparent and principled predictions, enhancing prediction accuracy as well. We test the efficacy of our framework in fair classification, link prediction, and node classification tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate its versatility in graph fairness for regression-based tasks. Our results are supported by theoretical foundations, and the source code is available for further reference. 

Disclaimer: The existing analysis of our approach is grounded in fair representation theory. Notably, there aren't any existing studies on neighborhood sensitivity in GNNs, and the use of diffusion bridge to measure node pair distance is also novel. Although our approach resonates with distribution constraint, our approach offers a novel combination of incorporating distance metrics for more accurate and fair graph learning.

By analyzing 35.9 fb^-1 of data collected with the CMS detector, researchers explore multiple low-M_{\chi^0_{1}} scenarios in which the lighter chargino decays into a neutralino. Several scenarios, including models of gluino production with significant squark contributions, are also evaluated and constraints placed on their parameter spaces. With the assumption of up to 60 jets in these scenarios, the search spans masses in the range of 400-600 GeV for gluinos and 300 GeV in the neutralino-mediated scenarios. Additionally, regions of parameter space in the compressed low-M_{\chi^0_{1}} scenarios, where the CMS detector is not efficiently sensitive, are identified through theoretical predictions and analyses of events with two jets. By combining these results, researchers place limits on SUSY models that have not been previously explored, such as neutralino-excess scenarios with high MET and low jet multiplicity, as well as split SUSY models where the lightest neutralino is essentially massless. For certain regions of parameter space, the search achieves sensitivity to points with neutrino-rich metastable states and compressed low-M_{\chi^0_{1}} scenarios that surpass the analysis's theoretical expectations. By applying constraints to split SUSY models, researchers obtain upper bounds on the gluino's production cross section, limiting its creation to less than 0.04 fb when assuming a 100% decay into the neutralino. Moreover, for metastable \chi_1^{\pm} points with high diphoton decays, the search's theoretical expectations can be raised to mass thresholds of 210 GeV, which significantly advances the analysis's performance. However, without additional assumptions, the search's constraints provide little relief from the parameter space in models of split SUSY, where the lightest supersymmetric particles remain undiscovered. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. Furthermore, the source term of the path integral was dealt with using a factorization similar to the Feynman-Kleinert factorization or through a linearization technique. Results from these methods converged when high precision was applied, demonstrating the methods' consistency. A discussion on the advantages of each technique is included. Time-dependent driving led to the development of a discrete-time lattice algorithm that effectively replicates the ground state |gs) when driven oscillations die out over time. Again, calculations of the position expectations were carried out with each method producing similar results. These were compared to available literature. Additionally, the source term of the path integral was dealt with using a rotation technique or the variable transformation technique. A similar convergence was observed in these time-dependent simulations. Suggestions for incorporating these methods into a quantum algorithms toolbox for near-term quantum simulators are provided. Position measurements were also carried out with a minimal number of sampling points when estimating expectations, while the path integral was based on an extensive sampling of all auxiliary variables for high accuracy. A study on the scaling of the source term sampling bias in a simple test case is included. A comprehensive analysis of the methods employed in these simulations is provided in an accompanying PhD thesis. Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which are hard to understand for users, and also fail to consider the variability of reviews' effectiveness based on user and item context. To overcome these challenges, this work proposes the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) that aims to provide more accurate reviews-based predictions and intuitive interactions. To achieve this, SIFN employs a two-part structure where the first part identifies relevant reviews for users and engages with their content, while the other part calculates the impact of these reviews and combines it with user and item features to make predictions. To ensure the network's adaptability and review effectiveness consideration, SIFN uses a dynamic review sampling method and a multi-layer sentiment-aware fusion module. Experimental results show that SIFN significantly outperforms other methods on several real-world datasets including Mmovie, BookCrossing, Bolep, Amazon, Ciao and Yelp. For example, on the Amazon dataset, SIFN performance is improved by 2.19% compared to other methods when evaluated using APC score. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/lingpengzh/IFN/tree/main/SIFN. The model's deployment on a GPU is demonstrated in this document. Furthermore, APEC score, which was used in this research, is available at https://github.com/lingpengzh/IFN/tree/main/utils/. The model's performance can be visualized through rating prediction results as shown in Figure 7 in the paper. The model's performance is shown through MSE and APC metrics in Table 1, where MSE is calculated by taking the average of the difference between predicted and actual ratings, and APC is calculated by taking the ratio of the difference between predicted and actual ratings to the standard deviation of the actual ratings. The motivation for developing this research stems from the fact that review-based prediction methods often suffer from less accurate and less intuitive interactions. To address this, this research aims to develop a more adaptable and more intuitive interaction mechanism, which is implemented through the sentiment-aware interactive fusion module. The research also explores the impact of review effectiveness on prediction accuracy and user interaction. The results demonstrate that SIFN significantly improves over other methods when evaluated using MSE and APC score. For instance, on the Amazon dataset, SIFN improves its performance by 2.19% and 1.66%

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to grow CS datasets by altering words, which preserves the underlying linguistic characteristics. We examined three word replacement techniques in the Arabic-English language pair and assessed their impact on maintaining the CS data's inherent properties. We evaluated the techniques through two exercises: one targeting lexical characteristics and the other involving a CS categorization task. Our analysis revealed significant variations among the three techniques in terms of maintaining the CS data's attributes, with one method, $LSTMAI$, performing better than the others in both tasks. Additionally, we discovered that incorporating a maximum of six word replacements maximized the retained CS data characteristics. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent controls over animal presence and agency cues was used to test both hypotheses within a hierarchical structure. Our findings show that a multi-layered neural network accurately models the animacy hierarchy and that the middle layers, corresponding to the core of human ventral temporal cortex, are particularly skilled at integrating agency cues. Furthermore, it was observed that early layers prioritize animal presence cues and that the final layers consider additional factors, including sociality. Overall, data suggest a nuanced view of animacy, where agency-driven sociality is a primary distinguishing factor, and that the hierarchy can be split into agency-driven and feature-driven parts. Therefore, it was concluded that the animacy organization arises from the interplay between these two components. Future research will explore the broader implications for understanding the cognitive processes of agents. The current study's findings also highlight potential drawbacks of binary classification approaches in neuroscientific studies. In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, standard approaches like mesh refinement and data smoothing, which are commonly used to address these issues, can also preserve inaccuracies and even intensify them. A novel and comprehensive approach to filtering has emerged as the most reliable method, but its high computational demands and potential for instability have hindered its widespread adoption. A new convex optimization filter overcomes these limitations while retaining the superiority of mesh-based filtering, with the added benefit of being mesh-independent, thus reducing computational costs by orders of magnitude. Through comparisons with advanced mesh-based filtering techniques, it has been proven to be just as effective or even more so in various numerical simulations, including the resolution of the 1-D heat equation and the nonlinear elasticity equations at different scales. Additionally, it has been successfully applied to the simulation of multidimensional cardiovascular blood flow, which further highlights its practical utility in complex simulations. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with significant margin and excels on visual localization tasks, topping rankings on two prominent benchmarks. Additionally, our method offers a notable advantage in computational efficiency. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources and offer a quantitative metric to assess and correct bias in scenarios where reference data is unavailable. By comparing smooth Bperp maps with corresponding observations obtained from spectropolarometric data, a metric of relative bias (ABperp) can be calculated. This metric is then used to assess the impact of different regularization and data residuals on Bperp in a simulated framework. Furthermore, to alleviate bias in a more natural manner, an inversion approach using a prior in the form of a Gaussian distribution is introduced. This technique constrains the possibility of achieving Bperp values and demonstrates the importance of selecting an appropriate dispersion value. Additionally, it is demonstrated that determining the optimal Gaussian distribution parameters requires minimal a priori knowledge of the solar physics background. By employing these methods in a realistic scenario, it is shown that treating data in a diagonal manner can greatly reduce bias in Bperp. The techniques presented are then applied to a map of the coronal region derived from AIA 3310 Angstrom data and compared with a map obtained through direct inversion, revealing reduced bias in the corrected dataset. Finally, it is observed that the techniques presented are transferable to other types of inversions and could potentially be applied to the characterization of 3D scenes of the solar atmosphere obtained through coronagraphic observations, where reference data is also available. Several possible future applications of these methods are then discussed. One such application is the creation of intrinsic magnetic energy maps, where correcting bias in a smooth Bperp map leads to a significant reduction in noise and thus increases the likelihood of identifying structures of magnetic energy comparable to the kinetic energy. This ultimately enables the identification of regions where magnetic reconnection occurs more easily than usual on the Sun's atmosphere, paving the way for further research in understanding the dynamics and behavior of the Sun's environment. Finally, it is proposed that the techniques presented can be employed to characterize structures of magnetic energy in 3D scenes of planets' atmospheres that display similar layering behavior observed in the solar corona, where magnetic energy can serve as an essential factor in understanding planetary atmospheric dynamics. The characterization of magnetic energy in these celestial objects not only aids in advancing our understanding of their respective physics but also sheds light on fundamental aspects of magnetic energy transfer. This research explores a real-world scenario in which consumers aim to minimize their energy costs by scheduling their energy usage in advance, with a billing system that instantaneously adjusts for high peak periods. To effectively respond to pricing variations, we apply a game-theoretic approach, enabling a large group of consumers to strategically coordinate their usage and create a aggregated load demand. We develop an efficient algorithm to solve this issue and illustrate its efficacy through numerical examples, showcasing how coordinated consumer behavior results in reduced transaction energy losses in smart grids. Additionally, we demonstrate that in the absence of real-time communication among consumers, the aggregated load still achieves a significant reduction in transaction energy losses. Our study also highlights the potential of interactive billing systems to foster consumer cooperation. Our proposed approach is evaluated using pricing models from actual smart grids in Europe and North America. The results indicate that by coordinating their energy usage, consumers can achieve a substantial decrease in transaction energy losses, with varying levels of success depending on the type of pricing model employed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even in the context of non-interactive billing, the aggregated load still exhibits a notable reduction in transaction energy losses. Our research showcases the potential of instantaneous adjustable billing to facilitate consumer cooperation during autonomous demand side management. With the ability to instantly adjust costs based on actual peak demand, we may be able to successfully coordinate consumer behavior and minimize transaction energy losses. The feasibility of implementing such a billing system relies on advanced metering infrastructure, which must be further investigated. The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity. We illustrate this with various examples derived from one-dimensional Schrödinger equations and convex functions of Toeplitz matrices. We also examine how this behavior extends to infinite ergodic Markov chains. Furthermore, empirical findings for chaotic systems, including the Lorenz system and time-series data from a chaotic invariant manifold, support these theoretical predictions. Finally, the findings from these theoretical models align with observations documented in the literature. The notable findings include that (i) converging averages in long-term simulations of chaotic systems experience slowing down (ii) simulations of chaotic systems, including a notable case involving the Lorenz system, exhibit oscillating convergence that is linked to periodic motion and (iii) time-series data exhibit oscillating convergence at a frequency similar to that present in the data. We provide a theoretical explanation for these phenomena along with evidence that these behaviors are widespread across chaotic systems. We also show, across a range of examples, that weak convergence and the empirical findings from these examples are consistent with the spectral properties described in the Lorentzian Theorem. Consequently, this evidence suggests that this theorem be renamed as von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. The primary contribution of this work is the finding that (i) as sequences of time tend to infinity in a manner linked to a spectral measure with a spectral value of one, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on weak convergence. We argue that this relationship holds for any ergodic system. The proof requires that systems exhibiting a spectral gap exhibit uniform convergence and that systems lacking a spectral gap exhibit weak convergence. We argue that this relationship holds through two principles: the ergodicity of the system and the use of a Lorentzian Theorem. Consequently, this work provides an extensive exploration of the nature of convergence rates in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, a topic previously unexplored. We choose to utilize von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem as the foundation for this work due to its foundational significance and the ease of applying these principles to a system. We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a substantial portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated. Conversely, principal component analysis within languages that share a common ancestor reveals that only a limited proportion of variation is shared. This suggests that, over time, changes in morphological complexity compel new dimensions of complexity to emerge independently. Furthermore, our findings indicate that an annotation-based metric of complexity is linked to an encyclopedic measure of complexity, despite them measuring distinct aspects of typological complexity. This connection holds even after controlling for language characteristics. Nonetheless, cross-linguistically, most of the variation in complexity is found to be unique, suggesting the necessity for further investigations into the distinct facets of morphological complexity that these measures assess. This study also highlights the importance of interpreting correlations between linguistic characteristics as causal associations when analyzing typological data. Additionally, analyzing languages that share a common ancestor using hierarchical linear models helps to distinguish between form and content aspects of morphological complexity. However, our study reveals that annotational morphological complexity is not a proxy for syntactic complexity, nor does it play a significant role in phonological complexity. Consequently, future annotations should be approached with caution, particularly when used to make cross-linguistic comparisons. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach addresses this by adapting the 'fastica' algorithm, an open-source Fast ICA implementation, to work with a wide range of kernel models, including novel sine and hyperbolic tangent based kernels, which are derived from the classical multi-layer perceptron ('MLP') neural network and are shown to be competitive with established kernels such as Gaussian and Laplacian. The proposed approach is evaluated using the open-source KNICTK library on diverse datasets including those found in computer vision and genomics literature, with results suggesting significant performance improvements when using the proposed kernel when compared to the existing Gaussian and polynomial kernels. With its ability to perform feature extraction, the proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach represents a viable tool for tasks such as feature selection, classification, and other data analysis techniques. Additionally, open-source code for implementing the approach has been made available. Finally, the research explores a range of possible extensions to the m-ar-K-FastICA algorithm, offering scope for further investigation and development. Specifically, while classification and feature extraction share some similarities, they have distinct objectives and thus different design strategies, leading to a new method, m-ar-K-Discriminant Analysis ('m-ar-K-DA') which achieves both classification and feature extraction through a combined approach. Additionally, another extension, Regularized Partial Marginal Likelihood ('R-PML') which tackles model selection and regularisation issues in ICA by adopting a combined approach with Lasso regression and regularization. Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating or responding to urgent situations such as emergencies. An innovative approach for monitoring social media updates based on geographical tags has been developed. This framework leverages an in-memory data store and NoSQL database to enhance real-time event detection, enabling the aggregation of multiple social media posts linked to specific locations. By comparing chronological order of aggregated events with a fixed-time interval, the system differentiates new events and avoids duplicate analysis. An optimized event detection strategy has been implemented using a distributed in-memory database and canonical normalization of SQL queries for improved performance and data handling. The effectiveness of this innovative method has been evaluated through experiments and benchmarking tests. Moreover, the technique has been successfully applied to real-world data by analyzing combined datasets of Twitter and Flickr images to identify notable events such as festivals, disasters, or location-specific landmarks. The resulting application demonstrates the ability to visualize events over time and provide detailed information upon mouse click. An additional feature enables users to customize and save their preferred spatial locations for further analysis. The technique has also been successfully tested on large social media datasets consisting of 600K Flickr images and 42M Twitter posts. The source code of this innovative method has been made publicly available for others to use. An online demonstration of the technique can be accessed via a web-based interface. Users can replicate the results by analyzing their own geographical locations and observing the events detected in real-time. The technique has the potential to be potentially useful for analyzing various types of data with temporal and spatial attributes. The method could be enhanced by incorporating deep learning algorithms for more sophisticated event detection and exploring other applications such as crowd monitoring. The technique may also serve as a foundation for developing more sophisticated systems in the future. The source code is available on GitHub at the specified repository.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization due to high transition metal content. By utilizing computational searches based on fundamental laws, researchers predicted 37 cobalt-rich compounds, specifically 17 YCo$_{16}$ and 20 YCo$_{20}$, which were identified as stable with a high likelihood. These cobalt-rich alloys were discovered to exhibit increased phase stability at elevated temperatures, attributed to increased vibrational entropy. Notably, YCo$_{16}$ and YCo$_{20}$ displayed enhanced magnetization and Curie temperatures compared to the extensively studied compound Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$, specifically 0.22 T and 204 K for YCo$_{16}$, and 0.29 T and 204 K for YCo$_{20}$. These findings highlight the capacity of computational searches to uncover novel, cobalt-rich compounds, which were previously unknown in experimental studies. Further investigation into these compounds is suggested to confirm their magnetic properties and stability. Our results also demonstrate that it is possible for the 1-2 at. % rare earth concentration, traditionally considered essential, to be reduced to nearly zero in the cobalt-rich compounds of the Y-Co-Fe system, which requires further research to expand on this discovery. Additionally, we suggest exploring the cobalt-rich compounds as potential permanent magnets, given their increased Co content. By reducing the rare earth proportion, the cost of materials and the complexity of processing can be significantly reduced. Cobalt-rich compounds, with their increased Co content and reduced rare earth proportion, may potentially replace traditional compounds in the development of advanced permanent magnets. These compounds could also shed light on the relationships between chemical composition, microstructure, and magnetic properties that contribute to their magnetic excellence. Existing research gaps and promising avenues are identified in the discussion as potential areas for future investigation. In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the ad impression and optimal bid price. Nevertheless, existing bidding strategies often overlook the randomness of user behaviors, such as click-through rates, and the uncertainty surrounding costs resulting from auction competition. In our study, we explicitly take into account the uncertainty associated with estimated ad impression values and the risk tolerance of a DSP under specific conditions via a sequential decision-making process. A novel bidding algorithm, grounded in reinforcement learning and incorporating budget constraints, is introduced. This method utilizes uncertainty propagation and a risk-adjusted performance metric to estimate the expected return from bidding. Additionally, it integrates an adaptive recovery mechanism to recover lost opportunities due to uncertain clicks and auction competition. Using real-world data, we evaluated our proposed approach against various baselines and observed notable improvements in our algorithm's risk-adjusted performance compared to traditional bidding strategies. Moreover, our results demonstrate that our method can adapt and thrive across diverse risk levels and data environments. [Introduction to] A Risk-Aware Real-time Bidding Algorithm.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in certain scenarios, specifically aiming to establish that one necessarily leads to the other in specified contexts. To accomplish this, we examine quantum steering in systems with distinct degrees of freedom, as well as in Gaussian states within various scenarios, and find support for the argument through positive permutation entropy, which indicates the presence of nonclassical correlations. However, we do find an exception in certain bipartite systems, where Wigner negativity can exist without quantum steering, and we discuss the implications of these findings. Further research could focus on identifying a universal criterion that links quantum steering and Wigner negativity, and thereby better understanding their interrelation. Additionally, the study suggests that examining nonclassical properties through permutation entropy has utility in investigating these features. Permutation entropy itself lends itself to analysis via mathematical tools, including dimensionality reduction techniques, and therefore has potential for being a key feature in identifying Wigner negativity and quantum steering. Finally, the study explores the idea that these nonclassical properties can serve as indicators of fundamental quantum behavior in continuous-variable systems. This study is further discussed in [21]. Moreover, recent discussions on Wigner negativity in [22,23] are pertinent to the subject. Our work is the first to link permutation entropy with quantum steering, however, similar approaches can be found in the literature for other nonclassical properties, for instance [24-26]. Relevant works on continuous-variable entanglement in general are [27-29], and the topic of hybrid approaches to identify Wigner negativity and quantum steering shares similarity with approaches in [30-33]. These related works offer a comprehensive overview of nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems. The study presents novel insights that connect permutation entropy with quantum steering, but it builds upon existing work in the field. Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed, precise QKD secure boundary analysis. Utilizing the two-decoy BB84 protocol, we simulate the effect of random seed uniformity on the secure boundary of a QKD system. Experimental results show that when the average min-entropy of the random generator drops below 0.95, a QKD system's secure boundary is severely compromised. Furthermore, we found that when 1-bit error is tolerated in the quantum channel, an increase of 1.78% in 1-mean photon number can gain an 18.7% increase in secret key generation, but these gains come at the expense of reduced confidence in the secure boundary. We verify that when the random generator's average min-entropy exceeds 0.98, a QKD system's secure boundary is restored. Our research enhances the security evaluation of quantum information exchange and sheds light on the importance of random seeds in quantum key distribution. The findings have potential real-world applications in the development of quantum communication systems. The study also contributes to understanding the impact of random seed quality on the secure boundary of a QKD system by illustrating QKD key regeneration and continuous generation under varying random seed conditions. Furthermore, we speculate that our research could be applied to other quantum information exchange protocols, potentially revealing previously unexplored security threats. The study supplies quantitative security analysis methods that can be used to assess random seed quality in quantum information exchange systems. The impact of random seed quality on the secure boundary of a QKD system serves as a demonstration case of quantum information exchange security, highlighting a previously overlooked security vulnerability that could be exploited by an active attacker in practice. The study provides security reduction-based security analysis applicable to non-uniform random seeds, establishing a security analysis paradigm that accounts for random seed quality in quantum information exchange protocols. The effect of random seed quality on the secure boundary of a QKD system serves as a prototype example of quantum information exchange security, indicating that an active attacker could compromise QKD systems' security if the randomness of seeds used in privacy amplification is compromised. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. This paper also explores an analogous development within the context of semi-Euclidean geometry.
