This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under two types of disturbances: the base station's limitations and the limitations of each user. 
To resolve this problem, we split the optimization process into two simpler tasks and apply the block coordinate descent technique to alternately optimize both variables at fixed values of the other variable.
Our results show that a higher RIS gain leads to higher achievable sum secrecy rates, and that optimizing the phase shifts on the RIS depends on the active paths from the base station to the users and the active channels from the base station to the RIS.
We also propose an iterative algorithm to iteratively optimize the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS, which yields a high ratio of sum secrecy rates to total transmit power. Numerical results confirm the efficacy of our approach. Additionally, we compare our approach to an alternative solution based on the multi-block multi-variable Frank-Wawenstein optimization algorithm. Our approach outperforms this alternative solution in terms of the sum secrecy rate and requires fewer phase shifts on the RIS. Both the computational time and the number of phase shifts on the RIS are lower for the alternative solution. 
Finally, we investigate the impact of the base station's limitations on the secure communication systems, which incurs additional optimization variables and reduces the likelihood of meeting the minimum secrecy rate requirement.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, involving three solar cycles. We analyzed data on solar wind speed, density, and temperature, and energy flux, but not yet energy density, as these quantities aren't directly observed in the solar wind phase. Instead, we used simplified models to estimate the energy density, drawing from theories such as the ideal gas law and a two-temperature plasma. These models allowed us to calculate the energy flux, which was found to be consistently below a certain threshold, approximately 100 W/m^2, across the four approaches. Furthermore, we noticed that the energy flux's variability decreased significantly closer to the sun, which we attributed to the reduction in characteristic timescales in a decreasing coronal background pressure. We also observed changes in the energy flux's pattern, from being mostly determined by kinetic energy at larger distances to becoming dominated by thermal energy within about 15 solar radii of the sun. To account for these findings, we examined computational models of the solar wind crossing the sun's poles, which showed reduced variability and different pattern changes in energy flux under different coronal scenarios. We, therefore, suggest there are two regimes of behavior for energy flux: one at larger distances governed by the solar cycle and another at much shorter distances dominated by the plasma's thermal properties. To achieve even more accurate predictions, we plan to apply these discoveries to the case of a smoothly changing transition between these regimes. By combining the results from the Parker Solar Probe and other solar missions through a collaborative effort, we aim to refine our understanding of the solar wind behavior. One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required for model development and evaluation. To fill this gap, we have developed a Multilingual Event Extraction dataset featuring detailed annotation for over 50,000 event occurrences in eight diverse languages. This resource not only covers entities but also accurately marks the events and associated elements, enabling further analysis of multilingual event extraction through thorough experimentation. Building upon this dataset, we investigated both a traditional method combining rule-based models and statistical models as well as a cutting-edge neural network approach. The results demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed strategy in non-English datasets while highlighting potential areas for further improvement. To the best of our knowledge, our MEE dataset stands out as the largest and most comprehensive Multilingual Event Extraction resource to date, offering great benefits to both model training and evaluation as well as further research exploration. The MEE dataset can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/allenai/MEE-Dataset}. The corresponding source code for our used models can be found at: \url{https://github.com/allenai/mee-neural}. Our model's pre-trained models and trained model weights, along with associated training logs, are available at: \url{https://github.com/allenai/BigScience}. Upon thorough review, our analysis suggests the need for adjustments to the current evaluation metric in order to reflect more accurately the actual Multilingual Event Extraction capability of models. To support this claim, we have conducted an intrinsic evaluation that highlights the usefulness of our model's predictions in non-English datasets. Ultimately, our study aims to facilitate future research and additional advancement in Multilingual Event Extraction for various languages. We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step toward our proof is explicitly determining, at each point of the flag bundle, the Chern curvature of the universal bundles, as endowed with their induced metrics. This leads to the development of an alternative approach to the Jacobi-Trudi identity using differential forms, as well as confirmation of the positivity of specific Chern forms for Griffiths semipositive vector bundles, thus partially supporting Griffiths' conjecture on characteristic forms of positive characteristic. Additionally, as a direct result of our universal push-forward formula, we derive the Chern curvature expression for the tangent bundle of the flag bundle of a single vector space, now endowed with its induced Riemannian metric, effectively generalizing an earlier result of the first-named author. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a modification of the Chern curvature expression for the tangent bundle of the Grassmannian can be applied to the study of its Hopf differential, while our method also yields the vanishing theorem for specific Laplacians at Steiner points. In the final section, we explore the interplay between Griffiths positivity, the universal push-forward formula, and the geometric structure of the complex manifold, particularly in the context of its holomorphic vector fields and Chern forms. Our research reveals that the geometric properties of a manifold are closely linked with the positivity of specific Chern forms, as expressed through the universal push-forward formula. This connection allows us to formulate the positivity conjecture, which encompasses both the Griffiths conjecture and the geometric properties of the manifold's Chern forms. Positivity of these forms is confirmed for all Chern forms up to degree 4, while an alternative approach to the degree-five conjecture of Griffiths is provided, which involves an extension and refinement of an earlier result of the first-named author. Our research is completed by the identification of a particular class of vector bundles, as defined by their closed and nonnegative Chern curvature, which satisfy both the universal push-forward formula and the conjecture of Griffiths. (The method of the last section was inspired by conversations with the late Professor M. Schneider.) Our work is the first to link the geometric properties of a manifold with the positivity of specific Chern forms, while our research also has implications for the study of K\"ahler manifolds

We analyzed a 7.22 day dataset from the Cyg X-1 Hard state Observations campaign and discovered notable changes in the X-ray spectrum and timing properties within the dataset, attributed to the approach of a dense wind patch. Corroborating evidence from UV and optical measurements confirmed four such events, although we only analyzed the X-ray data from the following stages: interstellar wind, approach of the patch at ~7.4 ks, peak absorption at ~7.8-7.9 ks, and post-spike periods at ~8.3-8.4 ks and ~9.3-9.4 ks. Notably, we observed a delay between the direct transmission through the wind and the delayed Compton upscattering, quantified as 2.7 ksec. When the wind density increases, delayed Compton upscattering becomes the primary origin of the observed delayed hard X-ray emission, explaining the intrinsic quasar nature of this delayed emission. We observed a notable, delayed soft X-ray flaring phenomenon on the order of 10-20% in different time intervals when the wind density increases, which can be attributed to localized heating caused by fast-moving clumps in the wind interacting with the quasar's radiation, although we couldn't precisely quantify this effect. We propose that these localized heating and cloud breakdowns due to radiation force feedback can collectively account for the observed rapid hard X-ray variability. The observed phenomenon suggests that these effects are more prevalent in Cyg X-1's hard state due to enhanced accretion rates, although observing such events in other BHB states was unsuccessful likely due to differences in wind properties between the different states, namely the presence of a larger inner wind cavity in the soft state. The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger is a highly plausible event, which could generate a burst of gravitational waves if the jet is directed at a nearby neutron star. We've investigated the characteristics of the jet-proximity effect observed in previously simulated scenarios of the postmerger accretion disks, focusing on a specific scenario where a black hole with a mass of 1.4 solar masses is involved. We've found that the disk's magnetic field plays a pivotal role in determining the amount of neutrino-driven tension in the disk. When the disk's magnetic field is relatively weak, the tension leads to a slingshot effect that ejects matter into space, primarily in the polar direction. We've observed that these ejecta have diverse properties - some disks experience initial ejections fueled by the disk's instability, while others are launched due to an uneven neutrino-natured sink. As a result, the jet properties show a significant variation depending on the simulation. We've observed that the resulting jets could potentially reach 1% of the speed of light within a thousand kilometers of the disk, which is consistent with previous studies. We've also discovered that the resulting ejecta could potentially reach tens of kilometers in size, resulting in a distinct optical and infrared glow if the jet is directed at a nearby neutron star. Depending on the angle of the jet, the resulting luminosity could be as high as 10^48 erg/s, which could potentially be detectable with a combination of ZTF, ASAS-SK, and DES. Our study suggests that in-order to accurately simulate the disk's magnetism, the entire disk should be studied with Garching-style resolution to allow for a slingshot effect and accurately simulate neutrino-natured and magnetically-driven ejecta. The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. Our software allows for the optimization of other systems with similar constraints, and can aid in determining performance metrics until experimental results are achieved. The model is made available for download at https://github.com/Norfair/CPA_NLO_Sim. Additionally, we present an inverse design example where we use a modified version of this software and the knock-out method to design a power amplifier, and then corroborate the results with experimental data from an actual device. Our approach leverages a knockout-empowered genetic algorithm to find the optimal design, and the accuracy of the CPA-NLO model is verified by comparing predicted and measured output spectra. The source code for this inverse design is available at https://github.com/Norfair/InverseCPANLODesign. The specific modification involves removing an unphysical penalty from the frequency-dependent fluence, which causes the optimal design to converge to an impractical state. By leveraging knowledge about the CPA-NLO model's behavior, we rectify this issue and obtain the optimal design, and the results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in high-power laser design. Implicit methods, such as detection layers, enable a model to identify out-of-distribution (OoD) samples without compromising its primary task performance. Various approaches have been attempted, such as distilling self-supervised learning or utilizing clustering and anomaly detection techniques. However, we found that the majority of these methods struggle to effectively detect OoD samples on real-world datasets. In contrast, a novel streamlit application demonstrates the potential of Distributional Gaussian Processes (DGP) layers, crafted by combining the principles of DGPs, which distribute data in a more explicit manner, and neural networks, which handle data implicitly. DGPs layers outperform other approaches on OoD detection tasks across multiple public datasets, according to our analysis. Additionally, we provide explicit-implicit data utilization as a trainable loss function, which contributes to the improvement of DGP layers. Users can find more information and interact with the model at https://dpd-gp-od.darwin-ai.tech/. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/DarwinAI/dpd-gp-od. In a breakthrough finding, our analysis reveals that DGP layers excel in variational Gaussian processes, which rely heavily on the choice of inducing points. By treating these inducing points as learnable parameters of an implicit distribution, we develop a training procedure that outperforms the conventional method. Quantum systems driven periodically experience heat build-up due to resonant excitations, typically leading to a random thermal state. In contrast, our findings reveal that an isolated system driven by a Gaussian phase-modulated light can develop a pure state composed of a coherent mixture of a few long-lived discrete modes, even when the driving is much slower than the characteristic time for relaxation. We attribute this phenomenon to the creation of a self-sustaining "firewheel" mechanism, where the driving enables a specific mode to transfer energy to other modes, and then enables a "spinning" of the accumulated energy back into the initial mode. Notably, our proposed approach may allow for the creation and maintenance of a Bose-Einstein condensate on a large scale using laser technology that is highly resistant to heat. Building upon this concept, we demonstrate that it is feasible to create a system of two interconnected "resonant lasers" separated by hundreds of thousands of atoms by leveraging the creation of a coherent state through heat-induced self-organization. We show that this binary system can be utilized to create an entangled state between two modes, as well as to generate heat-resistant modes that persist in systems with weak dissipation and dephasing. Ultimately, our approach may facilitate the attainment of a quantum many-body system that is robust against local errors. Although our initial analysis is confined to one-dimensional systems, we show that two-dimensional systems can be explored with similar driving strengths that are only one to two orders of magnitude larger than the one-dimensional counterparts. However, in two-dimensional systems, we anticipate the emergence of a rich interplay between Floquet states and quasi-long-range order, as well as the need to prevent the driving from creating excitations on the "edges" of the system. We propose that this can be accomplished through shaping the light with a pattern that has nodes along the perimeter, as this can protect the system from excitations for certain driving powers. Notably, the concept of using a "dark-state" for protection against excitations has a long history in quantum information, with recent findings indicating that this approach can be applied to a "dark-band" in quasi-periodic driving. However, our proposed approach is expected to provide additional insights into the light-driven quantum system, as well as to enable faster development of coherent states that are resistant to decoherence. Ultimately, our initial analysis points to a new direction for exploring quantum phases that are robust against decoherence. It is anticipated that this approach may allow for the creation and maintenance of quasi-long-range ordered states

The advent of Software Defined Networks (SDN) has simplified the management of network resources by decoupling it from the control plane, allowing programmers to focus on applications without navigating individual switches. Despite this, ensuring real-time communication across diverse SDN implementations can be challenging due to varying implementations and the complexity of network topology. To address this, our proposal leverages a unified fog computing platform to support the management of networks in a scalable manner. This platform circumscribes individual device capabilities, enabling fault-tolerant communication through the validation of multiple fault-recovery plans. Concurrently, it employs an online optimization algorithm to distribute resources efficiently, thereby reducing energy consumption and ensuring timely communication. The simultaneous execution of these operations fosters a balance between fault prevention and energy-efficient real-time communication. Through comprehensive evaluation, our proposal has demonstrated better performance in comparison to current best practices. This research was published in IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Computing. The source code is publicly available for review on our GitHub repository. This code can serve as a valuable resource for researchers exploring fog computing and network resource management. The proposed reason is a lack of fundamental understanding of text-generation objectives and how they impact the learning process during model training. A novel theoretical framework has been developed for generating text in dialogue, surpassing existing theories by allowing analysis of multiple goals inherent to text-generation. The new framework also provides theoretical guarantees for learning to generate effective task-oriented dialogue. The proposed algorithms based on this framework demonstrate superior performance in a learning-to-generate setting, significantly surpassing state-of-the-art methods in a simulated environment and achieving human-level diversity. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-residual for generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma = \BS(m,n)$. Further, our results demonstrate that a solvable group G possesses property $R_\infty$ if and only if every quotient of G by a nilpotent subgroup has $R_\infty$. Consequently, our work yields that $\Gamma = \BS(m,n)$ possesses property $R_\infty$ if and only if $n=1$ or $m=n^k$ for some natural number $k$. Additionally, our analysis extends to twisted conjugation invariants and the classification of nilpotent quotients of $\Gamma = \BS(m,n)$. Finally, our results also address the confluence of Quillen systems and its application to generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups. To accurately explain the progression of chemical reactions within extremely short timeframes, powerful lasers are used to stimulate and observe molecules. However, the intricate dynamics may be concealed in the resulting data, requiring sophisticated analysis that is also prone to interpretation errors. We propose a novel data processing approach that utilizes a comprehensive database of possible molecular behaviors and optimizes it using the results of these experiments. We developed a specialized software to create a cohesive model of molecular behavior from start to finish, and our example involving the breakdown of nitric oxide shows that this method is effective. This new technique has the potential to be more efficient if the molecule's behavior is already understood, as it can be based on a reduced set of possible scenarios, and it automatically detects any inconsistencies in the results. This technique has the potential to be a major breakthrough in the study of molecular reactions that are highly complex and take place rapidly. Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has intensified due to their potential for controlling the communication environment and combating multi-path interference effectively. Nonetheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems is significantly compromised by the increased risk of phase error resulting from hardware imperfections and reduced effective cyclic prefix (CP) length resulting from insufficient CP in original time-domain signals. To tackle these challenges, an advanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM)-based channel estimation method (eELM-CE) is introduced to provide accurate and reliable channel estimates. Building upon a model-driven framework, this approach leverages an efficient neural network that can handle various adverse factors including hardware nonlinearities and shortened CPs. The proposed method, eELM-CE, incorporates a conventional channel estimation algorithm as a pre-processing step to rectify its shortcomings in handling insufficiencies, demonstrating its superiority through numerical simulations showing a notable reduction in Mean Squared Error (MSE) of approximately 31.45% and 9.55% respectively when compared to ELM-CE. Furthermore, eELM-CE outperforms other conventional channel estimation methods by reducing the MSE by more than the reduction rate of ELM-CE in channels with non-linear hardware errors, in addition to significantly improving the rate loss resulting from shortened CPs. The proposed method's success lies in its ability to enhance the precision of channel estimates. The outcomes of the simulations demonstrate the resilience of eELM-CE to non-linear amplifier errors as well. Total model size for the proposed eELM-CE is largely independent of the number of training data, while the corresponding neural network for CE has a limited number of trainable parameters, while the trainable parameters for the neural network used in channel estimation occupy approximately 0.62% of the total parameters for original time-domain signals and 1.75% for shortened time-domain signals with 128 subcarriers at a given instance, indicating the feasibility of deployment. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus having far-reaching effects worldwide. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been widely adopted.  However, this technology poses significant concerns regarding user data security, leading to hesitation among the public to utilize contact tracing apps.  Despite the numerous proposals of anonymous contact tracing methods, there is a shortage of scientific research evaluating these proposals from a security standpoint.  To bridge this gap, this research assesses Coronav\'irus-SUS, an anonymous contact tracing app, focusing on user privacy through an in-depth analysis of store ratings, federal and state law protection, and the identification of potential vulnerabilities in the app's operation.  Furthermore, this research demonstrates an attack on the Coronav\'irus-SUS anonymization process, revealing that although the app provides anonymous identification using Android ID and Facebook account information, this information can be compromised through a combined cyber attack on the Android operating system and Facebook, enabling the disclosure of user data.  Consequently, this research emphasizes the importance of employing secure by design techniques to safeguard user privacy in contact tracing COVID-19 operations.  Moreover, this research proposes an evaluation framework to assess the security of contact tracing COVID-19 systems, which can inform and guide similar initiatives to ensure secure contact tracing.  Finally, considering the Coronav\'irus-SUS vulnerabilities an initial and elementary case, this research highlights the need for general best security practices in contact tracing COVID-19 to prevent the exposure of user data.

In order to tackle this inquiry, we introduce a broadened understanding of information utilization, which incorporates both distance metrics (propagation speed) and local data encoding methods (propagation waveforms). Applying these concepts to a neural network and a quantum system made up of spin-1/2 particles, we determine that the latter achieves higher information efficiency due to its capacity for more intricate encoding as demonstrated by examples in which local quantum operators exceed their neural counterparts. Nevertheless, it's also possible for neural systems to compensate for this disparity through enhanced propagator encoding as shown in an experiment involving a photonic quantum system and a neural network employing adaptive gradient-descent training. Such optimizations may offer an avenue for addressing the significant challenge of scaling quantum computers, thereby paving the way for potential applications in fields such as biology and medicine. Our approach to analyzing information utilization may also provide valuable insights for designing and implementing efficient computational methods within both classical and quantum systems. The study presented demonstrates the value in leveraging different perspectives on computational models in order to devise novel, adaptive algorithms for both neural networks and quantum systems, which are increasingly being used to facilitate data analysis and forecasting. Specifically, the proposed method could be applied to a variety of practical applications such as visual object recognition, weather forecasting, and others. The study presents a mathematical description of the proposed model, an analysis of its potential applications, and discusses the broader implications and future developments in this area. In particular, the study presents a mathematical description in the form of operator field equations that capture the key characteristics of information utilization in both neural and quantum systems. We introduce the concept of information propagation waveforms that facilitate more intricate encoding and discuss the role of global propagators, which are central to both neural and quantum systems. This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of products involving the solar irradiance function, as defined by ASTM standards, and user-defined smooth functions. The method's ability to produce accurate results with minimal evaluations is particularly beneficial due to the solar irradiance function's non-smooth, highly oscillatory nature. The accompanying Julia software facilitates the computation of the desired quadrature rules through a scalable approach enabling the computation of rules for any degree of quadrature via the Nevalmaa method, and solving the associated algebraic eigenvalue problem using eigenvalue decomposition or the QR algorithm. Three distinct solutions are presented, each catering to a distinct scenario: (I) the general case involving an arbitrary degree and degree-bound polynomial solar irradiance function; (II) the case of degree-one functions; (III) the case of functions whose products with the solar irradiance are constant. The software implements two solutions for case (I), which demands the resolution of a real, tridiagonal generalised eigenvalue problem. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. This phenomenon, studied across ten languages spanning nine countries, reveals inconsistent connections between a word's meaning and its grammatical gender, yet demonstrates a notable, albeit uneven link regardless of a word's intended gender. Compared to monoseismic languages, inanimate objects in polysynthetic languages tend to have more tenuous associations with their assigned gender. This peculiarity raises intriguing questions about the role of linguistics in shaping our understanding of the non-human world and its potential impact on artificial intelligence's representation of language. An examination of how this impact influences artificial intelligence's representation of inanimate objects in polysynthetic languages is particularly noteworthy. Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting estimated time of arrival. Our method involves extracting multiple feature sets - node flow characteristics, segment-based attributes, and similarity-based properties, which we used to train a model based on decision trees with gradient boosting. Our results demonstrate exceptional predictive capabilities across three cities - London, Madrid, and Melbourne - and even surpass some graph neural network-based approaches in estimating travel times. Our source code is available at https://github.com/c-lyu/Similarity-based-Traffic-Forecasting.

Secondly, it is equipped with graphical processing units (GPUs) which facilitate data processing at relatively low computational costs. REALTA successfully detected two transient events: the Solar flare 20220112T08:35:00 and the Pulsar 1929-05A flux calibration. Images were generated with the lofarCDRL software at a rate of $0.1^{\circ} \times \text{sec}^{-1} \times \delta t_{\text{integration}}$. REALTA also applied a real-time analysis approach with the lofarCDRL software at a rate of $1^{\circ} \text{per minute} \times \text{intervals of 1 minute}$ to discover a radio transient event associated with the UGC 12158 galaxy. This program is set to utilize the lofarCDRL software at a rate of $8^{\circ} \text{per minute} \times \text{intervals of 1 minute}$.

Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the research community due to its various potential uses. A significant feature of commercial plenoptic cameras, it captures the spatial and angular properties of light in a single exposure. However, the capture structure of plenoptic cameras necessitates high data storage and transmission costs, limiting practical applications. Recent advancements in computational optics have led to the development of novel image-based light field compression methods. Despite their potential, these methods typically require substantial processing capabilities, causing processing delays during real-time communication. This research presents a practical image-based compression solution, suitable for both live previews and real-time transmissions. A key component of this framework is a model that predicts viewing angles based on spatial images and local disparity information, enabling efficient evaluation of virtual views. This evaluation is then leveraged by a texture-encoded block-based light field compression method that offers high quality and low bit rates, achieving compression without significant processing delays. The proposed solution's quality and efficiency are demonstrated through extensive evaluation on four standard light field datasets, showcasing its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of compression ratio and peak signal-to-noise ratio. Notably, it successfully compressed a 4K x 4K light field to just 12 megabytes while maintaining near-lossless image quality. This practical solution has the potential to expand the scope of light field applications to real-time communications. Further analysis of the method's structure suggests numerous potential avenues for further research, including structured encoding and other optimization techniques. The source code for this framework has been made available online for the research community.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each approach excels and falls short. This study combines 
the benefits of these two frameworks through the development of a semi-interactive 
mechanism that constructs a non-interactive framework but unites document embedding 
with multiple associated queries in parallel, thus enabling interactive-style cross-lingual 
feature acquisition. By leveraging the word embeddings and a minimal character-ordering 
operation, we propose a novel character-based approach that surpasses current standards in 
cross-lingual IR and showcases state-of-the-art performance on all evaluated datasets. Our 
method also stretches the boundaries of current best practices, incorporating substantial 
English text for training and expanding the scope of multilingual datasets to 60 languages.

In order to mitigate this problem, previous solutions employed practical techniques, such as weight clipping and gradient penalty, to restrict the capabilities of the discriminator. In this work, a more systematic approach is presented as an alternative to tackle this problem by adopting a relation network for the discriminator, which is proven to be more effective and flexible. However, real-world datasets like ImageNet are marked by significant disparities between real and fake images, prompting the integration of triplet loss to broaden the discriminator's understanding of image variations. In this research, triplet loss is incorporated into the relation network-based GAN framework, offering superior results on various benchmark datasets, specifically ImageNet and CelebA, while providing a more theoretical justification for this fusion. Furthermore, this technique is applied to the state-of-the-art StyleGAN2 model and produces outstanding results on the ImageNet dataset, representing a notable improvement of over 1.0 in FID score. The proposed method is expected to contribute to the production of high-quality, diverse, and semantic images, particularly in the fields of computer vision and generative modeling. A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our approach categorizes time into two distinct frameworks: reference frames and quantum frames. Reference frames serve as a basis for establishing a universal phase reference, allowing us to achieve TF-QKD without the use of phase locking. Through data post-processing and an efficient fast Fourier transform-based algorithm, the phase reference can be reconciled efficiently. As a result, TF-QKD without phase locking is made feasible over a wide range of distances on standard optical fibers. At a distance of 50 kilometers, our system is able to achieve a secret key rate of 1.27 megabits per second. Moreover, our approach enables repeater-based TF-QKD without phase locking at a distance of 500 kilometers, producing a secret key rate of 1.05 megabits per second. Our experiments validate the efficiency of this method and provide secure quantum communication across various channels, including a single fiber and multiple fibers with different loss levels. Furthermore, our approach enables TF-QKD without phase locking over a long distance of 1500 kilometers via a fiber network consisting of multiple fibers with diverse loss levels, producing a secret key rate of 1.05 megabits per second. This method offers new possibilities for long-distance quantum key distribution using TF-QKD as a quantum channel in quantum communication networks. In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the Fock space over $C^b(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for a specific number of dimensions, focusing on the 'bounded symbol' class. We establish the equivalence of three representations of Toeplitz algebras: classical, commutative, and sample-wise. However, this equivalence does not exist for all Toeplitz algebras with symbols in $C^b(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Additionally, in the case of one dimension ($d=1$), we analyze the weighted Fock space, denoted as $F^2_d(\mathbb{R})$, and derives a non-trivial, closed ideal within the Toeplitz algebra of bounded symbols, using the symbol $e^{\frac{x^2}{1-x^2}}$. Furthermore, in the Bergman plane over $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{R}$), we find that the Toeplitz algebra of bounded symbols fails to contain a particular universal representation. Moreover, in the case of odd dimensions ($d=2m$, where $m$ is a positive integer), we identify the Toeplitz algebra of bounded symbols as the closure of the algebra consisting of Toeplitz operators with polynomial symbols, valid for $m\geq 2$. However, for $m=1$, we find that this statement does not hold true. Lastly, in the setting of the weighted Bergman spaces over $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R})$, we identify the Toeplitz algebras of symbols in $C^b(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for specific weights, but find that the equivalence of representations does not exist for an arbitrary weight. Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been proposed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small number of base categories used for training. To mitigate this constraint, we present a technique to automatically produce pseudo annotations of diverse objects using image-caption pairs and pre-trained vision-language models. This technique then employs these pseudo labels for training object detectors, leading to notable improvements in object detection accuracy on various benchmarks. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object detectors by significant margins, with performance boosts of up to 8% AP on the COCO novel category dataset and others. Code implementing this method is available for download on the GitHub repository 'PB-OVD'. Our research demonstrates that, without additional data, object detectors can be trained on diverse object categories by leveraging pre-trained vision-language models and image-caption pairs through the proposed PB-OVD technique. This advancement has the potential to further enhance the accuracy of object detectors through larger, artificially created training data. Furthermore, our proposed PB-OVD technique can be combined with other data augmentation techniques to train high-accuracy object detectors on under-explored environments with minimal supervision. Our research expands the possibilities of open-vocabulary object detection without relying on time-consuming data preparation processes. Analysis of our results reveals that our proposed PB-OVD technique is superior to existing methods, leading to significant improvements in object detection accuracy. Importantly, our approach is scalable, as demonstrated by its application to various challenging datasets, including the NovoBD-COCO dataset and others. This work presents a comprehensive investigation of open-vocabulary object detection, with a detailed examination of its performance on 10 different datasets. Our object detection evaluation code is available on the GitHub repository 'PB-OVD'. Our research aims to increase our understanding of open-vocabulary object detection, with a thorough analysis of this topic. To further advance this area, our code is available for download on the GitHub repository 'PB-OVD'. Our research is led by Manoj Changpury, a postdoctoral researcher, along with co-authors Saptarishi Grover, Abhishek Das, and Alan S. Yu. This work presents a novel technique, 'PB-OVD', for training object detectors without supervision, utilizing pre-existing image-data and vision-language models.

A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function applications. Moreover, their straightforward architecture allows for seamless processing of diverse modalities such as images, videos, and text. Due to their strengths, Transformer models have shown promising results in various computer vision tasks, leading to a growing interest in this area. This review aims to provide an in-depth overview of the current state of Transformer models in computer vision, starting with an introduction to key concepts behind their success, including attention mechanisms, their applications, and parallel processing. We then delve into pioneering works in image classification, object detection, segmentation, and other related tasks, followed by an analysis of the current state of research in this field, culminating in a discussion of potential future directions and challenges. Along the way, we identify notable benchmarks and datasets that have facilitated progress in this area. Due to the breadth of topics involved, this review operates under a slight bias toward the perspectives of computer vision experts. Notably, we refrain from delving into comprehensive surveys of natural language processing domains. The primary goal of this review is to provide an in-depth understanding of the applications of Transformer models in computer vision, including a comprehensive list of related works at the end of this document. Although some aspects of computer vision have already adopted Transformer models, this review is positioned as a general overview rather than a comprehensive guide for specialists in specific subfields. In addition, we do not aim to provide an exhaustive review of the current state of the art; instead, we strive to offer insightful discussion and reflection on the topics discussed. Mortality forecasting models, which use macroeconomic and demographic factors to predict death rates, have been successful but have overlooked the inherent non-stationarity in these rates. This oversight means that models relying on a constant structure are inadequate, as death rates exhibit significant fluctuations over time. In our research, we demonstrate that employing a factor model with time-varying loadings effectively addresses this issue, resulting in a more accurate prediction of changing mortality rates. We also introduce a novel method for estimating time-varying loadings, which is then applied to forecast Italian and French mortality rates, yielding superior results compared to existing models. Crucially, incorporating a prior distribution based on the average loading over historical periods significantly improves the predictive power of these models. This finding highlights the importance of incorporating temporal characteristics, ultimately leading to a notable improvement in forecasting mortality rates. We estimate that models with time-varying loadings can reduce MEPE by 30% and decrease MSE by 40% in comparison to models with constant loadings. Furthermore, the inclusion of a prior distribution yields an additional 60% improvement in efficiency (MSE reduction) and 25% improvement in efficiency (MEPE reduction) respectively. We conclude that factor-based models with time-varying loadings, accompanied by the incorporation of a prior distribution, emerge as the most effective mortality forecasting approaches. We also introduce a new method for forecasting the dynamics of factor loadings that, in combination with these models, results in substantially improved forecasting performance. In particular, models with time-varying loadings accompanied by a prior distribution and autonomous evolution of factor dynamics (i.e. models that predict both mortality rates and the dynamics of factor loadings) result in a 100% improvement in efficiency (MSE reduction) and 100% improvement in efficiency (MEPE reduction) respectively in comparison to models that only predict mortality rates. Moreover, models that predict both mortality rates and the dynamics of factor dynamics exhibit relatively small losses in terms of MEPE when compared to models that only predict mortality rates, specifically losses of about 1% and 3%. Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a popular strategy. However, due to interference from other models, there is often a poor correlation between predicted accuracy and actual performance of the child models. This study investigates the cause of interference by comparing how similar the effects are of training on one model with how similar the effects are of training on different models. It proposes a new method called cross-recurrent interference estimation that uses the effects of one model to estimate the interference caused by other models. This method is able to significantly reduce the difference between predicted and actual performance. Additionally, a new approach called batch-wise cross-recurrent interference estimation is proposed, which predicts the interference caused by groups of models rather than individual models. This method further improves the correlation between predicted and actual performance. Experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in reducing the cost of NAS. For instance, without any data from the target dataset, our approach allows the top model to be trained on 87% fewer data samples compared to the top model trained without any NAS. Furthermore, without any data from the target dataset, our method allows the top model to have a valuation score that is within 4.53% of the valuation score of the top model trained using Bayesian optimization with 131k samples from the target dataset. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of cross-recurrent interference estimation in reducing the cost of neural architecture search. Several variants of this method are also evaluated and compared, and guidelines are provided to help users choose the most suitable variant based on the results of an offline evaluation phase. In particular, cross-recurrent interference estimation is evaluated in three different offline environments: random, Bayesian optimization, and gradient-based architectures. Experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of each environment, and the most suitable variant is chosen based on the results of an offline evaluation phase. Finally, the main ideas of this research are evaluated through a discussion of related work and suggestions for potential future research directions. The evaluation demonstrates that our approach can significantly improve the correlation between predicted and actual performance, and these improvements have the potential to be sustained even when training is extended to several epochs. Moreover, our approach can be easily extended to other optimization methods such as evolutionary algorithms, and the offline evaluation phase can provide valuable guidance on the most suitable variation to use in each case. These are promising research directions that could lead to even better results than what has been achieved so far, and they could also be used in other areas of application. Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured with temporal characteristics like location, spread, and correlation. These properties can be used for both descriptive and diagnostic purposes, such as diagnosing patients with diseases or examining weather conditions. In the case of pathological data, time-based features like duration and count are relevant. However, when dealing with large datasets, manually extracting these features is impractical due to the labor-intensive process involved. This limitation is compounded by the limited advanced time series analysis capabilities available in existing R packages. To address these challenges, we introduce a unified framework that provides users with a seamless and efficient experience, automatically detecting events, extracting key features, and performing statistical analysis. This solution leverages popular tools like shazoo and deepblue. Our comprehensive approach is divided into three phases: detection, extraction, and analysis, allowing users to customize their approach by selecting the suitable R methods for their specific needs. Additionally, we have developed an R package called theft to offer a set of algorithms for automatic event detection and feature calculation. To showcase the effectiveness of our method, we have performed a comparative analysis using data from the DeepBlue project. Using a dataset from the GeoLife project, we have demonstrated that our approach is capable of producing reliable results with minimal variance. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that by combining temporal characteristics with geographical information, we can conduct spatial analyses at a deeper level. For instance, we have conducted a spatial correlation analysis, predicted chronic conditions, and examined the self-recovery process of patients. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating temporal factors into spatial analysis, and the resulting models have shown improved accuracy. The related R code and data are publicly available through the following repositories: https://github.com/feature-based-analysis/geolife-chronic-risk-assessment and https://github.com/feature-based-analysis/geolife-spatial-risk-assessment. To facilitate the reproduction of these results, we have employed the theft package, which includes the following components: GEOFIL RUTILS, GEOFIL, and geolife. We have provided the corresponding installation commands and data retrieval methods. Our research aims to contribute to the advancement of feature-based analysis by showcasing the automatic detection of events and subsequent extraction of key features using the theft package, and to demonstrate the development of predictive models through deep learning. Human-assisted Translation Verification via Reranking aims to maintain translation quality by reassessing existing translations. In order to rerevaluate, we first need to calculate a translation reliability score based on similarities between a baseline translation and optimal equivalents, which is typically done in a supervised environment. However, when working without a perfect reference, as commonly seen in domain adaptation, we must adopt a different method. This paper introduces a new approach that relies on a Bayesian statistical model to develop a reliable translation metric that resists domain shifts. Furthermore, we propose an unbiased estimator to avoid relying on questionable data. Experimental outcomes confirm our proposed model's ability to resist changing environments and surpass state-of-the-art benchmarks in a translation task. It's worth noting that our proposed model can also be applied to other problems where confidence measures are necessary. An accompanying repository containing all the necessary data, code, and datasets can be found at https://github.com/jaysell/TransBayes. An implementation in more advanced frameworks can be found at https://github.com/allenai/pari, with specific guidance outlined in the original research paper.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Research indicates that the expected value of these tickets in an initial model increases over time, but no study has explored the dynamics of this process or how to identify the best moment to initiate training. We examine the effectiveness of various techniques for determining when to start training the ticket and find that using the expected return after each training epoch at random achieves better results than starting at any fixed epoch. Additionally, the best time to initiate training is average model performance epoch and we explain this outcome statistically. Furthermore, choosing which tickets to train is another critical factor, and selecting the ones with the highest return at random is more effective than using the gradient-based method. Our findings also suggest that the best time to buy a ticket is when the return starts to decline, and we explain this empirically. Overall, our study advances the understanding of the ticket dynamics by providing a model-agnostic statistical approach that can replicate these results statistically, and may lead to improved outcomes in future studies. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on creating a model-simulation-optimization framework for a single-limbed robot to navigate a deformable terrain. A simplified model for a single-limbed hopper was developed, incorporating force distribution, spring stiffness, and dampening. This model also included a simulation component, where the shape of the deformed terrain and the position of contact points were calculated using the finite element method. Our results show that varying terrain shape and boundary constraints have a significant impact on the optimisation process. Due to the non-convex nature of this problem, it was transformed into a convex form using a penalty method with a barrier term. This allowed the problem to be solved using an iterative algorithm with a pre-defined penalty parameter, and we demonstrated the convergence of this method. Our results also show that this method results in a local minimum that approaches the optimal solution as the penalty parameter increases. Finally, we compared the performance of our proposed framework with existing control strategies, including pre-planned trajectories and ramp-like motions, and found that our method outperforms these approaches when navigating uneven terrain. This outperformance was measured by reducing the actuation work required to overcome the deformable terrain. This research showcases an effective model-simulation-optimization framework for legged robots to navigate deformable terrain, and our proposed penalty method achieves local convergence without resorting to approximation methods or relaxation. Our results also show that our model can efficiently generate stable and robust open-loop motions for hopper-type robots. This research can be further developed by exploring the real-time implementation of this method to enable agile and efficient deformable terrain navigation. Such a real-time implementation could significantly enhance the capabilities of legged robots in various applications. Our proposed framework can be adapted for other robots if a suitable replacement for the FEM-based contact model is found. The exploration of quantum machine learning has demonstrated the potential for
groundbreaking insights in both areas of research. Experimental findings indicate
that quantum computers could significantly outperform traditional machines in
certain machine learning tasks, although they may also be susceptible to
adversarial threats. These threats involve introducing small, manipulative
distortions to legitimate data that can lead a completed trained model to
predictive errors. This study is the first to uncover examples of these
threats—both universal and targeted—effective against quantum neural network
classifiers, regardless of the origin or structure of the data being processed.
Moreover, our results reveal that quantum computers may have an advantage over
classical systems in generating these adversarial examples, which could also be
utilized for innovative applications such as universal amplifiers and perturbation
sensitive algorithms. These findings hold great significance for the growing
quantum computing applications and underscore the necessity for robust models in
quantum machine learning. They also raise new questions and possibilities for
quantum-based anomaly detection and universal applications in machine learning.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on ray tracing and physical wave propagation laws, provide precise predictions but require significant computational resources and can only utilize traditional geographical data. In this article, a groundbreaking approach to radio propagation modeling using deep neural networks is presented, demonstrating substantial performance gains over conventional methods. Additionally, this study sets the groundwork for data-driven modeling of radio propagation, paving the way for future research to leverage diverse, fine-grained data. A novel approach to generating open-source simulation data via game engine technology is also described. This data is then utilized to train a convolutional neural network, allowing for the generation of a portable propagation model. Two variants of this model were developed, one designed for indoor and the other for combined indoor/outdoor use. The proposed models were evaluated on a vast dataset covering 30 nations and 526 cities. In comparison to the widely-used umi propagation model, our results show a marked decrease in absolute error rates - the indoor model demonstrated a nearly 7-fold reduction in median error, and the combined model exhibited a reduction of up to 9-fold. Moreover, a significant performance boost of up to 30% was observed in numerical computation time. A comprehensive study involving numerical computation time analysis and theoretical performance is provided to validate the model's efficacy. A detailed model evaluation and analysis, complete with code and data resources, are made accessible on GitHub. The deep neural network model's high precision, portability, and computational efficiency have the potential to significantly contribute to future research and development in mobile networks. Furthermore, it may find practical applications in real-time propagation modeling, allowing it to be deployed as a web or cloud-based service. The model's current combined variant can be directly used for indoor scenarios, highlighting its versatility. Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs associated with meeting demand. Through case studies involving capital-intensive wind power in three regional systems, our analysis reveals that model sensitivity varies greatly, even within the same power system, depending on the location of additional capacity. Additionally, our results suggest that modeling technical constraints is more critical than employing non-linear optimization for models evaluating large-scale resource integration. Ultimately, this framework can be utilized to refine power system expansion planning models and accurately estimate the costs associated with integrating renewable resources. By identifying areas of high model sensitivity, decision-makers can focus efforts on modifying parameters or adding new variables, particularly in areas corresponding to local maxima, thus enhancing the precision of power system expansion planning. Additionally, our approach demotes the importance of theoretical model evaluations in favor of testing and validation. When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for change, described using everyday language and involving relevant technical terms. The task requires identifying key terms related to the request's technical context, allowing developers to locate relevant sections in the source code and apply the desired changes. Unfortunately, developers often struggle to craft effective search terms for their tasks. This paper presents a new approach, STRICT, which uses machine learning and information retrieval to automatically determine suitable search terms based on a change request's description. The proposed method leverages two techniques: TextRank and POSRank, to analyze the request and assess the importance of specific terms based on their relationships and contextual connections. Experimental results on a dataset comprising 1,939 requests from eight systems reveal that STRICT outperforms baseline search terms in approximately 52-62.9% of cases, with a top-notch variant achieving even higher accuracy of 60% or more in around 51-61.5% of cases. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that using text summarizers can enhance the search results, with a notable improvement of up to 4% when employing this additional feature. The study also highlights areas for improving the overall performance of the STRICT approach. The proposed method was compared with the DMS tool in an experimental study, which is still in progress. Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized, is linked to the formation of micro-cracks within the gel structure, which can either repair or remain intact after the vibrations cease. Moreover, ultrasonic waves significantly reduce the gels' strength against external forces and expedite their transition into a liquid state under stress. Our study paves the way for the manipulation of gel properties and flow behaviors through ultrasonic manipulation, offering exciting avenues for future modeling and exploration of rheo-acoustic materials. This research has been published in the journal Nature Materials. A related data paper has been uploaded to http://doi.org/10.21973/YMQH41. Further simulation data is hosted at https://andreaskrouphal.github.io/rheoacousticgels. The Institute of Materials for the Future's website provides additional information and results. The Institute of Materials for the Future is a research and training center focused on the intersection of materials science with artificial intelligence and quantum simulation. Our work is expected to lead to future applications in soft matter and flow phenomena, which can be modeled and explored using advanced simulation methods. This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then generalized to encompass even sequences as well. By proving the conjecture's validity for this broader class of sequences, it ultimately leads to a proof of the original conjecture. The method employed in this research showcases the underlying sequence patterns in a different light. By representing sequences using functions defined by combinations of exponentiation and addition, the argument relies on evaluating how these functions interact at even and odd positions within the sequences. The key insight lies in representing numbers that are multiples of 2 using an additional variable, represented as $2^x$, and examining how this formulation affects the behavior of sequences during the Collatz process. The method also makes it possible to determine the starting point of odd sequences given their indices in the set of odd sequences or vice versa for sequences with an even starting point. By leveraging this insight, the research paper establishes a bijection between certain even and odd sequences. The method also enables describing which odd sequences have a specific remainder when divided by 2 and allows for a generalization of this approach. The work further includes a representation of natural numbers using functions defined by combinations of exponentiation, addition, and multiplication. The researchers use this representation to analyze the properties of sequences with specific properties, which is then applied to prove the conjecture. The method also leads to a generalized form of the conjecture. The proof of the conjecture relies on evaluating how numbers change during the Collatz process by expressing them using the identified functions. By proving that numbers in certain sequences with a starting value of 2^k do not exceed 2^(k+1), the researchers extend this finding to sequences with a starting value of 2^(k-1). By considering the properties of even sequences, the researchers establish that even sequences with a starting value of 2^m do not exceed 2^(m+1), which leads to a similar result for sequences with a starting value of 2^(m-1). Ultimately, the researchers combine these results to prove that even sequences do not exceed 2^(k-1) and demonstrate that this result can be generalized for sequences with a starting value of 2^(p-2), where p is an odd prime number. To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field or subfield, accurate document categorization is crucial. Despite the importance of this task, current classification methods may not effectively account for the unique characteristics of each field. A recent approach, known as Mathematical Entity Linking, enables the identification of fundamental concepts within scientific documents but often falls short in providing comprehensive categorization. To address this limitation, a novel technique is presented that integrates MEAL, an existing tool, to support full text categorization across various subjects. This proposed method, titled MEAL-CAT, was evaluated utilizing a dataset comprising multiple disciplines and was found to outperform established document classification methods, including those leveraging external informatics and those based on existing categorization frameworks. Furthermore, a user study revealed that MEAL-CAT's errors were largely linked to subject areas in which MEAL itself underperformed. Both MEAL-CAT's performance and MEAL's capabilities offer potential solutions for categorization challenges in fields such as Mathematics and Computer Science where it demonstrated relative strength. Additionally, MEAL-CAT provides a highly customizable system, allowing for the use of MEAL or any other mathematical entity linking model to support both document categorization and, to a limited extent, topic modeling. Ultimately, MEAL-CAT's success suggests the value of incorporating domain-specific features, like MEAL, to enhance document classification. In these domains, MEAL-CAT's performance surpasses that of existing models, even when they have access to complete informatics.

highly unreliable in assessing human quality and limit the variety of generated
summaries. To overcome these limitations, a novel evaluation metric called
SummScore has been developed. This innovative approach utilizes a CrossEncoder
to compare the semantic meaning of original text and summaries, thus preventing

assess summaries written by humans or generated by various models across
various domains, providing a comprehensive assessment of summary quality.

including both human assessment and automated evaluation methods. Furthermore, in
human evaluations, it is observed that high-performing automated summaries, as
evaluated by SummScore, frequently exhibit coherency, preciseness, and
variety. To facilitate wider adoption, the SummScore is made available for
public use. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/allenai/SummScore,

A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented. This type of correlation is common in fields such as optics and seismic analysis, but the additional dimension creates an inverse problem bottleneck as the number of variables quadratically increases. Our solution simplifies this by only solving for the diagonal of the signal matrix, where variables increase linearly. This is made possible through a specialized "noise absorber" that filters data that does not provide signal information. This results in a linear solution at a similar cost to linear measurements. Our theoretical findings confirm exact signal recovery under clean data conditions, with zero false positives even at noisy levels, as well as an improved signal recovery rate proportional to the number of data points. Numerical simulations validate our claims. This method can also be used for parameter estimation in fields like optics. Our signal recovery algorithm has been implemented in a new MATLAB package, MEQ, whose source code is publicly accessible.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted in 1965, this scale, denoted as $r^*_{\rm{B}}$, depends solely on the Brunt-V\"{a}is\"{a}l\"{a} body force, not the Reynolds number or any other flow characteristics. This process is identified as an energy-loss mechanism resembling the pre-resonant enhancement observed in supersonic rotors producing sound. We hypothesize that in the absence of determining scales, thermal fluctuations may generally disrupt and slow down turbulent decay, although their impact on the turbulent energy transfer process remains unclear. Conversely, when determining scales are present, as in mechanical flows or certain biological systems, $r^*_{\rm{B}}$ no longer sets the scale for energy exchange. Instead, it falls within the inner turbulence, an area defined by the smallest critical or determining scale, and it resides in a second interaction zone, an area where external and internal fluctuations are hybridized. Thus, when determining scales are present, thermal fluctuations only need to be considered when the external flow characteristics and determinate scales are known. Furthermore, as illustrated in two examples, thermal fluctuations may induce an apparent anisotropy due to an irregularly positioned observation sphere, which disrupts and distorts the isotropic turbulence in the dissipation range. These concepts are also applied to understanding fetal fluid turbulence during pregnancy.

This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. H-STREAM's micro-services dynamically adjust their techniques according to the stream producers, data velocity, and available processing resources to ensure seamless online processing and delivery to users, including real-time data visualization on demand. H-STREAM offers micro-services for stream aggregation, query execution, and data storage using in-memory and out-of-memory data repositories. Furthermore, a distributed data lake is used for long-term data archiving and analysis. In this study, we elaborate on H-STREAM's architecture, its functionality in handling stream and data processing pipelines, and demonstrate its capabilities through various evaluation experiments using Big Data streams. We also discuss the implications of online micro-service composition for real-time data analysis and visualization across multiple resource nodes. Finally, we identify areas for further development and expansion beyond current limitations. The source code for H-STREAM is openly available on GitHub, facilitating its adoption and adaptation by researchers and practitioners. Additionally, a related demonstration is showcased at the present conference.
