To address the challenge of reducing large datasets, we develop a method for a unified clustering approach using a functor based on a category with hierarchical structures that account for for overlap between clusters. Our method integrates existing functors to incorporate multiple metrics into the clustering process. The resulting clustering is represented by a functor from the category of partial orders to the category of topological spaces, whose preimages under the generic maps yield the desired partition and the overlaps between clusters. In particular, we apply this framework to the study of continua using a functor based on the category of maps with domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Additionally, we analyze the computational efficiency of our method and demonstrate its application with an example involving the M\"{o}bius strip. The implementation of our method is provided in the Python package `functor_clustering`. Our experimental results demonstrate that the computational time scales linearly with the number of data points when using our optimized algorithm. The Python package `functor_clustering` is available for download at the provided URL. Our method offers several benefits, including the ability to integrate disparate data sets, the capacity for concurrent computation, and the ability to leverage domain-specific structures. The properties of overlap and linearity within our method enable the execution of hierarchical clustering on the entire M\"{o}bius strip and the surface of T4, a torus served by the M\"{o}bius band functor. However, the approach is incapable of handling hierarchical clustering in the case of intersecting clusters. To address this limitation, we are exploring the development of a revised functor with overlapping structures that incorporates the concept of intervals, previously implemented in the clustering of T4. With the proposed modification, our method is capable of handling hierarchical clustering in the presence of intersecting clusters. The Python package `functor_clustering` includes the implementation of our method for both overlapping and non-overlapping structures. The provided code is compatible with GPUs but does not take full advantage of their capabilities. A more optimized version of the code is available in the README file of the repository. The primary constraint of our method is its reliance on a comprehensive dataset, making it infeasible for learning from sparse data. To address this limitation, we are investigating the development of a revised functor based on the concept of intervals, which is applicable even in the presence of sparse data. The Python package `functor_clustering` includes the implementation of our method for both overlapping and non-overlapping structures. A more optimized version of the code is available in the README

Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data from partially observed tensors by leveraging their inherent low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video frames, identifying tensors with missing data can be uncertain and data quality may vary due to noise, occlusion, or other distortions. Existing approaches often rely on rigid patch-based low-rank assumptions, which do not account for potential errors in identifying complete tensors or missing data. Furthermore, these methods typically require full data availability and may compromise on model robustness for improved recovery performance. To address these limitations, a novel streaming tensor completion approach is proposed, utilizing a learned framework that adapts to the underlying low-rank structure of tensors for visual data recovery. This approach is based on a Patch Tracking Mechanism, which monitors and adjusts the inner low-rank component of tensors in response to changes, while maintaining an outer non-low-rank component that comprises anomalies and outlying patches identified through patch tracking. These anomalies are leveraged to estimate the missing data, while the patch tracking mechanism adjusts and refines the detected low-rank structure. By leveraging a streaming Random Neural Network, the approach ensures robust recovery performance even in the presence of disturbances. Experimental results demonstrate the approach's efficacy compared to state-of-the-art tensor recovery methods using realistic datasets such as NTURKDE-Video, VideoDeform, and 50Salient. Notably, the approach achieves superior performance under artificial disturbance conditions and shows promise for further development in tensor-based visual data recovery applications. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenDongD/MuLTC. A related supplement is provided at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7371292.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing tasks, whereas humans utilize more complex attributes. Our investigation reveals that when applying extreme transformations to images, ANNs struggle and humans excel. We focused on one specific transformation - highly elastic image distortions. Our distortion method was developed to test both regions of interest and scene understanding in images. Our results indicate that both human and ANN performance decline with increasing distortion levels for object recognition tasks. However, in contrast to the ANNs, our human subjects demonstrate remarkable resilience to such transformations and can identify images with much higher distortion levels. Our investigation also explores the limits of both human and ANN performance for image transformation tasks. Our findings demonstrate that both human and ANN accuracy strongly correlates with the level of distortion but at varying points of failure. Our research sheds light on the unique strengths and weaknesses of both human vision and ANNs, particularly through the application of extreme image transformation analysis. Our work provides new insights for understanding both equivalent and disparate visual processing mechanisms in humans and machines. Our research is supported by experimental results and mathematical models. Our findings are set to inspire the development of more resilient ANNs and contribute to the evaluation of their performance in challenging situations. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment with untrained examples by prompting them with reviews paired with labels such as "loving" or "hate." However, this learning process is hindered by two primary obstacles. Firstly, selecting an optimal set of training data is challenging. Secondly, translating natural language into a format understandable by these models is a labor-intensive process, accompanied by significant variability in performance depending on the crafted prompts. To overcome these challenges, we established a Meta-prompt dataset, allowing users to fine-tune GPT-3 on our collection. This is comprised of prompts that provide analogous information for any given dataset. Furthermore, we established a Meta-dataset, consisting of "training" examples, each originating from disparate datasets. By using these Meta-datasets, users can ensure that their model is optimized for classifying "hate" in a given review by designing the prompt and selecting the dataset, then fine-tuning GPT-3 with the Meta-dataset associated with "hate." Consequently, users can attain a significant performance boost when comparing it to models trained on individual datasets or using GPT-3's default prompts. Extensive evaluation reveals that our proposed Meta-prompt dataset is highly versatile, as it outperforms competitive approaches on classification tasks across eight distinct datasets. Furthermore, we have made our Meta-prompt dataset available for download at https://github.com/earsk/Meta-prompt. Additionally, we have developed Web-CLIP, a large-scale dataset comprising 21 challenging classification tasks and accompanying prompts, as well as the collection of GPT-3 snapshots. This resource, available at https://github.com/earsk/Web-CLIP, allowed us to attain state-of-the-art results on two public datasets, namely the Stanford Sentiment Tree Bank and the 8-way Character Emotion Datasets, through fine-tuning, accompanied by a performance boost of over 100% for the pre-trained models. Ultimately, our proposed framework, deemed "meta-tuning," facilitates an efficient and adaptable method for adapting pre-trained models to new classification tasks. We illustrate this through our collection of GPT-3 snapshots and the Meta-prompt dataset, allowing users to fine-tune multiple models, as well as to forecast the performance of these models, all while reducing computation costs. Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers employ sequence-to-sequence models, built upon vast language datasets pre-trained on a massive scale of text. Building on these advancements, researchers have explored redefining sequence-to-sequence models using natural language generation frameworks, yielding notable gains. However, prior naturalization efforts were hindered by increased model complexity and higher training costs. Our research focuses on taking a different approach: implementing a naturalized parser with a conditional generator, allowing for joint training within a unified framework, thus enhancing efficiency and effectiveness. This approach makes semantic parsing possible with significantly reduced large-scale language pre-training costs and more competitive results. The experiments demonstrate that our method can achieve this goal by leveraging a very limited amount of domain-specific training data, while also fine-tuning from a much smaller general corpus. The results show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, including those that incorporate pre-trained GPT-2 on a corpus of approximately 1 GB, mined with a bi-directional transformer encoder, on a semantic parsing task involving real-world commands. The additional processing time required for joint training is significantly reduced, enabling the parser to handle a much wider range of commands, including up to 30 words, and maintain its performance even with as few as 50 training samples. The ability of our method to achieve this result marks a major breakthrough, opening up new possibilities for the development of more sophisticated and competitive semantic parsers that can be deployed effectively in real-world applications. The source code used in this research is now publicly available and can be accessed at https://github.com/githubacid/seq2seq-nat-gpt2. The dataset we employed for our domain-specific training is available at https://github.com/githubacid/sdp-dataset. The results of our method have also led to its deployment as an essential component in the development of a highly interactive, publicly accessible platform for human-product interaction, available at https://research.github.com/2021-07/robot-voice-assistant.html. The platform at https://githubacid.github.io/robot-voice-assistant displays real-time functionality of our method as it was implemented during the development of the system, while the video illustration of its operation can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a9r4cSxk1Gc. Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the reliability of other SFR measurement techniques, specifically infrared radiation (IR) and Hα (rest-frame wavelength 656.3 nm) based on their relationships with H30α and [NII] (a line often used to correct Hα emissions) emissions. Our goal is to compare SFR values derived from these methods to those obtained from photometric data at nearby UV-blue wavelengths. We also calculate the K-band to far-IR SFR ratio and analyze the physical properties of young stellar populations in NGC 5253, including their masses and ages. Our study shows that the 70-160 μm IR SFR value is 0.16 times that of the H30α-based SFR, indicating IR radiation overestimates the SFR by ~60%. Furthermore, our age and mass error analysis for 10-Myr old, 6,400 M☉ stars reveals a roughly 30% margin of error in both compact (r < 40 parsecs) and extended (r < 160 parsecs) star formation regions. Our study suggests that near infrared to sub-millimeter frequency SFR measurements using certain emitters are 10% more reliable than Hα-based measurements. We finally estimate a 10% accuracy for H30α-based SFR predictions, similar to other wide-band SFR metrics. Our study proposes a novel, low-interference SFR technique that could be applied to large nearby galaxies and those with similar low metallicity properties due to less hydrogen recombination emission interference. Our study sets the stage for future investigations into the properties of low-metallicity, low-recombination emission galaxies, allowing for exploration of the potential interplay between these factors in galaxy development. Our study expands the scope of the sample to include dwarf galaxies with extremely low metal content and T~10^9-10^10 Lux, which can be analyzed using ALMA's H30α emission (for galaxies with M_H > 10^4 M☼) to provide more accurate SFR estimates, along with additional galaxy analysis. Our study also includes a discussion on the potential sensitivity of this technique to hydrodynamic galaxy center feedback, which could lead to a more efficient conversion of gas into stars through enhanced star formation efficiency. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation. Simulation scenarios are also conducted to demonstrate the observer's performance in various epidemic scenarios. Furthermore, it is shown that the observer can be designed without knowledge of the reproduction number, provided the infection rate is known. This observer can also be applied to other nonlinear systems, potentially addressing the correlation issue in state estimation for coupled dynamical systems. Moreover, an extended Kalman filter is developed as an alternative design for the observer, although it may not account for the nonlinearity of the system as effectively as the observer designed through the approach outlined in this research. This Kalman filter, however, enjoys a key advantage in the form of simplified design and less computationally-intensive implementation compared to the observer designed through the approach outlined in this research. Simulation scenarios are conducted to illustrate the performance of both the observer and Kalman filter for state estimation in nonlinear epidemic models. Above all, it is hoped that the approach outlined in this research may contribute meaningfully to the design of other nonlinear systems, including coupled dynamical systems, through the development of optimal state observers, which hold significant potential in the form of advancing our understanding and estimates of COVID-19 spreading dynamics - a topic of growing urgency, particularly in the context of SARS-2 COVID virus, which has caused over 400,000 deaths worldwide to date. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings, such as link prediction. Several recent studies have proposed the use of time-dependent embeddings that capture variations in relationships over time. Despite their potential, models reliant on temporal-variant embeddings often fall short when requiring extensive data for training. In response, we present a new static model formulation for link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs. This approach, dubbed LSTME, makes use of long short-term memory layers for encodings that can function across an unlimited number of time points. By leveraging static models, LSTME offers a more efficient and accurate link prediction method in comparison to state-of-the-art temporal and non-temporal models, even when dealing with a limited amount of training data. Additionally, we develop and present several datasets that represent real-world scenarios where link prediction based on temporal knowledge graphs is applicable. These datasets, along with the implementation of LSTME, are made publicly available. Experiments using the newly introduced dataset demonstrate that LSTME achieves state-of-the-art results on link prediction tasks. Moreover, we provide evidence that several widely-used benchmark datasets contain errors, such as duplicate triples and inconsistent time points. The source code for LSTME has been made available at https://github.com/Microsoft/LSTME. By analyzing films of two different thicknesses, the study finds that a 3D photonic band gap crystal can enhance absorption by 50% compared to unstructured films, exceeding the limiting efficiency predicted by a simple homogeneous damping model.  Moreover, the benefits of the photonic crystal increase as films become thinner, showing potential for significant efficiency gains in devices with thicknesses as low as 0.1 $\mu$m.  Lastly, the study assesses the feasibility of the proposed design using computational optimization techniques to identify a suitable crystal geometry that maximizes absorption while being easily manufacturable.  Specifically, the researchers identify a specific geometry with enhanced absorption capabilities that can be made from a material with reduced thickness, opening up new avenues in the development of efficient thin-film silicon solar cells.  Ultimately, the addition of this photonic band gap crystal boosts the efficiency of these thin films, bringing them closer to their theoretical maximum possible efficiency, estimated by considering factors such as the wavelength-dependent light absorption in a homogeneous sample.  Notably, the photonic band gap crystal offers notable benefits when the thickness of the active layer is as low as 0.1 $\mu$m or even smaller, surpassing expectations established by a straightforward homogeneous damping model.  Specifically, the optimized design determined through this study exhibits a relatively compact size with a width and height of approximately 1.2 $\mu$m, as well as a thickness of around 380 nm, demonstrating that a simple modification to the underlying material could yield a substantial improvement in its efficiency.  Ultimately, the integration of this photonic band gap crystal into thin-film silicon solar cells holds the potential for significant performance enhancements, especially when thinness is a key characteristic of these devices. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science and combinatorics, facilitating numerous applications such as testing functions, probabilistic inference, and querying datasets. Although high dimensional expanders share some similarities with graphs, few methods of construction based on generic principles exist. In our research, given any high dimensional expander $X$, we present a method to construct a new high dimensional expander $Y$, possessing a similar dimension and size, through a simple and straightforward process that involves a simplicial complex derived from a specific type of space - a cover. This method can be applied even when $X$'s construction is unknown, in which case $Y$ can be obtained by repeating a random process a fixed number of times. In addition, we demonstrate that $Y$'s construction can be made deterministic at the cost of increasing its dimension by a fixed amount. This is the first time a straightforward, deterministic approach to constructing high dimensional expanders has been described in literature. As part of our contribution, we outline several novel applications of the constructed complexes, including semi-private function testing, data streaming, and query complexity. These applications demonstrate that $Y$'s construction is not only theoretically significant, but also holds practical implications. Utilizing our method, we present two concrete constructions of high dimensional expanders - a construction based on the hypercube and one rooted in property testers. Importantly, our method may lead to new insights on high dimensional expanders, inspiring further research in this area. Finally, our work is closely related to the conjecture claiming high dimensional expanders cannot be expressed as a product of simple, low dimensional complexes, a statement that remains unsolved. Nevertheless, our research provides evidence of the potential advantages of adopting a new perspective rooted in topology. Three distinct data sets were developed from actual Twitter activity over a 12-week period, each comprising 450 local UK users who provided geographically-specific content. Our investigation into depression detection employed supervised machine learning from six trained models, while our broader analysis of social media content involved topic modeling and network analysis. The discovery of distinct topics and demographic influence on content was revealed, along with evidence of a closed network where users primarily interact with one another. Additionally, our investigation into depression detection indicated that only users who openly expressed depression, rather than those who suppressed it, could be identified. In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation policy accordingly, based on inferred user intent. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform. Our results demonstrate that modeling user intent using our approach yields better recommendation performance, as measured by various metrics. For instance, promoting intent-aligned items to users leads to a 10% increase in overall usage and 5% decrease in unhelpful engagement (e.g., X marks the spot without content engagement). Our work highlights the importance of modeling user intent to ensure the long-term quality of the recommendations provided. We believe that the techniques described in this research can be applied to various other online content domains where understanding user purpose is crucial for long-term success. For example, in video content, modeling user intent helps ensure that users are presented with relevant information upon watching a video. If a user intends to learn the product features, the recommender should focus on recommending similar products rather than irrelevant content such as commercials and ads. Similarly, in text domains, if a user is reading an article to learn more about a particular topic, the recommender should focus on providing similar content rather than distracting users with irrelevant suggestions. To sum up, we've developed an innovative approach to modeling user intent using variational autoencoders and a recommendation policy, which we've successfully tested and validated through both offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform. Our results consistently demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, yielding 5% decrease in unhelpful engagement and 10% increase in overall usage. Ultimately, we hope this research contributes to the development of the next-generation latent user intent models required for long-term user engagement and success in the future. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. Additionally, our approach is demonstrated to be applicable to various practical applications, including satellite networks and formation flying systems. Our analysis from fossil records reveals that slow-changing ecological and evolutionary processes that unfolded over this timescale have deep roots and significant impacts that eventually influence dynamics on shorter scales. We explore the interplay between these long-term processes and shorter-term eco-evolution, particularly as it relates to changes in climate and geography. We also examine modulators of change rates, which play a crucial role in understanding when these changes are gradual or abrupt. Finally, we discuss the implications of this understanding for both fossil-based and contemporary eco-evolutionary studies. Our analysis reveals the importance of considering various rates of change and long-term processes in eco-evolutionary studies, particularly if we want to integrate deep-time fossil history and contemporary species interactions. By doing so, we can develop a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the complex and multifaceted nature of eco-evolutionary dynamics. Our research also opens up new avenues for studying climate change, suggesting that ecological and evolutionary responses to this threat could be anticipated and prepared for by recognizing how changes in environment translate to changes in rate modulators. Our analysis closes by highlighting the need for new tools to help predict tipping points in slow-changing eco-evolutionary systems, which could lead to unexpected and potentially catastrophic outcomes if these changes suddenly shift trajectory. However, it also shows that by anticipating these changes and acting early, it may be possible to avoid catastrophic outcomes. Our discussion includes examples of potential applications, including the rapid evolution of disease-resistant forms of fruit flies and the impact of glacial cycles on the ecology of large mammals. Our primary contribution is developing a new framework that integrates deep-time fossil history and contemporary species interactions, which has far-reaching implications for our understanding of eco-evolutionary dynamics. Our analysis also identifies specific and testable hypotheses about modulators of change rates and suggests ways to anticipate and prepare for abrupt shifts in eco-evolutionary systems. Our discussion includes examples of potential applications, including the evolution of large mammals in North America during a period known as the Irvingtonian. Our analysis ultimately reveals the importance of considering various timescales and rate modulators for understanding and predicting complex eco-evolutionary dynamics. This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional coordinates of objects, such as streetlights. Furthermore, the approach is shown to progressively improve in performance over time as the amount of collected data increases. In contrast to other object-localization algorithms, this method exhibits increased resilience to biases in labeling, thereby ensuring that the localization results are consistent with actual physical distributions of objects within the cityscape. Under optimal conditions, this method is capable of achieving precise and accurate results within a few meters of actual object locations, as evidenced by an analysis of our experiments. Additional information about our experiments, including associated image data and three-dimensional reconstruction results, is publicly accessible through our website. Keywords: three-dimensional reconstruction, urban environments, voting-based algorithms, large-scale data sets, visual decision-making, decentralized information processing. Subcategory: computer vision. Additional category: robotics. We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm utilizing proximal averaging for optimization, which we translate into a deep learning framework, naming it NuSPAN. Our evaluation indicates that NuSPAN outperforms other approaches in revealing details from synthetic signals and achieves comparable results for real-world seismic data that matches expectations for this application. Additionally, NuSPAN displays a notable capacity for generalization over its counterparts. Our study also performs a comparative analysis of computational efficiency among the tested methods. The implementation details of NuSPAN can be found in the accompanying open-source repository. Our results suggest that NuSPAN could effectively enhance seismic inversion if the underlying signal characteristics align with its assumed model characteristics. However, the predicted outcomes for actual seismic data are more complicated and require further investigation. A potential enhancement of NuSPAN is explored in the accompanying paper titled, "Improving Seismic Reflection Imaging with NuSPAN Enhanced Multichannel Gabriel deconvolution". A related project is available at https://github.com/GuopengLi123/NuSPAN. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on phi for semigroups to act on BMOA_p and VMOA_p. We derive connections between our results and those on integral operators. Moreover, our article compares the notions of strong continuity and boundedness within the context of semigroups of operators. Our research involves the construction of a semigroup consisting of composition operators that is adjoint to another, providing an example of a semigroup that is not adjoint to any. This is achieved by leveraging operators related to discrete singular integrals and the use of MWOA_p and its dual VMOA_p to establish this relationship. Lastly, our article examines the relationship between our results and those on MBOA_p and VMOA spaces. Further comparisons are drawn with recent work on BMOA_p and VMOA spaces by P. Zhang and Y. Zhang. Additionally, our article introduces a new notion of weak continuity for semigroups of operators and derives connections between our results and weak continuity. Finally, additional research is conducted to extend our findings to multi-variable settings. Our goals are to extend our results to operators with weighted compositions, those with multiple variables, and to establish connections between our work and the concept of bounded mean oscillation in various contexts. However, due to technical difficulties, this part of our research remains an open topic for future study. To place our research in context, our methods of proof are categorized according to their connections with existing works in the literature and the relationships between them are outlined. At the same time, our research encompasses several novel aspects that are likely to contribute to future studies. Ultimately, not all of these contributions can be thoroughly explored within the scope of this dissertation. Further research is an essential next step. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task in linguistic research, but current machine learning-based methods face significant challenges, particularly with ancient languages and historical texts. These methods rely on extensive corpora of annotated records, but even with large training sets, they can generate inconsistent and contradictory tags. In response, a new approach called set-valued prediction is proposed, allowing machine learning models to accommodate multiple possible tags per word, rather than assigning a single POS tag. The model can also learn to predict the probability that a POS tag is certain, uncertain, or impossible for any given word. The evaluation of this approach on Greek and Old English texts has shown a substantial improvement in tag set prediction and probability prediction accuracy, surpassing traditional single-valued methods. The proposed method has been found to be robust to common linguistics datasets biases. Additionally, a new dataset of ancient English text, the Casie Corpus, has been compiled and made available to the research community. The respective models, dubbed H-GAN and OE-H-GAN, achieved impressive results, demonstrating a 98.28% accuracy in predicting POS tags, a 98.40% accuracy in probability prediction, and a 98.65% accuracy in combined accuracy (F1-score) on the test set of the CoNLL-2006 dataset. Furthermore, models for three other languages have been fine-tuned using transfer learning, yielding notable results: 87.57% accuracy in Latin, 93.69% accuracy in Armenian, and 85.87% accuracy in Sanskrit. The models discussed above can be accessed through the following repository: https://github.com/constantin-opleanu/set-valued-POS-tagging. The new Casie Corpus can be found at: https://github.com/constantin-opleanu/Casive-Corpus. The adaptation of set-valued prediction in machine learning-based POS tagging has led to a substantial leap forward, enabling these models to sustainably annotate large historical corpora. The accompanying videos of this research can be accessed at: https://www.youtube.com/watch? v=MkR8hXKLuQo and https://www.youtube.com/watch? v=U6HgJeJe6Xo. The proposed machine learning-based approach allows for an assessment of the reliability of automated POS annotation. This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that ensure the candidate meets the necessary conditions for differentiability. These criteria are associated with the candidate's first- and second-order derivatives. We also establish that utility functions derived from weakly differentiable demand functions are weakly differentiable. Furthermore, we show that locally Lipschitz demand functions have unique, weakly differentiable representations within a specified domain. We apply the method to the linear demand function p = a - b/x and the log demand function p = log(a/x) for a, b > 0. Through numerical examples, we examine how various values for a and b affect the utility functions and their derivatives. Additionally, we determine the convergence properties of a general class of utility functions derived from linearly combinations of utility functions. We also obtain convergence results for a specific example of combined demand functions. The proposed method can be used for a broader class of utility functions, including those with interior singularities. However, this approach may not work for utility functions with non-empty singular sets. Such cases require an alternative method involving the utility function's absolute value. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain errors or ambiguities in their language-based descriptions. Converting these demands into formal specifications is a time-consuming and intricate process, largely due to the expertise required. This paper presents AutReq, an innovative, intuitive interface that simplifies the transformation of city officials' requirements into precise, machine-understandable specifications. AutReq draws on knowledge from multiple sources to complete missing information and clarify uncertainties in the demands. We have tested AutReq with real-world data from three cities and observed a significant reduction in the time needed to complete the specification process when using our tool compared to other methods. Moreover, AutReq's usability has been proven through successful collaborations with city officials who found the specification process effortless and acquired new skills in formal specification creation as a result. This successful interaction not only contributes to the requirements engineering process in smart cities but also contributes to the extension of the AutomataLight formal language with additional features that enhance the specifications' expressiveness. You can access AutReq through the website: https://autreq.cs.umass.edu/. For our technical evaluation, a video and the experiment's results, including written city requirements, formal specifications, and usability test results, have been submitted to https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04923. Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit improves. This strategy has been successfully demonstrated through the implementation of a QAOA circuit on a superconducting quantum device using IBM's QASM and Qiskit tools. Results indicate that inverse gate implementations can yield significant reductions in cross talk noise and the optimal performance often occurs with an intermediate number of inverse gates. This approach not only enhances circuit resilience but also facilitates faster convergence towards optimal outcomes. Furthermore, we examined the computational expense of implementing these inverse gates and found that certain error reduction methods can be achieved with minimal additional resources, making this method a promising low-cost mitigation strategy for reducing the impact of noise in complex quantum circuits. This method has potential applications in enhancing the performance of variational quantum eigensolver, quantum chemistry simulations and other related applications where high-quality quantum states are essential. Future research will focus on adapting this method for real-time applications and exploring its potential in addressing multi-qubit cross talk. The associated code can be accessed via the following repository: https://github.com/kayladrake/hidden-inverses-NoiseMitigation. The code can also be found through the following reference: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-17755-2_25. The corresponding author can provide access to the latest version of the code. The experimental setup utilized an IBM Washington grid quantum computer with 5 qubits. This device features a linear architecture which is beneficial for executing circuits but also increases the impact of cross talk. As a result of this limitation, certain qubits exhibit notably higher error rates than others. The implementation of inverse gates can help mitigate these differences. In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not yield a partial order. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the category. This work explores conditions ensuring the existence of these cofibered images, which can be seen as a form of saturation. Specifically, we identify sufficient conditions involving injectivity and cocompleteness in the context of regular categories. Moreover, we consider an equivalent formulation in terms of a categorical analogue of Cantor's theorem and show that these conditions find applications in three areas: the characterization of equivalence relations, the construction of bimodules in tri-modules, and the solution of an equation involving partial codes and families of relations. As a standalone result, our approach to equivalence relations in categories satisfies more stringent requirements than existing works in the field. Our text also contains an in-depth examination of the history of the problem, as well as a comprehensive overview of the relationship between pullback and direct image in several relevant categories. Finally, our method of proving the fundamental theorems involves an innovative pullback to a subcategory of $\mathbb E$, specifically a subcategory ensuring the existence of the desired cofibered images, which allows for an accurate description of these images as the pushout of the original preorder above the epimorphism, and ultimately enables the derivation of the partial order properties of these images. This original method of proof distinguishes our approach from other existing works on the topic. Furthermore, our text contains an annotated bibliography of recent papers on categories satisfying regularity conditions. Our work is positioned at an advanced level and is intended for readers with a strong background in mathematics, particularly in category theory. Moreover, our text contains several typos and is currently under revision for even more precise formulation. However, the current version can still be accessed via the URL https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/tex/CLROM17/CLROM17.html. Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed, wave height, and sea surface temperature is examined for the North Atlantic Ocean between 2007-2015. A novel method using a spatial extreme value model with non-constant shape parameters links wind speed and wave height extremes, while considering temperature as a fixed covariate. Model selection is performed through information criteria and the model's predictive performance is evaluated through a simulation study. An extreme event on 12-13 October 2013 is identified as a key test of the model's accuracy, with simulated wind speed and wave height observations matching historical patterns. This model can inform marine navigation and operation decisions, such as those made by the UK's Met Office when issuing weather warnings, and is particularly beneficial for the maritime industry due to its applicability in tracking spatial extremes during events like storms. A major limitation of the model is its assumption that the response variables must be non-negative, which is violated in practice due to the presence of errors-in-variables, particularly in the case of wave height estimates. A proposed solution involves applying a transformation to the estimated wave heights, while also adding uncertainty to the estimates to mitigate the effect of measurement error. A companion package is provided in the supplementary material to aid in the model's implementation, which includes functions for generating design-based estimates, calculating transformation parameters, and simulating from the model's distribution. Additionally, the MetOffice using this model provides critical weather information to the UK's government and industry to inform decision-making in the face of extreme weather events. A particularly notable instance of this is during a 12-13 October 2013 extreme weather event where the model's predictions accurately reflected the wind speeds and wave heights observed in the event. A major limitation of the model is explored including recommendation for further research and potential ways to mitigate this limitation. A possible future work could extend the model to accommodate the presence of non spatial variables that correlate with the covariates of the model such as temperature which in this case does not appear to have a significant relationship with the extremes according to the model diagnostics. A possible future work could also explore the impact of the assumption of non constant shape parameters assumed within the model. A possible future work could also explore strategies to test the model's performance including a sensitivity analysis and a reliability analysis which could also help to shed some light in the limitations of the model. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 operator shifting strategy, we expand the applicability to broad classes of noisy matrix problems. Our research also delves into the limitations of this technique and makes recommendations for future investigation. Additionally, we examine the computational implications of utilizing non-hermitian matrices due to their relevance in various scientific fields. Using a time-dependent electronic structure model as a real-world application, we observe a substantial reduction in computational time when utilizing non-hermitian matrices. Our research concludes with potential avenues for further study related to this technique. Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which holds specifically for $F$-rational local rings. If the ring is $F$-rational, we demonstrate the coincidence of this polynomial with the Hilbert function, thus offering a diagnostic tool for that property. As an application, we prove the $F$-rationality of certain Noetherian local rings with dimension one, based on specific conditions involving the tight Hilbert function. These conditions include vanishing or taking on a particular value for certain coefficients, which relates directly to known rationality criteria for one-dimensional local rings. These criteria include requirements such as positivity or non-monotonicity, which provide explicit conditions for $F$-rationality, particularly in rings with reduced, locally free, or torsion-free ideals. Our analysis also encompasses the Hilbert function of powers of the ideal $\mathfrak{m}^t$. If the ring is $F$-rational, we identify a specific value, say $t_0$, such that for any $t \geq t_0$, the Hilbert functions of $\mathfrak{m}^t$ exhibit constant behavior, which we determine explicitly, by relating it to the degree of a specific polynomial associated with the ideal. Conversely, we define a new class of local rings, which we call $F$-tightly rational, by imposing certain conditions on this constant value, which allows for a positive characterization in terms of $F$-rationality. These new concepts provide the foundation for a deeper comprehension of local rings with one-dimensional spectra, which is reflected in a comprehensive theorem, which offers an equivalence between certain conditions for $F$-tightly rational, $F$-rational, and strongly $F$-rational local rings, thus providing a complete classification of these concepts. These results extend, expand, or provide complex generalizations to several significant results, which include works by Goto and Nakamura, Matsudo, Miyazaki, Bruns and Kiss, and the authors' previous work. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based promising outcomes with ML models, there is an underlying barrier to integrating these into clinical practices due to issues of interoperability.  The DICOM standard provides specifications for the representation, storage, and exchange of digital images and related information but the standard's broad nature hinders its adoption in the ML research environment.  Therefore, there is a need for a balanced standardization that can facilitate the exchange of information between ML models and clinical ML practices.  Consequently, we developed highdicom, a Python library that supports the standard's use in ML applications through simplified processes of writing ML model outputs in DICOM format as well as reading DICOM images that adhere to the standard.  The key functionalities of highdicom are: (a) converting ML model outputs into DICOM format, (b) reading DICOM images that adhere to the standard in popular libraries such as OpenCV and numpy, (c) writing ML model outputs for standard-compliant datasets, and (d) converting ML model outputs into widely-used ML datasets.  Additionally, we have provided practical applications of highdicom by testing it in ML models developed for both radiology and pathology applications.  The source code for highdicom has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/cungi-co/hicdicom, and it has been included in the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository at https://pypi.org/project/hicdicom/.  The source code repository has been released under the terms of the Apache 2.0 licence, and the library itself is also released under the Apache 2.0 licence agreement.  Finally, we believe that releasing highdicom will facilitate the exchange of information between ML model outputs and DICOM standards, thus promoting their integration into clinical practices.  An illustration of highdicom's functionality is showcased at https://highdicom.cumannigh.eu/demo. In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often presents itself in the form of a vast DNA sequence dataset requiring extensive computation for thorough analysis. In such a scenario, representing DNA sequences in a lower-dimensional space can streamline task performance and accelerate training, ultimately optimizing model performance. The objective of our study is to develop an unsupervised method for representing DNA sequences in a compact representation while enhancing the overall representations of downstream tasks. The end result of this study is an innovative approach, ReSeq, which leverages an attention-based self-encoders model to extract meaningful representations from DNA sequences in an automated manner. We evaluated the efficacy of our proposed method on three distinct tasks: reducing the dimensionality of a cancer-related DNA sequence dataset, classifying DNA sequences based on their anti-microbial potential, and predicting the functional domains within a DNA sequence. The results demonstrate that our method successfully extracts task-specific insights from DNA sequences in an unsupervised manner, ultimately yielding better performance when incorporated into a downstream task model compared to using randomly initialized sequence encoders. The implemented code is now publicly accessible via our GitHub repository at https://github.com/sterbichev/ReSeq. Additionally, we have also released our pre-trained DNA sequence representation models through the PyTorch HUB. Our findings highlight that by uncovering the underlying patterns in DNA sequences, ReSeq successfully improves the performance of various downstream tasks. The uncovering of such patterns also has the potential to contribute to a greater understanding of the meaning behind DNA sequences. The model can be utilized in response to pressing scientific questions, such as identifying new compounds with antimicrobial properties, which may have a significant impact on society and the economy. Furthermore, with ongoing advancements in DNA sequencing technologies, our model holds the potential to significantly impact the future large-scale analysis of sequence-to-sequence prediction tasks. The model's results could also shed light on the less understood processes of antimicrobial actions, which may lead to the development of novel treatment approaches for diseases with poorly understood mechanisms, such as sepsis. Ultimately, the results of our study have the potential to pave the way for the precise, large-scale synthesis of antimicrobial peptides with even more sophisticated activity than natural ones, which could lead to the development of highly effective and inexpensive treatments for sepsis. The metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films is investigated using a combination of scanning tunneling spectroscopy, low-energy spectroscopy, and transport measurements. Our study compares the transition in two different surface terminations, V$_2$O$_3$(0001) and V$_2$O$_3$(1$\bar{2}N)$\times$2, and finds that they exhibit distinct behavior. Our results demonstrate that the metal-insulator transition occurs at the same temperature in both types of films but reveals a notable difference in their temperature dependence. Additionally, our investigation examines the electronic properties at vortex cores in both films and finds that the metal-insulator transition is associated with a change in the electronic density of states at the Fermi level. We attribute the observed differences between the films to the varying degrees of vanadium height and the presence of oxygen vacancies at the surface, which have a profound effect on the electronic properties. Our study provides a deeper understanding of the underlying physics of the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films and is likely to be applicable to other transition-metal dichalcogenides and dioxides. Our work also reveals the immense influence of surface termination, which highlights the significance of controlling the crystal orientation during film growth to modulate the electronic properties of materials at the nanoscale. Ultimately, our investigation opens up a new area of research focused on the design and engineering of layered materials with regulated stacking sequences to achieve exceptional properties. By mastering the manipulation of surface terminations, it is possible to unlock a wealth of fascinating materials with unique electronic structures, paving the way for a new generation of devices and applications. Our study provides a crucial insight into the design of materials with metal-insulator transitions and demonstrates that ultra-thin films can be used as a platform to precisely adjust the metal-insulator transition temperature. Our findings also reveal that metal-insulator transitions in thin films provide an exceptional level of control over the transition temperature, which can be fine-tuned over a wide range of temperatures by adjusting the film thickness. Our study provides an important understanding of the potential to design and engineer materials with metal-insulator transitions in response to changing external stimuli, which could lead to the development of metal-insulator switches and memory devices. Our investigation provides an essential insight into the development of materials with metal-insulator transitions that can be activated by simple adjustments to the film thickness and surface chemistry, which opens up a new area of research in the design of functional materials. A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, which under specific conditions can represent the process of Lie-Poisson systems canonization. Consequently, we demonstrate how symmetries in momentum maps are associated with mathematical invariants. Furthermore, we derive a new form of Hamiltonian Poincare equations for the elliptic Gelfand-Dikii integrable system using the Clebsch canonization. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experiments with datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, VLCS, and LSID, have demonstrated the superior performance of our OCN method over state-of-the-art deep learning approaches that handle pose variations. Our findings have further highlighted the crucial role of proposing effective filters in enhancing the robustness of image recognition tasks. The related code can be accessed via https://github.com/mit-plaid/OCNs. Additionally, our project page, including extra results and related tools, is available at https://plaidcs.mit.edu/OCNs.

We develop a systematic method to study the dependence of heavy quark masses
on mass terms in QCD, specifically using a sequence of momentum-virtuality
representations. A detailed investigation into the effects of light quarks is
carried out using the light-cone expansion of the QCD Green's function,
accounting for the evolution of momentum-virtualities and a deep Breit frame
limit. The top quark mass, calculated at two-loop order in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$
scheme, reveals a dependence of up to $10^{-5}$ on the masses of u, d, s, c, and
b quarks. Our results accurately predict the numerical values in the
$\overline{\text{MS}}_{\text{g0}}$ scheme at third-order accuracy. Additionally, we
establish a systematic method to study the evolution of the coefficients and
scale dependence of heavy heavy-flavor masses. Specifically, we demonstrate
that, at the two-loop order, the scale dependence of the bottom quark mass is
entirely accounted for by the scale dependence of the gluon transversity,
confirming a previous finding. Moreover, we demonstrate that, at the three-loop
order, the scale dependence of the tau quark mass is entirely driven by the
scale dependence of the u and d quark masses. Finally, we outline a general
framework for applying our results to the mass relationships between the top,
bottom, and charm quarks. However, a detailed calculation is performed only for
the relationship between the top and bottom quark masses at the two-loop order.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces incorrect results; in contrast,
computed tomography scans offer high accuracy but involve radiation exposure
and increased risk for those who need to take multiple scans. Human physicians
interpret CT scans by identifying characteristic patterns of lung lesions, but
their accuracy depends on experience and can vary. A computer-based approach
using machine learning is more consistent and independent of radiation, using
chest CT scans to diagnose COVID-19 by either detecting patterns or creating new
models for comparison, yet it remains uncertain whether such methods can
accurately diagnose COVID-19 or not, and what degree of experience is needed
for proper diagnosis. A proposed two-stage capsule network model, capable of
diagnosing COVID-19 from low-dose CT scans with only a few samples, was
trained with data from various sources, even if some samples were not labeled,
and when tested it demonstrated the capacity to diagnose COVID-19 similarly to
human physicians with years of experience, suggesting a significant potential
for clinical use. This study confirms that capsule networks can diagnose COVID-19
as accurately as human physicians with extensive experience using low-dose CT
scans, even with a minimal number of training samples, thus reducing the need
for RT-PCR and low-dose CT scan-related radiation. A future study will involve
labeled samples from various datasets to confirm robustness and generalization.  Additionally, further research is needed to expand the network's ability
to recognize patterns by training it with data from various COVID-19-related
datasets, and to assess the diagnosis of COVID-19 using scans from different
sources, in order to identify the key characteristics that humans and machines
use for diagnosis, and whether there are any differences between these two
approaches. A human-centered machine learning system has the potential to reduce
the diagnosis time and variability, while also increasing transparency by
exposing the specific patterns that humans and machines use for diagnosis. A
proposed diagnostic toolkit is capable of analyzing and visualizing CT scan
patterns, as well as capsule network and gradient-weighted class activation
maps, using data from various COVID-19-related datasets. This study reveals the
existence of distinct patterns associated with COVID-19 diagnosis, and why some
human physicians may struggle to diagnose COVID-19. Furthermore, it shows how
machines, despite their accuracy, fail to understand the underlying patterns
that humans use for diagnosis

As numerous satellite constellations plan to launch into a Low-Earth Orbit (LEO), there's growing concern about obtaining necessary licenses and potential risks of interference with existing systems. To address this issue, it's crucial to understand space occupancy in LEO, which involves determining the likelihood of collisions with operational satellites. To quantify space occupancy, we've represented it as a probability density function near the equator in LEO, taking into account the spatial distribution of operational satellites. Our analysis focuses on objects orbiting at 0.1 to 0.4 LEO radii off-center, approximately 10 degrees off the equatorial plane, and within 10 kilometers of any given point. By examining the occupancy probability density, we've found that in LEO, approximately 8, 30, and 150 operational satellites are found in such off-center positions with probabilities greater than 50%, 20%, and 10%, respectively. Our analysis utilized an database that identified over 5,800 satellites launched between 1957 and 2021. Our results demonstrate that in LEO, approximately 60% of all operational satellites have a probability of occupancy greater than 50%, whereas only about 0.5% have a probability of occupancy less than 10%. Our analysis has significant implications for determining the required separation distances between satellites, and the results of our study will be useful for determining the minimum separation distances required for newly launched spacecraft. Additionally, the results of our study can assist both launch and test operators in assessing collision risks in LEO. Our methodology allows operators to obtain relevant statistical information regarding occupancy probabilities for satellites they are interested in, and demonstrates that through a large database, trends and statistical information regarding occupancy probabilities in LEO can be effectively determined. Our study analyzes a variety of occupancy probabilities, and demonstrates that a database with a sufficient number of terms is required to accurately determine occupancy probabilities for satellites that have completed their operational lives and are no longer active. With a database of over 5,800 satellites, we have shown that a Gaussian distribution effectively models the data, and that a Gaussian distribution is a sufficient statistic for accurately determining occupancy probabilities for satellites that are operational. Ultimately, the results of our study demonstrate that a database with a sufficient number of terms allows operators to effectively mitigate collision risks in LEO. To facilitate further research in this area, we have provided a set of raw data that we have compiled, including the data used for our study as well as additional information that is not presented in the paper. To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created, which allows for intricate quad configurations due to its unstructured layout. Subsequently, we build upon this foundation with a flexible T-mesh structure, which can be manipulated to optimize the mesh topology by assigning varying lengths to its arc segments. Utilizing advanced optimization techniques in the form of integer linear programming, we efficiently resolve the mesh simplification process and refine the resulting topology. Ultimately, we extract high-order quadrilateral meshes from the optimized framework, showcasing excellent results on various CAD models through rigorous testing that highlights its speed, robustness, and strict adherence to original design features, as well as notable improvements in mesh coarseness and overall quality. Compared to other high-order mesh generation methods, our approach significantly outperforms the results in terms of mesh quality, particularly when generating meshes with fewer triangles. Additionally, we have developed mesh fixing techniques to maintain high-quality results even when the optimization process produces meshes with flaws, thus ensuring accurate mesh generation. Our method's efficiency has been demonstrated in the mesh generation competition, where it surpasses the performance of topological pyramid methods by reducing the mesh size, improving the results, and scaling better to large models. Furthermore, we have successfully applied our method to generate high-order meshes on complex 3D point clouds, where it outperforms the performance of mesh generation methods. Finally, we have complemented our method with mesh smoothing techniques that yield smoother results, thus expanding the capabilities of our approach. A comprehensive overview is provided of the empirical and theoretical underpinnings driving its development. Furthermore, a concise summary is provided of the S-matrix framework itself, accompanied by a presentation of its key benefits and accomplishments in relation to observational data. We examine two primary applications: one involving the subeath probe scenario in which gravitational field patterns around Earth emerge from an out-of-vacuum S-matrix, and another involving an alternative theory of gravity in a quark-gluon plasma environment, characterized by a non-vacuum S-matrix. We highlight the practical utility of the S-matrix framework in tackling quantum gravity and quantum gravity phenomena that arise in black holes, holographic information and the Swamplifting of effective theories. We outline a strategy for extending the S-matrix framework to address quantum gravity and illustrate the importance of observational constraints in distilling a theory's predictive landscape in the context of quantum gravity. We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to demonstrate the stability of this system through a finite-dimensional feedback control. This control is designed to be localized and applied to a small area within the domain, and we show that it can achieve uniform stabilization across a wide range of relevant function spaces. Specifically, this control is effective so long as $q$ lies between 1 and infinity. This is an improvement over previous work because it covers a broader range of values and accounts for a larger class of possible initial conditions and forcing functions. The key innovation of our work is a novel decomposition that allows us to represent the state of the system in a more flexible way. This decomposition relies on a critical theory of functional spaces that takes into account the scaling of the system. The structure of our decomposition is informed by a representation formula that describes how the state of the system evolves over time. This decomposition is then used to derive an approximation formula that estimates the error caused by approximating the system in a way that is both stable and accurate, and we use this result to show that the control is effective across a wide range of values of $q$. This work builds upon the work of many authors who have studied the properties of Navier-Stokes systems in different functional spaces, and it draws on a critical theory of scaling which is a key innovation of the theory. The structure of our decomposition is inspired by the work of Cannone and the work on representation formulas by Chemin and the methods developed in the critical theory of scaling. This work has been published in an article in 2012, and it is an extension of the authors' previous work on the topic. The key innovation of our work is a decomposition that is new even in one-dimensional systems, and it is an important contribution to the theory of Navier-Stokes systems. The control we use is simple to compute, and it is based on a small number of variables that are chosen through a procedure that is simple to execute. Research has shown that local information helps training robust models to perturbations. We are investigating the scope of this phenomenon and the factors that contribute to it. Our key discovery is that the influence of local information depends significantly on the characteristics of the data distribution and the approach used to process the local data. We created the $\beta$-sandwich dataset family to examine how the local density affects the utility of local information. Our results reveal that denser local data leads to more informative labels, even at higher adversarial robustness levels. Additionally, we found that certain data augmentation techniques can amplify this effect. Our findings also highlight the benefits of combining several local information sources from different perspectives. Ultimately, his helps demystify the success of self-supervised learning methods, particularly those using transformations as labels. Our analysis provides insights into the design of effective augmentation techniques for generating valuable local information. Furthermore, it sheds light on the circumstances under which the theoretical robustness guarantees based on local information can be realized in practice. Our experiments, encompassing various benchmark datasets, empirically substantiates our theoretical findings. At the same time, our study also uncovers situations in which local information is less helpful and the over-reliance on it can diminish model performance. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/protogee/reverse-validation. https://github.com/protogee/reverse-validation offers the accompanying code.

4  Certain data augmentation techniques can amplify the effect of local information and improve model robustness.
5  Combining multiple local information sources from different perspectives leads to increased robustness.

7  The design of effective augmentation techniques for generating valuable local information is also elucidated.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into the characteristics of a kernel matrix with linearly aligned triangular elements and utilizes its mathematical properties to further enhance Sinkhorn iteration performance. A novel permutation matrix is developed based on the kernel matrix's diagonal entries and row minimum product, enabling the creation of an approximate optimal transport map in a single iteration with reduced computational overhead by combining two Sinkhorn iterations. This results in exceptionally fast and efficient approximate solutions for optimal transport problems, particularly evident in large-scale applications where numerical precision may not be crucial. Interestingly, the proposed method also yields an exact solution for specific problems with limited domain sizes (less than 256x256), achieving $O(N)$ complexity at near-optimal convergence rates without relying on regularization as an intrinsic form of numerical stabilization. This method further includes a novel vectorized kernel evaluation without scalar multiplications, an extremely fast and accurate approximation of the kernel matrix, and a detailed analysis of numerical stabilization techniques for the Sinkhorn algorithm. The proposed method's performance is extensively validated through a variety of numerical experiments and real-world applications, culminating in a $10^{7}\times$ speedup over established OT solvers for problems with a $256^{2}$ domain size, with exact solutions achievable for sizes up to $256^{4}$ through approximate scaling. This method is expected to greatly expand OT availability and usability in real-world data settings. By combining these with existing X-ray observations, we examined how its energy output changes across different wavelengths. Our research indicates that the star's coronal and UV radiation frequently exhibit little to no activity, though this is likely due to ongoing stellar wind, which could also explain the depletion of the planets in the system. By comparing activity levels in the FUV and X-ray bands, we have established a relationship between these emissions in the young star AU Mic. Our research implies that similar systems may experience little to no X-ray emission in the course of regular stellar activity, with most of the radiation coming from high-temperature coronal components. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks. Models leveraging character-based techniques surpassed their word-based counterparts, who struggled with the task. Additionally, incorporating a task-specific learning model, namely the ROMANCE-HATE task, did not yield favorable results in comparison to character-based models. An examination of the models' predictions revealed various types of derogatory content, including hate speech, racial slurs, and graphic sexual content. This insight could aid in the development of future models by recognizing the limitations of previous models in accurately classifying such content. Our analysis also uncovered the frequency of ambiguous and emotive words in both derogatory and non-derogatory content, which has the potential to greatly impact the accuracy of future models. It was also observed that using an approach that extracts key sentences from the text can be ineffective in identifying hate speech. Ultimately, our team recommends a refined dataset with more precise annotations, as well as a reconsideration of the two subtasks, due to what was perceived as an unusually difficult task for NLP models. Our paper provides an in-depth analysis of the provided dataset, including both strengths and weaknesses, which has the potential to aid in the understanding of NLP models and their limitations.
