The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture synergizes a sequential encoder with tree-structured decoding, utilizing syntax-aware decoding through a tree-structured DRNN model with syntactically linked connections. Furthermore, this paper seeks to optimize tree-structured decoding in Neural Machine Translation and Parsing tasks. Experimental evaluations on the WMT15 English-to-German and English PARSL datasets demonstrate that Seq2DRNN yields notable improvements in translation accuracy and parsing performance. Notably, when used as a syntax-aware parsing approach, Seq2DRNN outperforms other state-of-the-art models, achieving higher F1 and LA scores on the English PARSL dataset. Moreover, when employed in Neural Machine Translation, Seq2DRNN with a conventional Transformer baseline exhibits increased BLEU scores without additional computation, while its computed proxy metrics indicate improved translation accuracy and model robustness. Finally, although incorporating syntax through Seq2DRNN does not lead to natural-sounding translations, this issue could potentially be addressed by incorporating a stress rule model in future enhancements. Therefore, although the translations produced by Seq2DRNN are formulated in a less natural way than those of Transformer, this architecture demonstrates promising results in both translation and parsing tasks, opening up further possibilities for optimization. Analysis of the theoretical translation costs based on the Seq2DRNN model reveals a direct relationship between its connection matrix and the R score from the constituent parsing model. By reinterpreting the Seq2DRNN model as a constrained sequence-to-sequence task, the paper derives an expression for the model's maximum translation cost using the connection matrix, providing insights that could be applied in other tree-structured decoding tasks. Analysis of the Seq2DRNN model's data-driven R score also enables the evaluation of its connection matrix, offering a new way to examine syntax-aware decoding through the Seq2DRNN model. Ultimately, this architecture may be used in other tree-structured decoding tasks, while the obtained R score can serve as a common metric to assess various neural models with tree-structured decoding. Analysis of the Seq2DRNN model's data-driven R score also enables the evaluation of syntax-aware decoding efforts. The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the fundamental requirement that they map unique inputs to unique outputs. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the phenomenon where models capitalize on non-functional inputs, i.e., inputs that do not provide any explanatory value. To address this issue, we develop several practical methods for introducing sibylvariance into text data, thereby allowing for broader input coverage. Experimental results indicate that our methods are effective in enhancing the input coverage capabilities of well-known NLP models, while also demonstrating that sibylvariance can be harnessed to improve the robustness of these models in face-to-content and face-to-context Scenarios. Furthermore, our techniques result in substantial reductions in the cost of training these models by at least one order of magnitude. Our work aims to make text generation more robust and efficient through the concept of sibylvariance. Additionally, all of our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/wzhang2005/sibyl. What's more, we also revealed a surprising connection between sibylvariance and the problem of avoiding memorization in text classification. This finding has the potential to contribute positively to ongoing discussions around model robustness. Our study also raises important ethical considerations for text generation in a multi-turn setting. In particular, we highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of the potential harm caused by biased and low-coverage language models, especially in high-resource scenarios. In one of our experiments, we show that language models can sometimes "lie" by transforming a given input into a specific word when it has no actual knowledge about that word but is capable of generating it. This phenomenon holds significant implications for a variety of applications, including fact-based articles, where accurate text generation is critical. In general, our research points to the need for a more balanced approach to promoting diversity in text data, one that avoids extremes but instead strives to expand the model's input coverage while maintaining its explanatory power. Ultimately, our work is part of a broader effort to enhance model robustness and efficiency through text transformation. Several of our techniques are adaptable to various NLP tasks, while our study is part of a class of research focused on text generation. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear features. In particular, we demonstrate that, with careful task scheduling, $O(MK)$ samples are sufficient to ensure that these features are learned correctly, where $M$ represents the number of tasks, and $K$ is the number of data points per task. This theoretical bound nearly matches existing lower bounds, which signify that our design is largely optimal. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across multiple tongues without prior knowledge of target languages. We've found that by treating speech as unlabelled data, it's possible to bypass language prediction and learn a single model that handles unseen target languages with ease. Our experiments on Indonesian to English and Mandarin to English reveal that this model's performance closely matches that of our districted multi-step model, yet it eliminates the need for target language designation. Moreover, this model's capabilities in the out-of-vocabulary target language surpass that of our baseline model, and it even outperforms a direct translation model in the bilingual setting. Our findings suggest promising avenues for research in zero-shot speech-to-text translation. The pre-trained models we've developed are available for public use.

Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans is a top priority, yet challenges arise from the extensive time required for manual analysis due to the rapid spread of the virus. Consequently, large-scale, manually annotated datasets are difficult to establish, posing a significant problem for traditional segmentation algorithms. We propose an innovative solution using weakly supervised learning techniques, allowing us to develop a robust COVID-19 detection model from data marked only with lung boundaries. Through an iterative process, our approach not only facilitates accurate detection but also generates precise segmentations. We tested and validated our method on the CoronaCTDash 2021 dataset, where our results demonstrate a substantial improvement in detecting COVID-19 presence (AUC: 0.8561 vs 0.7888) and accurate segmentation (mAP: 0.7825 vs 0.5558) compared to existing lesion detection models. The successful implementation of our framework on the CoronaCTDash 2021 dataset serves as a model for tackling similar challenges in medical image processing. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, the complexity of spinal anatomy and the presence of artifacts or positioning errors hinder reliable localization and identification. To address this challenge, a novel approach has been developed by expanding existing deep learning-based solutions to handle unusual positions, postures, and imaging conditions. The method involves a multi-stage framework that starts by correcting the spinal column in each slice and then uses optimized criteria to identify the vertebrae, leveraging knowledge about the spine's anatomy to refine a initial prediction. The framework demonstrates exceptional accuracy, with results comparable to those achieved with vertebra-based references on a large dataset containing diverse subjects, even in cases with image quality issues or at the extremes of the spinal column. Notably, this approach outperforms existing CT localization and identification methods in most scenarios. The developer of this approach has made the related code and models available for further research into the challenges of accurate vertebrae localization and identification. The anatomic constraints-based optimization technique has also been applied to the task of unsupervised spine segmentation and served as the foundation for the development of an end-to-end approach that segments and identified vertebrae in the absence of vertebral identifiers, detailed in our companion paper. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated through central pattern generators, whose parameters are fine-tuned to rapidly develop an open-loop controller for walking. Following this, we implement reinforcement learning to enhance the existing controller's resilience to parameter uncertainty. We then employ the developed techniques to tackle running locomotion, again utilizing reinforcement learning to fine-tune the new gait. Our novel approach allows for a controller overhaul in just two hours, resulting in substantial improvements over older strategies. Experimentation has shown that this new model-free controller results in increased endurance and speed. Specifically, our method has yielded a remarkable 71% boost in endurance when compared to an older model-based approach. Notably, our closed-loop system has achieved a speed of 2.9 m/s, representing a 111% improvement over this comparable benchmark. A well-documented phenomenon, microtearing modes, occurs due to the electron temperature gradient in a plasma and causes fine-scale magnetic field changes resulting in the formation of magnetic islands. Prior research in a slab geometry setting showed that as plasma collision frequency decreases, these modes survive for longer before damping. Additionally, experiments in a different setup revealed that as the amplitude of the magnetic field variations decreases, the growth rate of these modes decreases in a specific manner. Studying a small-scale tearing mode with nanosecond timescales and micrometer spatial scales in a collisionless plasma, this study found that reducing the amplitude of these fluctuations in a specific manner affects their growth rate in agreement with previous experiments. Furthermore, these modes exhibit a dependence on electron scales in their magnetic structure and are characterized by the formation of magnetic islands with densities varying across different poloidal passages, an observation consistent with electron redistribution. Lastly, experiments in various electron temperatures and densities show the mode growth rate depends on electron temperature in a specific manner but demonstrates only weak dependence on electron density. Investigating the cause of this mode in a slab geometry setting remains an ongoing area of research. Analyzing the drive and damping mechanisms through both linear and nonlinear simulations, this study found that electron temperature gradient drive is the primary mechanism but that damping mechanisms partially counteract this effect in a nonlinear manner. Though this counteraction is not sufficient to prevent the mode from surviving for longer than linear theory predicts in experiments. Researchers propose that this mode might be a possible explanation for the observed "fluctuation-driven transport" in various plasma settings where enhanced mixing could occur due to these modes, an effect that could be mitigated by adjusting the amplitude of these fluctuations in a specific manner for increased stability. A surge in demand for image retrieval technology has driven advancements in modern computational photography and visual understanding. Fashion companies seek to capitalize on these benefits but face challenges in image retrieval tasks, largely caused by the need for extensive annotation costs. In response, this paper outlines a novel semi-supervised attribute manipulation approach, allowing for the creation of numerous images with specific attributes using limited original images and target attribute settings. We propose a dual model framework consisting of a fine-grained image generation network and an attribute control module, both trained in a semi-supervised manner using a shared feature extractor. Through adversarial training and a latent space constraint, this framework produces photorealistic manipulated images with desired attributes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in fashion image retrieval, showing that it significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in retrieving images with specific attributes while increasing retrieval accuracy by 9.0% relative to conventional image retrieval methods. Furthermore, our semi-supervised attribute manipulation method outperforms a strong baseline model without attribute manipulation in both tasks. The proposed approach is available on https://github.com/kuoo/FashionImageRetrieval_Semi-supervised_Atmu. The images displayed in this summary were generated using our method, demonstrating attribute manipulation and image retrieval results. Visual examples of our method can also be found in the accompanying video. Experimental results can also be found on https://kuoo.github.io/FashionImageRetrieval_Semi-supervised_Atmu. The database used in this research, known as FashionIQ, will be made available in due course. FashionIQ is an extension of the TRECVID's e-commerce dataset and will be announced once it is ready. FashionIQ provides a wealth of data, including rich text, image, video, and HTML information, in the form of 49K web pages and 341K images, although only a subset of 10K images is utilized in this research. Through query-based retrieval, our method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in retrieval difficulty measures, including recall, 1-rank, and 5-rank scores. Our method produces a new state-of-the-art model that outperforms previous image retrieval techniques in TRECVID. The supporting code for this research is also provided at https://github.com/kuoo/FashionImageRetrieval_ebi. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image, which neglects occlusion or treats it as an area with no data. However, in reality, there can be significant differences in the views that are affected by occlusion. This paper proposes a novel cost constructor that is specifically designed to handle occlusion and outperforms previous constructors by leveraging a dark channel prior to detect areas affected by occlusion and then using a segmentation mask to mask out these areas before assembling the matching cost. The constructor's effectiveness has been tested on the light field datasets "Stanford Bowl" and "4D LF Stanford Bunny", with experimental results indicating its superior performance. The constructor's source code will be made available.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results. The paper notably resolves the motion equation ambiguity for String Newton-Cartan gravity that had previously been unaddressed. This research demonstrates that double field theory effectively encapsulates a wide range of alternative gravity theories, offering a promising path to explore these theories' quantum gravity limits. Additionally, it showcases a useful tool for linking constraints related to different versions of double field theory. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve their performance capabilities. The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-definition video streaming require networks with enhanced throughput levels and reduced latency. One effective strategy for achieving these goals is to deploy multiple access points within a given area, but this also raises the challenge of identifying the most suitable access point for each device. 

This study explores the potential performance enhancements that can be achieved in home WiFi networks through the use of secondary access points, or Extenders, by examining two main methods of optimizing WiFi networks: a standardized technique that determines the optimal backhaul link for each device, and a unique mechanism that facilitates device-to-Extender channel load balancing. The results of our evaluation indicate that both of these methods are effective at reducing the load on WiFi networks, but load balancing provides consistently better performance outcomes. 

The analysis presented in this study leveraged simulations of real-world scenarios, and the results were compared across various settings, including 40 and 80 devices within a network, and under different load conditions. The performance metrics that were used to evaluate the results included device offloading success rates, and the average throughput of both primary and secondary access points within the network. The results showed that both load reduction techniques are able to achieve consistent improvements in performance, but load balancing provides more stable throughput levels across a range of different simulation scenarios. Ultimately, the success of these methods in reducing load requires a limited amount of feedback information, and the results showed that they are compatible with existing WiFi standard protocols, specifically IEEE 802.11k/v.
